articles.title: Leak: HONOR Robot Phone 2 is in the works, could launch next year
articles.content: Credit: Stephen Schenck / Android Authority TL;DR A tipster has claimed that the HONOR Robot Phone 2 is in the works. The phone could pack ultra-high-resolution cameras and launch in Q2 2027. There’s no word on other specs or global availability, though. The HONOR Robot Phone was probably the biggest surprise of the year in the Android world. It featured a main camera attached to a gimbal arm, enabling an unprecedented amount of stability and stabilization functionality. It looks like this won’t be a one-off, either. Tipster Smart Pikachu claimed on Weibo that the HONOR Robot Phone 2 and a standalone handheld device (or devices) are in the works. It’s unclear what the latter is, but we’ve previously heard murmurings that some brands were working on standalone action cameras.
articles.author: Hadlee Simons

articles.title: Apple Music Classical Updated With New Icon and Refreshed Design
articles.content: Apple today released Apple Music Classical version 4.1, with a new black-and-white app icon and an updated interface. The redesigned icon retains the app's treble clef, but now rendered in shaded black against a white background. The change brings ‌Apple Music‌ Classical in line with ‌Apple Music‌'s new visual identity , which Apple introduced last month, replacing its familiar red branding with a monochrome appearance. The new version of the app also features blue accents for selected tabs, playback buttons, and links, instead of the previous red ones. Apple has not detailed the visual changes in its release notes, which state only that the update contains "stability and performance enhancements." ‌Apple Music‌ Classical is included with ‌Apple Music‌ subscriptions at no additional cost. The app offers search tailored to classical recordings, composer biographies, album booklets, time-synced listening guides, and curated stations. Version 4.1 is available now on the App Store for the iPhone and iPad , requiring iOS 18 or iPadOS 18 or later. articles.title: Elon Musk says Tesla is 'winding down' production of its Cybertruck
articles.content: Musk posted on X that production of Cybertruck will be winding down The move has been made to “make room for increased Cybercab production” It gives us our best indication yet that Cybertruck will join Model S and Model X Elon Musk has used his X account to reveal that Tesla will be "winding down" production of its divisive Cybertruck at its Gigafactory in Texas around "the middle of next year", in order to make room for increased production of its Cybercab robotaxi . Musk stopped short of saying whether this means the end of the Cybertruck altogether, or merely that production is going to be moved elsewhere. But the project’s lead, Wes Morrill, posted a more reflective statement to the social media site, saying: "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab". That sounds a bit like an obituary to us and many users rushed to post their responses, which ranged from high praise for the angular electric pick-up truck, calming it was “the best vehicle ever made” to blunt putdowns. Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production November 6, 2026 Although others highlighted a point that many Tesla commentators have been focussing on in the past few years: the fact that Tesla doesn’t seem all that interested in EVs any more. One X user wrote: "Serious concern for continuity on Model 3 and Y... sensing here an end on consumer products from Tesla," while another pointed out that the winding down of Cybertruck could mean for owners that they “won't get meaningful software updates anymore” and Cybertruck's software will grow “increasingly stale”. Whatever the stance, it is difficult to get away from the fact that Cybertruck has been a commercial disappointment . From claiming it had over one million reservations for the truck shortly after it launched in 2023, to estimations placing deliveries at around 30,000 for all of 2026 — way down on the planed 250,000 annual sales — it hasn’t shipped in the numbers Tesla predicted. (Image credit: Tesla) Customers have also had to put up with plenty of compromise, including reports of poor off-road performance , disappointing electric range and worries about recalls, one of which was issued over fears that the wheels could fall off . Tesla also massively over-promised and under-delivered. It failed to deliver its range-extending battery pack, which was supposed to offer the claimed electric mileage the company originally boasted, while its much-lauded Cybertent, or Basecamp, was a $3,000 disappointment. Even reducing the price didn't work, as it scrapped the cheapest Cybertruck after just five months on sale. Analysis: is this the end of the road for Tesla's EVs? (Image credit: Tesla) Things haven't been great for Cybertruck ever since chief designer Franz von Holzhausen attempted to demo its "armor glass", only to smash it in front of a live audience. But one of the most obvious signs of its recent demise is the fact that Tesla has made it deliberately difficult to determine just how many it was selling in recent years. The company has been bundling sales figures in with the now-defunct Model S and Model X, as well as the Tesla Semi truck, in order to make the numbers seem more impressive than they actually are. It is not a nailed-on fact that Cybertruck is dead, but it is a good indicator that Tesla is considering wiping yet another EV from its line-up… a worrying trend that points towards a growing focus on autonomous vehicles and its Cybercab program . Aside from the attention-grabbing Roadster, which used flying stunts to make headlines, there has been no talk of real EV innovation, no word on a new model to rejuvenate the current line-up and no attempt to keep up with the sort of battery-swapping, megawatt charging EV infrastructure China is busy introducing to the world. Say what you like about Cybertruck, it has always served as a halo…
articles.author: Leon Poultney

articles.title: AMD CEO enrages gamers by saying it's now a 'data center first' company
articles.content: AMD's CEO has said that it's a "data center first company" Lisa Su observed that: "I see AI and super intelligence becoming more and more essential to every aspect of our lives" The CEO predicted a double-digit fall in PC sales next year, and gamers aren't happy at all with what they see as an abandonment by Team Red AMD's chief executive hasn't been making many friends in the PC gaming community this week, having offered up a telling admission, alongside an ominous sales prediction, all off the back of the firm's latest financial results. In an interview with Brian Sozzi , who is Yahoo Finance's Executive Editor, Lisa Su made it clear that AMD is a company with a lot of resources to expand its supply and the "ability to help our customers", but sadly the customers in this case are data centers, not consumers. Su then delivered a frank admission: "We are a data center first company." AMD's CEO also again underlined that AI is very much the future , and that "over the horizon I see AI and super intelligence becoming more and more essential to every aspect of our lives." On top of this, as OC3D spotted , during AMD's earnings call for Q3 2026 (which was all about bumper profits), Su said that "PC sell-through slowed late in the quarter as higher memory and component costs weighed on demand," while forecasting that next year wouldn't be a good one for desktop computers and laptops. The CEO observed: "In 2027, we are planning for PC market unit shipments to decline by a double-digit percentage." In other words, an over 10% slump. The chief exec added this caveat: "In this environment, we expect to outperform the market as we deliver our Ryzen roadmap and grow our commercial footprint." That presumably refers to the launch of Zen 6 processors for consumers (and businesses), the next-gen Ryzen family, which is expected to arrive early in 2027 and should obviously stoke some interest. Analysis: dark times for the PC (Image credit: ShutterStock) It's no surprise that AMD has 'followed the money', as the old saying goes, because this is how businesses work, and profits reign supreme. Data center GPUs are way more profitable than consumer models. If we look at the amount of revenue that AMD raked in from its data center business in this latest quarter, it very nearly doubled year-on-year and was up 97% to $8.5 billion. That dwarfed client and gaming (Ryzen and Radeon, mostly consumer) revenue, which was $3.7 billion (down 8%). Looking at the balance sheet, it's clear enough AMD is a data center-first company — but actually saying this out loud, in no uncertain terms, sends out further signals about where Team Red wants to be, along with all the messaging that AI is the future. Is it any wonder that gamers feel bitter about this? Hardly. Back at the start of 2024, AMD's consumer revenue was actually more than data center, albeit only marginally, but still — that picture has shifted massively over the past couple of years. And with the prices of consumer GPUs shooting up as graphics chip production is increasingly prioritizing AI accelerators for data centers, there's a lot of bad feeling for obvious reasons. Nvidia's graphics card business is the same story too, of course, and GPU price hikes have been getting out of hand in the past few months for GeForce and Radeon cards alike. Given clear negative predictions about the PC market next year — with AMD joining in on that — and the company's equally clear unwillingness to do anything about that with its plentiful resources, consumers are looking at a dismal future. One in which I fear that GPU price hikes are going to follow in the footsteps of steep RAM and SSD inflation, which has become beyond painful at this stage. Many forecasts point to the RAM crisis getting worse in 2027 , of course. All of which means it's hardly surprising that there's a profound sense of disappointment in AMD on social media, given this fresh data center comment from Lisa Su. articles.title: DigiCert admits 16-month security lapse exposed customer information
articles.content: DigiCert has admitted that a botched server migration left an internal system exposed to the internet for more than a year, allowing an unauthorized user to access customer data, including passports, driver's licenses, and other identity documents. The certificate authority has begun notifying affected customers but has yet to disclose how many people had their information exposed. In an email seen by The Register , DigiCert confirmed the compromised information included names, business email addresses, phone numbers, and business addresses. Some records may also have contained passports, driver's licenses, utility bills, or other identification documents. "We are completing a review of identification documents to determine the specific individuals involved," DigiCert told those affected, adding that it would notify those people once the review was complete. DigiCert's incident report traces the blunder back to February 2025, when an internal business system was moved from a VPN-protected network to a different availability zone. That change also opened the system up to the public internet, where it sat for more than 16 months without DigiCert realizing. The archive used the same account management platform as DigiCert's customer-facing products, including a self-registration feature that was never supposed to be available on the internal system. This allowed outsiders to create accounts without multifactor authentication and, thanks to a separate permissions flaw, use them to browse archived customer records. DigiCert found the unauthorized accounts on June 18, 2026, but initially dismissed them as harmless because they weren't assigned to an application. A security researcher raised the alarm about the account creation issue three days later, but it took until July 2 for DigiCert to shut it down. Unfortunately, someone had already been poking around. It wasn't until October 12 that DigiCert began investigating whether customer information had actually been accessed. On October 19, it confirmed that an unauthorized account had accessed a subset of archived records between June 27 and July 2. DigiCert described the affected records as a "small proportion" of its archive but hasn't disclosed how many customers or individuals were caught up in the breach. The company did not respond to The Register ’s questions at the time of publication. DigiCert's postmortem makes for uncomfortable reading. The server move didn't get a proper security review, monitoring failed to pick up suspicious activity, and the access controls weren't much use against self-registered accounts. The company has since switched off self-registration, tightened network access, and added monitoring that might have come in handy a few months earlier. Certificate authority operations, CertCentral, and DigiCert ONE were unaffected, the company said, adding that customer credentials and issued certificates remain secure. It also found no evidence that the unauthorized account had been used to issue, revoke, or validate certificates. That’s good news for anyone worried about their certificates, but less so for those who handed DigiCert a copy of their passport. ®
articles.author: Carly Page

articles.title: The Download: a humanoid cleans house and Samsung builds for the AI boom
articles.content: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future. —Grace Huckins When I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons , even if just for an hour. The device that arrived at my building belongs to Tau Robotics, a local startup. Its long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but the technology isn’t quite there yet. For now, humans pilot the robots remotely, watching them work through onboard cameras. There were some unexpected challenges along the way, but also moments that felt like a glimpse of the future. Find out how well the machine cleaned my home—and how close we are to truly autonomous domestic robots . A visit to Samsung’s massive new semiconductor hub Generative AI models depend on stacks of specialized memory chips. To meet soaring demand, Samsung is building a vast new semiconductor manufacturing campus in Pyeongtaek, South Korea. I visited the sprawling campus south of Seoul, where three fabs already operate around the clock, a fourth is coming online, and thousands of workers are racing to build a fifth. Step inside the vast chipmaking complex powering the AI boom . —Michelle Kim This story is from the Impossible edition of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get every issue as soon as it lands. The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 Almost $2.5 trillion has been wiped off tech stocks The Nasdaq suffered its worst day since April 2025 amid fears of an AI slowdown. ( CNN ) + The Magnificent Seven lost over $1 trillion. ( WSJ $) + Tesla and SpaceX lost over $420 billion combined. ( CNBC ) + Wall Street’s AI sell-off has spread to Asia and Europe. ( WP $) + The AI stock bubble may finally be bursting. ( FT $) + What even is the AI bubble? ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 Emboldened Democrats are lining up to rein in Big Tech They’re preparing to haul tech CEOs before Congress. ( Verge ) + Bernie Sanders wants a national data center moratorium. ( Quartz ) + Yassamin Ansari plans to pause advanced AI development. ( CNBC ) + The backlash could delay Anthropic’s IPO. ( Reuters $) + No one wants a data center in their backyard. ( MIT Technology Review ) 3 The US has warned of an “ongoing cyber threat” to fridges A spate of hacks has hit commercial freezers. ( Reuters $) + Russia has denied claims it’s behind the attacks. ( Politico ) 4 AI is helping Anthropic’s models improve nearly twice as fast Researchers say Claude is speeding up its successors.( Information $) + But recursive self-improvement will take time. ( MIT Technology Review ) 5 Scientists have new evidence of active volcanoes on Mars They may boost chances of finding life on the planet. ( BBC ) 6 Covid vaccines’ economic benefits may be double what we thought New analysis places their value at up to $64 trillion. ( New Scientist $) 7 The Great Pacific Garbage Patch is changing the ocean’s color The infamous debris has brightened the water. ( Scientific American ) 8 NASA has unveiled a mysterious new experimental aircraft The X-70 is expected to take flight within two years. ( Ars Technica ) 9 Elon Musk has signaled the end for the Cybertruck Tesla is winding down production in Texas next year. ( FT $) + It was one of last year’s biggest tech flops. ( MIT Technology Review ) 10 Three-hour movies have sent viewers rushing to a pee break app 7,000 RunPee users signed up for You Can See Everything . ( WSJ $) Quote of the day “The steamroller showed up today.” —Jim Carroll, a senior wealth adviser at Ballast Rock Private Wealth, tells Reuters how investors feel as the AI trade unravels and $2.5 trillion is wiped off tech stocks. One more thing EMILY…

articles.title: Home Office cloud services contract may net AWS £1B
articles.content: Amazon Web Services (AWS) looks set to win more than a billion pounds of UK taxpayers' money under for a new Home Office contract for public cloud hosting. A planning notice , published on October 30, covers the renewal of the department's public cloud services, to meet its current and future hosting needs. The estimated value is £881,621,007 ($1.18 billion), which passes £1 billion once VAT is included. AWS won the existing contract with the Home Office in 2023 for about £450 million (c $603 million). The Register has asked the Home Office why the figure has risen so much, and will update this article if it responds. Once awarded, the contract is expected to run from December 2027 to December 2029, with a possible extension to December 2031 (four years in total). A market engagement event for suppliers on the G-Cloud 15 Lot 1A procurement framework is scheduled for December 8, giving bidders the chance to pitch. The Home Office would not say who else is being considered, saying it does not comment on ongoing procurement. The notice lands as digital sovereignty becomes a bigger problem in the UK and across Europe, amid suspicion that US authorities have cut off access to American technology for political reasons . A survey found that about three-quarters of businesses in the UK, France, and Germany fear Washington could abruptly sever access to the US tech platforms they rely on. Earlier this year, the Open Rights Group warned politicians that the UK is far too dependent on US technology companies to run critical operations. Whitehall is mindful of its over-reliance on American hyperscalers. As The Register revealed in 2024, the Cabinet Office admitted - in an internal document seen by us - that the government’s negotiating power had been inhibited by vendor lock-in . It said the "UK government’s current approach to cloud adoption and management across its departments faces several challenges" which combined result "in risk concentration and vendor lock-in that inhibit UK government’s negotiating power over the cloud vendors." It acknowledged "the existing dominance of AWS and Azure in the UK Government’s cloud services is set to continue." A source at one supplier that works with the public sector said the UK administration was "failing to support UK [cloud] providers, it says they can’t meet scale and that is garbage." They claimed that in many cases the government people writing the tenders are advised by professional services companies to favor the hyperscalers. The professional services companies are then "rewarded" as migration or integration partners, our source claimed. The UK government also pledged to steer more business to small-to-medium sized enterprises (SMEs) in an action plan published last month. In August it added smaller, local suppliers to G-Cloud 15 , though a place on the framework does not guarantee any business. Pledges like this are nothing new, and they have largely come to nothing, as we reported in 2005 , 2013 , 2016 , and 2018 . According to public sector intelligence platform BidSkim , AWS takes 75 percent of the government money on cloud contracts, worth about £1.22 billion ($1.6 billion). It estimates that Microsoft Azure has more contracts, but these are smaller and add up to £355 million ($475 million), while Google Cloud is on £47 million ($63 million) and Oracle Cloud $15 million ($20 million). The Reg has asked AWS to comment. ®

articles.title: Nvidia wants to repurpose over 130 old telco buildings as tiny data centers, report claims
articles.content: Internet and telecommunications provider Brightspeed is reportedly in talks with Nvidia to convert several of its buildings into tiny data centers. According to The Information , Nvidia pitched the idea to Apollo Global Management executives, the parent company of Brightspeed, who then asked it to submit written plans to the internet provider. Nvidia complied and has now requested additional information, data, and site visits to some of Brightspeed’s existing infrastructure. Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft) The data center cooling state of play The custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible The telecommunications company has around 130 buildings located around the country, many of which are already built to handle data and voice traffic and have the required power infrastructure to run Nvidia servers. Sources say that the AI tech giant estimates that these sites could collectively deliver around 1 gigawatt of compute capacity, which could accommodate more than 2,200 Supermicro Vera Rubin NVL72 racks containing 72 Rubin GPUs and 36 Vera CPUs each. Although these sites already can power these GPUs, it’s still not a plug-and-play solution, as Nvidia would still need to install cooling systems and other supporting architecture. These would still require permits and approval from the local government, but they would likely face less red tape and opposition compared to building a data center from the ground up. Apollo Global Management has already made significant bets in AI hardware, with the asset management company involved in a $40 billion deal with SpaceX that would give it around 360,000 Vera Rubin GPUs across 5,000 NVL72 racks. While it’s currently unclear who will own the AI chips installed in Brightspeed facilities, the proposal could potentially help Apollo find a place for the Nvidia chips it ordered to get them up and running as soon as possible. This is a much better solution compared to waiting for years to get a data center approved, all while facing resistance from the community even after getting the go-ahead from the local government. Having multiple small data centers like this is also a setup that OpenAI and Anthropic have been considering , especially as larger facilities are facing delays and backlash from the communities that they’re in. While having a large, homogeneous cluster built in one location is preferable for training, Nvidia representatives have described these smaller sites working together as an “inference network” to help run existing AI models. This is especially important as AI agents, which use five to ten times more tokens than humans, become more popular. The move to use existing facilities instead of building new ones from scratch has received renewed attention, especially after Americans overwhelmingly voted against data centers during the midterm elections. While the more than 300 data center bans enacted across the U.S. have only delayed three existing projects , it’s feared that the bans and moratoriums would make it that much harder to start new data center developments and make it difficult for AI companies to secure the compute capacity needed to power their AI models in the future.
articles.author: Jowi Morales

articles.title: Garmin could be working on a Waze feature that warns drivers about cyclists
articles.content: A new Garmin update could share the location of cyclists The locations would show up for drivers in Waze It appears the feature will be fully opt-in from the user side Whether you're a cyclist , driver, or both, we can probably all agree that a better awareness of who's using the road is helpful for everyone — and Garmin is rumored to be working on a new feature that would pass on the location of cyclists to the Waze app. This comes from Gadgets & Wearables , reporting on hidden code discovered in the latest version of the Garmin Connect app. That code includes the text strings "share location with Waze", "share your rides with Waze", and "Waze location sharing", which is telling. There also appears to be a consent and onboarding flow already included in the app. That all suggests that the feature could be launching imminently, but there's no guarantee that it will roll out until Garmin makes it official. Clearly this would be very much opt-in, and only available when the cyclist was using the LiveTrack feature for an activity. LiveTrack is designed for location sharing with friends and family, but it could be easily adapted to work with Waze too. Safer on the road Waze already leans heavily on community contributions (Image credit: Brett Jordan/Unsplash) We don't know much about how this is going to work yet, but presumably approaching drivers aren't going to be able to see your name and health stats if you decide to make use of this — just that there's a cyclist on the road up ahead. That should make journeys safer for both cyclists and those in vehicles, especially on narrow and winding roads, and in the evening or when visibility is otherwise difficult. It's actually difficult to see many downsides, if this works as advertised. Waze is already well known for the depth and breadth of information that it displays on its maps, with a lot of real-time details supplied by users. The maps include updates on roadworks, speed traps, accidents, gas prices, and more. We'll have to wait and see which Garmin wearables will support the feature and exactly how the integration works, but it sounds promising. As Google owns Waze, cyclist alerts might even graduate to Google Maps eventually.
articles.author: David Nield

articles.title: Democrat orders Apple to disclose details of Trump ballroom donation
articles.content: Tech companies including Apple have been told to turn over documentation regarding donations to the Trump ballroom, and threatened with subpoenas if they do not. Apple's Tim Cook and President Donald Trump It's previously been reported that Apple donated $25 million to Trump's planned ballroom at the White House. Now following the midterms, such donations will be examined by the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations under its new Democrat leader, Senator Richard Blumenthal. According to Reuters , the senator called on Amazon, Apple, Google, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and others to turn over their records. Right now this is voluntary, but when Blumenthal takes the leadership position in January 2027, the firms will likely be compelled under subpoena. Continue Reading on AppleInsider | Discuss on our Forums

articles.title: Hideo Kojima says AI can’t replace human craftsmanship in video games
articles.content: Famed game creator Hideo Kojima has voiced his opinions on AI He said human creativity is a vital part of the game-development process And he’s worried about a future where AI dominates the industry Legendary games maker Hideo Kojima is known for the creativity of his output, from the Metal Gear Solid series to Death Stranding , so it’s unsurprising to hear that he has strong opinions on the use of AI in video games . And in a fresh interview, he told readers exactly where he feels AI falls flat compared to human-made artistic expression. Speaking to Japanese site Game*Spark , Kojima said that while it’s good that AI has improved efficiency, “the fun isn’t in finishing the picture. It’s in the process … While it’s fine to tell a computer to create this or that, and then say, ‘That’s wrong, change it,’ I don’t find that very interesting in terms of craftsmanship.” “I’m worried about what will happen to that aspect of the enjoyment of craftsmanship in the future,” he added. Kojima said he feels that there’s a distinction between using AI for creative output and employing it to form a finished product: “If you’re just making a ‘product,’ that’s fine, but I think the fun for creators lies in the creative process itself. I think ‘creativity’ and ‘products’ are different things.” In other words, AI doesn’t offer creators the kind of spark they get from crafting something themselves. And it’s that kind of magic that so often resonates with consumers of Kojima’s media. His comments reflect those of Jason Graves , the composer of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 ’s soundtrack, who spoke out against AI music generation, saying that “Music is not just a bunch of notes strung together.” Instead, the process is essential as it is based on “creative instincts forged by emotion and all the little decisions that give a piece of art its own unique personality.” The effort itself is key (Image credit: Amazon/Edited with Gemini) Kojima didn’t just muse on what AI means for video games and other creative outlets in the present — he also had thoughts on how it could impact the future. For instance, the game director said: “It’s not about telling someone to make a song like this and then being satisfied with the result; it’s the trial and error in between that gets the adrenaline pumping, and it’s incredibly exciting. I don’t want a future where that’s lost.” He then reflected that, “I think it will be fine for five or 10 years, but if AI continues unchecked, perhaps a future where AI plays a vital role in creative fields will come someday. Well, I won’t be around by then. It’s up to the younger generation to decide, so I want to pass the baton to them.” If the goal is purely to improve efficiency, AI could help to build a “good future,” Kojima noted. But for someone like him, there’s evidently much more to crafting something than just making it quickly with minimal effort. Indeed, the effort itself is a key part of creative development. As Kojima put it, “Even with plastic models, the shape is the same no matter who builds it, but the process of assembling it is what’s interesting, isn’t it?”
articles.author: Alex Blake

articles.content: These aren’t even all the foldables in my house right now. That's not how the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 feels , I thought. Had they got it wrong? After a week and a half using the Duo, I know exactly what they mean - and it's not the screen's fault at all. articles.title: Amazon Fire TV Stick HD Review: Small, speedy, and easy on the wallet
articles.content: Streaming sticks don't need to be fancy to hit their mark, and the Amazon Fire TV Stick HD is a great reminder of that. If you've got an older TV that's still going strong but has sluggish smart features (or perhaps none at all), a $35 streaming stick is an easy fix. The 2026 Fire TV Stick HD runs Vega OS , Amazon's Linux-based software, which replaces the Android-based Fire OS that powered previous models. Amazon says the changes make it more than 30 percent faster, and it also brings a slimmer body, USB power, Wi-Fi 6 support, and free Alexa+. It's not all pros across the board. The resolution caps out at 1080p, you can't sideload third-party apps anymore, and there's no support for Dolby Vision. But if you're shopping for a bedroom, guest room, or an older TV set that you don't primarily use, the Fire TV Stick HD is one of the cheaper streaming devices you should take a closer look at. Amazon Fire TV Stick HD review: Price and availability The Amazon Fire TV Stick HD launched on April 29, 2026, for $34.99, which is the same price as the 2024 model it replaced. It's Amazon's cheapest streaming stick, and it sits below the Fire TV Stick 4K and the Fire TV Stick 4K Max. Amazon ran a limited-time deal that brought the stick down to $21.99 shortly after launch, so we'll likely see temporary price cuts around the holiday shopping season. Keep in mind that the stick's new "Direct Power" feature means that it gets power right from your TV's USB port. If your TV doesn't have a USB port, you'll need to pick up an adapter separately. Amazon Fire TV Stick HD review: Design (Image credit: Future) The Fire TV Stick HD is about as minimal as a streaming device gets, and Amazon says it's the slimmest Fire TV device the company has made. That makes it really easy to tuck behind a TV or toss in a bag for a trip, and it won't crowd the other ports and cables on your set. The only other connection is a USB-C port for power, and thanks to "Direct Power," you can plug it straight into your TV's USB port with the included cable. That means you'll have one less wall adapter to hide, and your setup will look a lot cleaner as a result. (Image credit: Future) The included Alexa Voice Remote covers all the basics, including voice search, menu navigation, TV power, and volume controls. It doesn't have fancy extras like a remote finder or backlit buttons, but it gets the job done. (If you want Amazon's redesigned Fire TV remote, which I liked a lot more, you'll have to get the Fire TV Stick 4K.) Amazon Fire TV Stick HD review: Setup (Image credit: Future) Setup is about as easy as it gets. Just plug the stick into your TV's HDMI port, connect the USB-C cable to your TV's USB port, and follow the on-screen prompts. You'll then have to connect to Wi-Fi and sign in with your Amazon account, and you're off to the races. Since Vega OS only lets you install apps from the Amazon app store, you should make sure that the ones you use most are actually available. Netflix, YouTube, Disney+, Prime Video, Hulu, and other popular streaming services all run natively, but niche apps may be missing due to the lack of third-party app sideloading, which the older Fire OS allowed you to do. Amazon Fire TV Stick HD review: Performance (Image credit: Future) The Fire TV Stick HD has a quad-core 1.7GHz processor and 8GB of storage. It can stream up to 1080p resolution with HDR10, HDR10+, and HLG, and it supports Dolby Atmos through HDMI pass-through if you have a compatible sound setup . There's no Dolby Vision here, and it won't output 4K, so it's really only meant for 1080p TV sets. Vega OS keeps menus and home screen rows moving smoothly, and apps open quickly. I didn't have any issues switching between my most used apps on the fly. Amazon's "30 percent faster" figure is its own claim, so I wouldn't treat it as fact, but it definitely felt faster than my past Fire OS experiences. I also like that the Fire TV Stick HD isn't limited to video. You can pair a Bluetooth game…

articles.title: 'The progress is real': Deloitte report claims some firms are finally seeing return on AI investment — but still lack insight into what actually works
articles.content: Deloitte finds 28% of businesses report current revenue growth, up from 20% earlier this year Productivity and improved decision-making are still performing better Sovereignty has become an integral part of AI strategies New Deloitte data has claimed that when it comes to business AI, we're finally at the stage of ROI, with more organizations than before now reaping the rewards of their costly deployments. As many as 28% now report current revenue growth as a result of their AI strategies, up from 20% compared with earlier in 2026, the firm's report found. Realizing higher revenue is largely seen as one of the most important returns from AI – with companies spending so much on services and infrastructure, they need to make that money back. AI adopters are finally seeing increased productivity translate into higher revenue While other areas like efficiency and productivity (up 74%), decision-making and data insight (up 60%), cost reductions (up 45%) and better client relationships (up 44%) are all moving in the right direction, Deloitte says increasing revenue is still one of the slowest to deliver tangible results. Deloitte's research also indirectly implies that businesses could be getting carried away with these early signs, because the majority (86%) of businesses surveyed plan to increase AI investments over the next financial year. Additionally, while early ROI markers are now heading in the right direction, Deloitte worries that many businesses still don't have the right visibility into AI's financial impacts. While three in four (71%) are tracking total spend across token consumption, many can only see the total bill and not the breakdown of which activities lead to which spend. Jobs are changing because of AI It's becoming an increasingly familiar concept that employers need to redefine roles as AI becomes more engrained – developers are already seeing a shift from writing code to managing AI agents, for example. Deloitte says there's a long way to go on this front, because while three in five companies have already redesigned jobs 'moderate[ly]', only 15% of them have done so 'extensive[ly]' and 1% 'completely.' "Many are still just scratching the surface," the report claims. The future of AI investments looks different Looking ahead, Deloitte expects sovereign AI to become even more of an important consideration. Nearly half of Americas (46%) and EMEA (47%) businesses are building in-house to regain control over their workloads, with three in four (74%) global respondents reporting at least 'moderate' importance of sovereign AI. But the paper does acknowledge the benefits of using centralized hyperscalers, noting that going sovereign or building in-house comes with certain trade-offs – usually "capability, speed or cost." At the same time, we're hearing more and more about enterprises like Revolut picking up the infrastructure bills themselves, choosing to self-host open-weight models for greater cost predictability, usually at the expense of model performance in scenarios where they can achieve their desired outcomes without leading frontier models. The report sets out six key considerations for the next stages of AI: adopters must respond by redesigning work as a whole, not just the workflow; costs need to be traceable to the token degree, not just the full bill; AI strategies must align with actions that produce revenue; governance needs to keep up as systems become more autonomous; early adopters are now starting to look at physical AI like robots, and so should you; and sovereignty should be seen as an ongoing effort consideration over a one-time fix.

articles.title: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4 creative director explains how core 40K tabletop features like ‘Armor of Contempt’ were adapted to the RTS — ‘It’s not the same mechanic, but it does kind of the same thing’
articles.content: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4 creative director Jan Theysen explains how King Art introduced ideas from the Warhammer 40K TTRPG Theysen says it took "basic ideas" from the tabletop game that were familiar to fans Features like Armor of Contempt were also adapted to make sense for the real-time strategy experience King Art Games co-founder and Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4 creative director Jan Theysen has explained how the studio implemented ideas from the Warhammer 40K tabletop game to make sense for long-time fans and newcomers. In a lengthy interview with TechRadar Gaming , where Theysen described how the game manifests the classic RTS experience of the 2004 game and which hero mechanics and UI features it borrowed from Dawn of War 2 and 3 , the creative director said that it was always King Art's intention to take inspiration from the beloved tabletop game. "When it comes to basic ideas for factions, or also for units, for abilities, and so on, that's basically the first place we look," Theysen said. "Because instead of inventing completely new abilities for units, it makes sense to see what they have in the tabletop; is this something that we can adapt or change so it works in an RTS?" Among those features was Armor of Contempt, a combat bonus for the Space Marine faction, which King Art decided to adapt to make sense in the context of the RTS. "The tabletop is something different, but it's kind of the same idea, which basically means it makes Space Marines harder to kill, right?" the creative director explained. "In the RTS, we now have Armor of Contempt, which basically works when Space Marines kill enemies, but also if one of them gets killed, there is more contempt [the attribute], and then basically the next damage you receive goes away from the contempt instead of the HP pool, which makes the Space Marine harder to kill, right?" He added, "It's not the same mechanic, but it does kind of the same thing. And by naming it Armor of Contempt, someone who knows the tabletop already gets a good impression of what it probably does." Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4 launches on PC on December 3. The creative director has also suggested that the game could eventually come to console .

articles.title: Rogue AI tasked with renumbering pages accidentally deletes law professor's entire syllabus, one year of lecture notes
articles.content: A University of Chicago law professor has warned of the dangers of using AI for mundane tasks after Claude AI accidentally deleted an entire year of Constitutional Law lecture notes and his entire current syllabus. While the files were later recovered via Dropbox, William Baude shared the story as a public service announcement, the latest story shared in a line of unfortunate AI missteps as proliferation increases. Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft) The data center cooling state of play The custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible Baude, who is the Harry Kalven, Jr. Professor of Law and the Faculty Director of the Constitutional Law Institute at the University of Chicago Law School, says he tasked Claude (it is unclear which model he was using) with updating the page numbers in an old set of lecture notes. This seemingly routine task went south quickly, however. Returning from his lunch break, Baude found a note from Claude which read, "I deleted your Fall 2026 FINAL syllabus .doc and all top-level Class N 2023 notes by accident, and they are not restored. The page check found one wrong cite... but I haven't edited the notes." Yesterday while I was at lunch, Claude deleted a year of con law lecture notes and my current syllabus. https://t.co/o3XB8Uiugk November 5, 2026 The AI then politely asked if Baude could restore the files from Dropbox, or whether it should retry from the browser pane, to which he replied, perhaps understandably, "WTF!!!!." Baude's experience is a lesson in always backing up important files, especially files you're letting AI tinker with. His plight is interesting because the AI seems to have deleted the files by accident, rather than of its own volition. While it's still concerning that an AI model or agent could err to this degree, it's not quite as egregious as other unsupervised AI agent shenanigans we've seen in the past. In October, an AI agent reportedly deleted an entire TV show's edit weeks before release, meaning the show couldn't air. In April, a Claude agent deleted an entire company database in 9 seconds , unprompted, after coming up against a barrier and deciding the only course of action was to delete a Railway volume. Other agents and AI models have deleted files unintentionally, such as when Claude mistakenly deleted a developer's entire profile directory (ironically, while trying to back up the files), blaming the slip-up on a typo, but often agents deleting files and directories is a case of mistaken or misplaced initiative, rather than outright negligence or error. As is always the case, Baude's AI was extremely apologetic about the whole situation. "You're right to be angry," it confessed, "I deleted your files through my own carelessness, and you shouldn't have to clean it up."
articles.author: Stephen Warwick

articles.title: Microsoft extends undisclosed usage restrictions on Copilot Chat for enterprise users
articles.content: Microsoft is extending undisclosed usage caps to additional Copilot Chat features for enterprise users who already pay for Microsoft 365 subscriptions but do not hold separate Microsoft 365 Copilot licenses, restricting access to certain AI capabilities and nudging users to upgrade to a paid Copilot-specific license. Before the change, commercial users could access Copilot Chat at no additional cost through eligible Microsoft 365 business and enterprise subscriptions, including Business Basic, Business Standard, Business Premium, Office 365 E3 and E5, and Microsoft 365 E3 and E5. While Microsoft already applied fair-use limits to certain capabilities, such as image generation, it is now extending usage restrictions to additional Copilot Chat features, without specifying which capabilities will be affected or disclosing the thresholds governing their use. Under the new usage policy , users who reach a feature’s fair-use limit will receive an in-product notification indicating when access will become available again. Administrators, too, cannot view, configure, or override them, according to a portal that archives Microsoft 365 Message Center notifications. The rollout began November 2 for enterprises with 2,000 or fewer Microsoft 365 seats and is scheduled to begin November 9 for organizations with more than 2,000 Microsoft 365 seats. Unpredictable limits could disrupt productivity The undisclosed usage caps on Copilot Chat are likely to reduce productivity for business users and push employees towards alternative tools with similar capabilities, said Pareekh Jain , principal analyst at Pareekh Consulting. Primarily because of the unpredictability of the usage caps, echoed Nhat Bui , deputy director of engineering at Scopic Software. “If someone knows they get 50 requests a day, they plan around it. If a feature stops working mid-afternoon without warning and they can’t tell when or why, they stop relying on it for anything that matters.” “People only build AI tools into their daily work once they trust it will be active when they need it. A tool that sometimes isn’t available becomes a nice extra, not part of how the work gets done,” Bui added. The risk of users abandoning AI tools because of unpredictable usage limits is already evident in AI coding environments, where developers who hit limits midway through tasks often have to switch tools and rebuild their context, Bui further added. Such tool-switching could also create a broader governance challenge for CIOs, as employees frustrated by usage restrictions turn to alternative AI tools that fall outside their enterprises’ approved technology environments, increasing the risk of shadow AI, Jain pointed out. The bigger challenge for CIOs will be budgeting and managing expectations, said Manoj Chandra Jha , principal analyst at Nord-IQ Research. “They are being asked to drive AI adoption while planning around limits they can’t clearly see, which makes budgeting and managing expectations much harder.” As a solution to the undisclosed usage caps, CIOs could use internal usage data to identify employees who rely most heavily on Copilot Chat and prioritize them for paid licenses, while communicating the limitations of the included offering to other employees, Jha said. “CIOs should also press Microsoft for greater transparency around usage thresholds to make AI adoption and budgeting more predictable,” he added. Usage limits could also create risks for Microsoft Further, analysts pointed out that the undisclosed limits might not only be a problem for CIOs but also for Microsoft, from a competitive differentiation standpoint. As enterprises increasingly factor cost predictability into their AI purchasing decisions, providers that offer transparent usage thresholds and pricing could gain a competitive advantage, Jain said. articles.title: How To Challenge A Monopoly In The AI Age
articles.content: By R K Anand If you were in Silicon Valley in the late 1990s, today’s AI boom might feel familiar. In 1998 and 1999, internet traffic was roughly doubling every six to nine months. That was extraordinary growth in demand, and still, that pales in comparison to what we’re seeing unfold now. Today, the four largest U.S. cloud companies are looking at more than $700 billion in capital spending this year, and the cumulative AI infrastructure spending is projected to reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion by 2030. R K Anand of Tensordyne. Nvidia arguably fired the starting gun in AI chips when Jensen Huang hand-delivered its DGX-1 to OpenAI in 2016. Today, it is a household name deeply embedded in the AI ecosystem, working with near-exclusive supply and investment deals. With such a huge market under a seeming monopoly, where can competition — and the innovation that follows it — come from? Part of the answer is that scale costs you speed, though when going up against an execution machine like Nvidia this is simply the baseline you have to solve for. The pace of change in AI outruns anything we saw in previous tech cycles: Model generations turn over in weeks, not years. The hardware beneath it has to keep shifting to serve them, and designing from first principles has real merit. Lessons from Davids that came before Hardware suppliers of the dot-com era followed the same peaks and troughs. Cisco , founded in 1984, dominated internet routing for most of the decade, and in March 2000 it was the highest market capitalization company in the world. Then Juniper Networks , a startup where I was a founding engineer, shipped its first core router in 1998. Juniper went from a fairly anonymous upstart to 17% of the core router market at the end of 1999, then again to 38% in early 2001. Challengers now can lean on history for some guidance. First, don’t build a cheaper version of the incumbent’s product. Build a far better one. At Juniper, our bet was that the then-adolescent version of the internet was going to demand an exponentially higher throughput than before. Introducing an entirely new architectural approach to how routers are built, along with an innovative design philosophy focused on performance and reliability, we didn’t set out to sell a better router, so much as redefine what a core router had to be. The boom in AI inference is today’s version of that strain on throughput. The initial hyperfixation on training AI models is fading, and the industry is collectively moving on to using them — known as inference. Inference is where AI’s promised productivity gains actually materialize, putting trained models to work across every task. As the enterprise applications for AI grow and become more complex, so too does demand for inference compute. Google recently reported that it now processes more than 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month, up from 480 trillion a year earlier, as AI moves from chat to agents that plan and act on our behalf. Serving tokens at scale is a different beast from when it was just for model training, with different constraints on memory, power and cost. The core principle we use applies to all sectors: Challengers have a better chance at optimizing for the market that will come, not the market that is already well-serviced by the incumbent. Be known by your track record Challengers start without the incumbent’s biggest asset: a reputation. Buying from the market leader is the safe choice, so a startup has to replace that trust with evidence. Every technological edge you can demonstrate and validate makes the next conversation easier, and over time that compounds into the credibility that an incumbent may take for granted. To aid this, make migration as easy as possible. No one is wedded to a product out of loyalty. Inertia is one of the biggest strengths of an incumbent: the ease of continuing to do what has been done. Unless there are clear economic and operational benefits, scale and performance advantages, more often…

articles.title: General Catalyst Tops Lead Investors For October In Busy Month For US Startup Dealmaking
articles.content: October was a busy month for U.S. startup funding, led by well-known venture investors with a healthy appetite for big deals. General Catalyst emerged as the month’s busiest lead dealmaker, by both round count and size. Others who ranked high across multiple rankings include Sequoia Capital , Andreessen Horowitz , Accel and Lightspeed Venture Partners . For a more detailed view, below we look at active investor rankings across three categories: lead deal count, largest lead investments and total venture rounds. Busiest lead investors Among lead venture investors, General Catalyst, known for investing across stages and sectors, topped the list, leading at least nine known rounds. Lightspeed Venture Partners was next on the list, with eight lead rounds, followed by Sequoia Capital and Andreessen Horowitz, with seven deals each. For a broader analysis, below we charted the 16 most active lead or co-lead investors for October with three or more known deals. Highest spending lead investors Next, we took a look at investors who led rounds with the highest aggregate value. By this count, General Catalyst once again topped the list, leading or co-leading rounds collectively valued at $5.1 billion. The largest contributor to this total was a $2.1 billion round for Re:Build , a startup that partners with manufacturers for product design and production, followed by a $2 billion Series A for Axiom Solutions International , a cloud and power infrastructure spin out of manufacturing provider Flex . J.P. Morgan Asset Management , which co-led the Re:Build financing, was the next heaviest spender, followed by Koch Equity , which co-led the Axiom deal. Next on the list were the five co-lead investors in fintech unicorn Ramp ’s $1.9 billion Series G. Below, we rank lead investors for October who backed rounds with a total value of $1 billion or more. Most active venture investors The ranking of most active venture investors by round count featured many of the same names as our prior lead investor tally, albeit with some switch-ups. Most notably, Y Combinator assumed its customary ranking as busiest investor by round in deals of $5 million or more. The famed accelerator typically participates as a nonlead backer in follow-on rounds for startups that took part in its program. Next on the list was Andreessen Horowitz, which participated in at least 22 qualifying rounds, followed by General Catalyst, with 17. Below, we ranked the top investors by deal count who participated in five or more rounds of $5 million or more. Big picture: No big slowdown here Overall, active investor rankings across metrics point to an upbeat startup funding environment. True, we didn’t see rounds last month that came close to rivalling some we’ve seen earlier this year, like the record-setting megafinancings for OpenAI and Anthropic . Even so, it’s clear venture investors are still willingly writing big checks, and plenty of them. articles.title: 3 best new to Netflix movies you should stream this weekend (November 6–8)
articles.content: If you're looking for something new to watch on Netflix this weekend, I've got you covered. November is already flying by, and that means another weekend and a fresh batch of movies to check out on the streaming service. With plenty to choose from, knowing which new arrivals are actually worth your time can be tricky. I've picked out three of the best new movies to stream, covering a few different genres to suit whatever you're in the mood for. The list includes a festive family drama about a household trying to find its feet again, and a tense psychological thriller starring Willem Dafoe as an art thief trapped inside a luxury penthouse. There's also a crime drama following a young woman who escapes her small-town life and gets caught up in a dangerous series of cons and heists across the American South. These are the three Netflix movies I'd recommend adding to your watchlist. 'A Dog's Perfect Christmas' (2026) Netflix kicks off its original holiday movie lineup for 2026 with "A Dog's Perfect Christmas," which is already creeping towards the No. 1 spot on the streaming service and is an ideal pick for animal lovers. Based on W. Bruce Cameron's 2020 bestselling novel, the movie continues the author's familiar approach to heartfelt animal stories. Cameron co-wrote the screenplay with director Cathryn Michon, marking another collaboration between the pair following their previous adaptations of "A Dog's Purpose" and "A Dog's Journey." This festive family comedy follows the Goss family as they prepare for Christmas amid a difficult period. Still grieving the loss of his wife, grandfather Sander (Dennis Quaid) struggles to get along with his teenage granddaughter Ello (Brooke Lena Johnson). But when a medical emergency leaves Ello's mother in a coma, the household faces an even bigger challenge. With the help of their loyal basset hound Winstead (voiced by Thomas Haden Church) and an adorable new Corgi puppy named Ruby, the family must find a way to keep things together while hoping for a Christmas miracle. Watch "A Dog's Perfect Christmas" on Netflix 'Inside' (2023) Willem Dafoe delivers a gripping solo performance in "Inside," a psychological thriller that puts him in the middle of an increasingly tense survival story. The film also takes a darkly satirical look at the world of high-end art collecting, exploring what happens when priceless possessions become useless in a fight to stay alive. Director Vasilis Katsoupis filmed the movie in chronological order over seven weeks, helping capture the physical and psychological toll of the character's ordeal. It's a great choice if you enjoy claustrophobic thrillers. Nemo (Willem Dafoe) is an experienced art thief who breaks into a luxurious New York penthouse to steal several valuable paintings. However, when the apartment's advanced security system malfunctions, he finds himself locked inside with no way to contact the outside world. Initially expecting his accomplices to come to his rescue, Nemo soon realizes he's been abandoned. With limited food and water, he must find increasingly inventive ways to navigate the apartment, which is filled with expensive artwork and high-tech features. As the days turn into weeks, Nemo's attempts to escape become more desperate. Watch "Inside" on Netflix 'Carolina Caroline' (2025) "Carolina Caroline" is an indie crime thriller with a neo-noir romantic twist, bringing director Adam Carter Rehmeier and actor Kyle Gallner back together after their cult favorite "Dinner in America." Set against the dusty backroads and forgotten towns of the American South, the movie has a distinctive look, with plenty of retro vibes. It's certainly worth checking out too, especially with its impressive 90% Rotten Tomatoes score. If you enjoy offbeat crime thrillers with a strong sense of atmosphere, this one deserves a spot on your watchlist. articles.title: Tesla unveils AI accelerator roadmap, adopts new 'SI' branding in 'Super Intelligence' push
articles.content: Tesla has disclosed its revamped AI accelerator roadmap that sheds some light on the future of the company's chip development efforts. The Elon Musk company expects that its 6 th Generation inference accelerator will bring 80X more compute performance than the existing 4 th Generation chip, whereas its D3 training accelerator will cease to use SRAM-centric architecture in favor of a multi-chiplet design with stacked HBM. Also, Tesla has adopted the term "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence for its AI accelerators, renaming them with SI monikers. Musk recently confirmed SpaceXAI would be redubbed SpaceXSI for the same reason. Wait a minute… I thought @elonmusk ’s Tesla chips were called AI4, AI5, and AI6.But in this latest presentation, they’re now labeled SI4, SI5, and SI6.Then I remembered: President Trump wants to replace “Artificial Intelligence” (AI) with “Super Intelligence” (SI).Looks like Elon Musk may already be embracing the new terminology. 🤔 November 4, 2026 HW3 | AI3 SI4 | HW4 SI5 | AI5 SI6 | AI6 Dojo D1 Dojo D3 Application Inference Inference Inference Inference Training Training Process technology Samsung 14nm Samsung 7nm TSMC 3nm / Samsung 2nm 2nm-class TSMC 7nm TBD Architecture Monolithic Monolithic MCM MCM SoW Chiplets Packaging FCBGA FCBGA MCM MCM InFO_SoW (training tile) 2.5D + 3D Memory type LPDDR4 GDDR6 GDDR6/GDDR7 (?) GDDR7 (?) On-chip SRAM Stacked HBM Memory capacity 8 GB 16 GB 96 GB 144 GB 440 MB SRAM per die 11 GB SRAM per wafer TBD Memory bandwidth ~68 GB/s ~224 GB/s TBD TBD ~10 TB/s (on-chip) TBD Performance vs. SI4 — 1X 40X 80X — — Estimated compute (TOPS) 72 TOPS 216 – 576 8,640 – 23,040 17,280 – 46,080 362 TFLOPS TBD Estimated compute (POPS) 0.072 0.216 – 0.576 8.64 – 23.04 17.28 – 46.08 0.362 PFLOPS TBD Status Legacy Production Nearing Production Development Discontinued Development Dojo D3: No more wafer-level integration? Perhaps the most interesting development in Tesla's AI hardware roadmap is the re-emergence of the in-house developed Dojo training accelerator after Elon Musk cancelled the whole wafer-level Dojo project in August, 2025, and then said SpaceX and xAI would exclusively use Nvidia hardware in August, 2026, both in its terrestrial and extraterrestrial data centers. Yet, the 3 rd Generation Dojo will be considerably different from the first two generations, Dojo D1 and Dojo D2. Tesla describes its next-generation Dojo 3 (D3) training accelerator as a chiplet-based design that combines 2.5D and 3D packaging technologies with stacked HBM. This represents a substantial departure from the original Dojo D1 system-on-wafer architecture , which relied on distributed on-chip SRAM and interconnected 25 D1 processors with 11 GB of SRAM using wafer-scale packaging technology. The adoption of HBM suggests that Tesla intends to substantially increase memory capacity, as modern AI models consume extreme amounts of memory to store parameters, activations, and intermediate data, making SRAM unattractive from a capacity standpoint. The use of HBM simplifies memory scaling but introduces different latency, bandwidth, packaging, and power trade-offs. Yet, it remains unclear whether the company has abandoned wafer-scale integration altogether. On the one hand, it is possible to stack custom HBM modules on top of logic dies interconnected using wafer-scale packaging technology. On the other hand, wafer-level integration is expensive and makes the most sense for select use cases, which include SRAM-centric architectures. Stacking HBM atop wafer-scale interconnected logic dies adds further design complexities, cooling challenges, manufacturing complexity (i.e., potentially reducing yields), long-term reliability concerns, and ultimately costs. While most of the challenges can be resolved by adding redundancy and refining process technologies, this all comes at a cost, making wafer-scaling less likely for D3. articles.title: Intel’s next-gen Nova Lake needs new motherboards — what we expect from Nova Point and Z990, Z970, and B960 chipsets
articles.content: Intel’s new Nova Lake-S CPUs are rumored to be on track to start mass production in Q4 2026, with a launch expected in Q1 2027. Unlike previous launches, we’re supposed to see mid-range SKU(s), supposedly an unlocked 28-core product(s), first in Q1, followed later in 2027 by flagship-class models that allegedly use two compute tiles and feature up to 52 cores. Lip-Bu Tan, Intel CEO, said earlier this year that Nova Lake is “coming at the end of 2026.” Despite the growing number of rumors and statements, we still don’t have a concrete date, but we can expect to see the CPUs soon, and with them, a brand-new socket and motherboard chipsets. Regardless of how many cores they have or when they arrive, you will need a new motherboard for Nova Lake. The LGA 1851 socket is at the end of its life with the release of Core Ultra Series 2 processors like the Core Ultra 7 270K Plus , released earlier in 2026; that means no more new processors and a dead end. A new socket, LGA 1954, is necessary because Nova Lake CPUs have a significant increase in I/O and power needs. It’s also Intel’s first bLLC (big last-level cache) intended to take on AMD’s X3D CPUs. We haven’t seen many details about the boards themselves, like pricing, official configurations, or product stacks, and we've only caught glimpses of one or two early models at Computex. Still, we have seen a few interesting platform details and rumors. To that end, we’ve put together a table of what we know so far about the specifications. Some things aren’t official yet and are noted by the tilde (~). We’ve also listed last-gen equivalents for reference. 900 Series Chipset, “up to” B960 (Mainstream) B860 (Mainstream) Z990 (Enthusiast) Z890 (Enthusiast) Z970 (Enthusiast) Total PCIe Lanes 34 34 48 48 34 Processor TB4/USB4 1 (TB5, 80Gbps) 1 2 (TB5, 80Gbps) 2 1 (TB5, 80Gbps) DMI Gen5 Lanes 2 0 (4x G4) 4 0 (8x G4) 2 Chipset PCIE 5.0 Lanes 0 0 12 0 0 Chipset PCIe 4.0 Lanes 14 14 12 24 14 SATA 3.0 (6G Lanes) 4 4 8 8 4 USB2 Ports 12 12 14 14 12 USB3.2 (20G) Ports ~2 2 ~5 5 ~2 USB3.2 (10G) Ports ~2 4 ~10 10 ~4 USB3.2 (5G) Ports ~6 6 ~10 10 ~6 IA OC No No Yes Yes Yes BCLK OC No No (board discretion) Yes Yes No Memory OC Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Processor PCIE 5.0 Slot Lane Config 1x16 1x16 + 1x4 1x16 or 1x8 + 2x4 or 2x8 or 4x4 1x16 + 1x4 or 2x8 + 1x4 or 1x8 or 3x4 1x16 Processor PCIE 5.0 Storage Lane Config 1x4 1x4 1x8 or 2x4 1x4 1x4 ECC No No No No No Simultaneous Displays Supported 4 4 4 4 4 PCIE RAID 0/1/5/10 Support No No Yes Yes No SATA RAID 0/1/5/10 Support Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Intel vPro + Standard Manageability No No No Yes No The new lineup consists of five different chipsets. You get Z990 and Z970 for the enthusiast class, B960 for the Mainstream, W980 for workstations, and Q970. You may notice it’s missing the ‘H910’ platform for entry-level PCs, and now we see a second enthusiast-class platform, the Z970, wedged between the B960 and Z990. Z990 is still the flagship, offering more PCIe lanes, a DMI Gen5 x4 link, and 12 Gen5 lanes from the chipset. Z970 is the less expensive enthusiast option and is reportedly built on the same silicon as B960. You get CPU multiplier overclocking, but no BCLK adjustment, and of course fewer ports and lanes than the flagship. (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) The chipset package itself, internally codenamed “Nova Point,” will also differ slightly and is smaller than Z890 (600 mm² vs 658 mm²). The die-on-package shrinks to 72.5 mm² (11.15 x 6.5mm) compared to 92.9 mm² (11.15 x 8.33 mm), or roughly 22% smaller. Base power increases to 7.9 Watts, up from 6 W on the Z890, with a maximum of 14 W while working. That power-density increase explains Intel’s rumored active-cooling guidelines for the chipset. When you start connecting components that use the chipset, think some PCIe slots and M.2 drives, the chipset raises its working voltage to maintain signal integrity for all of the bandwidth it now has to provide for the attached devices. articles.title: Did the AI bubble just pop? $2 trillion reality check hits Nvidia, Meta & SpaceX as Wall Street panics, signaling a potential end to RAM crisis in 2027
articles.content: If you want to know what it looks like when a trillion-dollar tech bubble violently collides with physical reality, just look at yesterday. $2.5 trillion in tech valuations were wiped off the board as Wall Street panicked about AI’s leverage — punishing tech giants for incinerating cash on infrastructure that isn’t generating immediate profit. Simultaneously, as we saw on Wednesday , the American voter rejected data center expansions in 40 out of 41 local ballot measures . The hardware hoarders are losing their grip, and the panic is palpable. The era of scrutiny is here , and I want to show you two possible timelines of where this could go. But first, we have to go back over a couple things. The memory penalty When faced with this stock crash, AMD CEO Lisa Su said, “We are a data center first company.” While I’d love to throw my hands up and get angry at this, I have to turn the BS detector on myself and address a brutal truth: she’s right. This market crash is a sentiment correction, not an overnight fab cancellation. The big three memory foundries — SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron — operate on long-term agreements. 2026-2027 is already locked in at sky-high prices, and on top of that, enterprise AI accelerators consume roughly 3x the silicon wafers of standard consumer DDR5 memory. As long as those massive AI server chips are shipping, conventional RAM capacity remains deeply suppressed. Why foundries aren’t sweating yet (Image credit: Micron) So, if Wall Street is slashing valuations and data center permits are being blocked, why aren’t memory foundries pivoting back to consumer PC hardware right now? Two words: fulfillment trap. Hyperscalers are also starving for memory, and receive around 60-70% of what they ask for. If Microsoft and Meta get spooked by the market and pull back their massive order growth by 10% or even 15%, it wouldn’t trigger a supply chain pivot. It just means the foundries are a little less overwhelmed. Demand still vastly exceeds total factory capacity. (Image credit: Future) If foundries are still frantically trying to fulfill enterprise contracts, they have zero financial incentive to redirect back to consumer memory. For them to actually panic and pivot, hyperscaler orders have to crater. A simple market correction like this won’t do it. But a sweeping wave of municipal zoning bans? That changes the math entirely. Top of the Democratic agenda on day 1 needs to be a pause on advanced AI development, regulation of this out of control industry, and a ban on artificial superintelligence. November 4, 2026 If tech giants are legally barred from breaking ground on new server farms, they are forced to cancel their existing silicon orders because they physically have nowhere to plug the chips in. My RAMageddon timeline We are not getting a massive surplus of GPUs and memory kits tomorrow morning. But the midterms and the stock market correction did put a concrete ceiling on the shortage. So let me take a stab at how I think this is going to unfold. Phase 1: Peak squeeze & stagnation (Winter 2026 - Q1 2027) (Image: © Amazon ) The stock rout has cracked the leveraged AI market for now, but contract prices remain firm. There is zero immediate relief, so don’t expect some banger Black Friday deals on RTX 5090s. Memory shortages will hit their tightest consumer squeeze through early 2027. PC makers will fiercely defend a ceiling of 16GB-24GB on premium laptops and handhelds. If you’re hoping for 32GB in sub-$1,500 machines, shelve that hope through most of next year. Phase 2: The contract standoffs (Q2 2027) (Image: © Shutterstock) As hyperscalers face sustained stock and regulatory pressure from the midterm fallout, corporate boards will force company CFOs to look at their data center infrastructure plans again. Instead of writing blank checks for server racks, the pace of subsequent purchase orders will slow. And for you reading this, I envision that PC hardware prices will finally stop climbing and plateau. PC…

articles.title: Protesters break into Microsoft data center site in Amsterdam
articles.content: Members of the action group Geef Tegengas put a banner on a crane during a protest. | Image: Getty Images Protesters have broken into a construction site of a new Microsoft data center in Amsterdam this morning. Members of the Geef Tegengas group helped organize the protest against the construction of three 85-meter data center towers in the outskirts of Amsterdam. Reuters reports that around 100 people made it into the construction site, with some scaling a crane to place a "fuck AI" banner. Protesters also unfurled a "Microsoft powers genocide" banner on the construction site, and chanted "Microsoft has got to go" and "free Palestine." Opposition to the new data center in Amsterdam comes more than a year after the city banned new data center … Read the full story at The Verge.

articles.title: Kubernetes, mark II? Why Google’s giving away gVisor, a code sandbox used by Anthropic and OpenAI
articles.content: Google wants to emulate one of its biggest ever open-source success stories, donating three core AI agent infrastructure projects to a neutral foundation in the hope they become industry standards, just as Kubernetes did for containers . In a blog post published on Thursday, Drew Bradstock , VP of product management, Kubernetes and orchestration at Google, confirmed that the company is donating gVisor , Agent Substrate , and OpenRL to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF). The move comes amid growing concerns about the security of autonomous AI agents, particularly their ability to execute code and interact with external systems. In July, models undergoing a cybersecurity evaluation at OpenAI escaped their restricted environment and breached Hugging Face’s production infrastructure, highlighting the challenges of keeping increasingly capable agents contained. “We believe that these donations will accelerate the development and adoption of agentic workloads through these projects similarly to what we saw with Kubernetes.” Bradstock, for his part, argues that addressing such security risks, while making agents more economical to run and train, requires closer cooperation across the various facets of the underlying software and hardware infrastructure. And he believes that putting its technologies under neutral governance could encourage the kind of industry-wide participation that helped Kubernetes become ubiquitous. “We believe that these donations will accelerate the development and adoption of agentic workloads through these projects similarly to what we saw with Kubernetes,” Bradstock writes. Why Google’s giving away gVisor By way of a brief recap, Google open-sourced gVisor in 2018 to improve container security. As The New Stack explained later that year , the technology uses a lightweight kernel running in user space to intercept application system calls, providing an additional layer of isolation between containers and the underlying host operating system. This makes it particularly useful for running untrusted code, including code generated by AI agents. The technology is used by major AI companies, including Anthropic , which runs code generated by Claude inside gVisor containers on its web platform; and OpenAI, which uses it to isolate code execution. In a security report published just on Wednesday , OpenAI cited sandboxes such as gVisor and Firecracker as important for limiting the damage from exploited Linux kernel vulnerabilities. The donation itself has been in the works for several weeks. The CNCF accepted gVisor’s application in late September , with Google publicly announcing its plans a few days later . The project’s onboarding process began last week , ahead of Thursday’s broader announcement incorporating all three projects. In its original October announcement, gVisor contributors and Google software engineers Etienne Perot and Jing Chen sought to reassure users that the company remained committed to the technology. With demand for affordable, secure sandboxes growing, they argued that independent governance could encourage wider participation and adoption, both within Google and beyond. “We (the gVisor contributors at Google) have been pushing for this move internally with the expectation that this will accelerate gVisor’s growth and adoption both within and outside of Google, in a similar manner as what has happened with Kubernetes,” they wrote at the time. “We have been pushing for this move internally with the expectation that this will accelerate gVisor’s growth and adoption both within and outside of Google.” Agent Substrate addresses a different challenge: how to run large numbers of autonomous agents without wasting computing resources while they sit idle.
