articles.title: Score a huge $600 saving on this RTX 5070 Ti gaming laptop from HP, now under $2,100
articles.content: There's a seriously good price on a HP gaming laptop right now with an RTX 5070 Ti and a top spec AMD Ryzen CPU. HP has cut this HyperX Omen Max 16 gaming laptop down to $2,099.99 right now , or slightly more if you fancy the OLED, giving you a $600 saving in the process. ● Check out this HP laptop deal The big selling point here is the current-gen Nvidia GPU, giving you the performance you'll need for gaming. The mobile version of the Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070 Ti isn't quite a match for the desktop version, and ships with a set of 5,888 CUDA cores and 12GB GDDR7 VRAM. This is still a 115W GPU with plenty of power for high-resolution gaming, however, especially compared to the CPU's integrated GPU you'd be stuck with otherwise. There won't be much of an issue here hitting high frame rates on this HP laptop's 1600p display. DLSS support, meanwhile, means you've got breathing room to boost to the best settings, with multi-frame generation able to cut some of the slack with AI-generated frames to give you an uplift in the most power-intensive games. This is an extremely competitive option for gaming with this discount, offsetting some of the criticisms we made in our HyperX Omen Max 16 review , and the build quality will remain the same, whatever spec you choose. If you change other components, like the RAM, GPU, and display, then performance will vary. HyperX Omen Max 16 (RTX 5070 Ti) 16z-ak100: was $2699.99 now $2099.99 This HyperX Omen Max 16 gaming laptop features a powerful (and customizable) spec sheet that includes the AMD Ryzen AI 7 450, Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070 Ti GPU with 12GB of GDDR7 VRAM, 16GB of DDR5 RAM, and a 512GB SSD. OLED and IPS LCD versions are available for this 16-inch laptop, offering a 1600p max resolution and refresh rate up to 240Hz, depending on your preferred option. View Deal That's because this laptop is heavily customizable, so you can switch up most of its specs, although that will impact the price. The rest of the specs include an AMD Ryzen AI 7 450. This Zen 5 CPU has eight cores, with a boost clock up to 5.2 GHz. This is a solid enough mid-tier mobile CPU and won't be a huge bottleneck for your ambitions at 1600p. If you need more juice, though, you can choose the 12-core AI 9 HX 475 instead for an extra $140. The build for $2,099.99 includes 16GB of DDR5 RAM, but you can upgrade to 32GB or 48GB if you want to pay a higher price tag. Likewise, the base model here comes with a 16-inch IPS display with a refresh rate up to 240Hz. If you have an extra $110, though, you can upgrade to an OLED with a refresh rate of 165Hz, or $190 will get you an OLED with a 240Hz refresh rate. A 512GB SSD is a compromise for the price, offering Gen 4 speeds. You can upgrade to 1TB or 2TB models for higher prices, though. Other areas of the laptop's build quality are worth mentioning, however, with a full-size keyboard that has per-key RGB lighting, as well as liquid metal cooling and a vapor chamber that helps to improve heat dissipation. You've also got several ports to choose from, including two USB-A and USB-C ports each, as well as HDMI 2.1, DisplayPort 2.1, and Ethernet, as well as Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4 connectivity. If your budget goes further, you can pick up an RTX 5080 model for $3,349.99 instead . This rig comes with a 20-core Intel Core Ultra 7 270HX Plus CPU, a 16-inch OLED with a 240Hz refresh rate, 32GB DDR5 and a 1TB SSD, along with one of Nvidia's most powerful GPUs. You're still getting a saving, too, with $650 saved compared to the list price. HyperX Omen Max 16 (RTX 5080) 16-ah1731nr: was $3999.99 now $3349.99 A high spec laptop from HP, this HyperX Omen Max 16 has an RTX 5080, Intel Core Ultra 7 270HX Plus CPU, a 16-inch OLED with 240Hz refresh rate, 32GB DDR5 and a 1TB SSD. View Deal Whichever rig you choose, there's a big saving to be had on these high spec HP gaming laptops. articles.title: Bank of England pours cold water on AI productivity boom
articles.content: Despite the billions being thrown at artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered little in the way of productivity gains for UK businesses, according to the Bank of England. In its latest Monetary Policy Report , the central bank found that AI has increased UK productivity by an estimated 0.5 percent over the past three years. That works out to just 0.1 to 0.2 percentage points of additional annual productivity growth since early 2024, hardly the economic revolution Silicon Valley has been promising. "AI investment appears to be contributing somewhat to current demand strength, but so far there is only evidence of a modest AI-driven rise in UK productivity growth," the Bank said. Even industries supposedly best placed to benefit from the technology have little to boast about. Productivity growth has improved in AI-heavy sectors such as information and communications, but has yet to exceed pre-pandemic averages. That's not to say AI isn't doing anything for the British economy. The bank estimates that AI-related activity has accounted for just under a fifth of UK GDP growth since the beginning of 2026, though much of that appears to come from companies developing and deploying the technology rather than businesses becoming more productive by using it. "The contribution to growth from AI to date appears to reflect activity in the upstream development and implementation of AI technologies rather than broader gains from their adoption elsewhere in the economy," the report said. In other words, selling AI is proving rather more lucrative than actually using it, The bank also cautioned against giving AI too much credit for Britain's recent productivity improvements. Much of the increase appears to reflect businesses hiring fewer workers while output continues to grow, partly as companies unwind post-pandemic staffing decisions and respond to higher employment costs. And despite predictions that AI will make vast swathes of the workforce redundant, firms responding to the Bank's Decision Maker Panel survey reported virtually no overall impact on employment so far. The technology is, however, making some employers less inclined to hire new staff or replace those who leave. Other studies suggest businesses are still waiting for the payoff. A Gartner survey published last month found that while three-quarters of corporate board members expected AI to improve productivity and cut costs, just 3 percent of organizations had actually achieved their targets. Meanwhile, 38 percent were already over budget on AI spending, yet 85 percent planned to spend even more next year. Another study involving nearly 6,000 executives , published in February, found that more than 80 percent of firms had seen no discernible impact from AI on either employment or productivity. Apparently, the answer to disappointing returns is to keep writing checks. That growing disconnect between AI spending and actual returns has also caught the attention of financial watchdogs. The International Monetary Fund warned last month that the AI spending spree could come back to bite investors if the promised profits don't show up, potentially dragging the wider economy down with it. The Bank for International Settlements sounded a similar alarm in June , comparing the current spending spree to the dotcom boom of the 1990s. Its concern is that tech giants are committing enormous sums to infrastructure on the assumption that AI will eventually deliver equally enormous returns, leaving them exposed if reality fails to cooperate. However, AI is already making its presence felt in one area: prices. The Bank of England noted that surging demand for AI-related products, including memory chips, has pushed up export prices in China and other Asian economies, raising import costs for Britain. So while businesses are still waiting for their AI-powered productivity windfall, the costs of the boom are already making their way through the economy. The bank isn't writing off the…

articles.title: I was struggling to wake up in the mornings until I found this free feature in the Apple Health app — now I’m sleeping better and waking up energized
articles.content: I write about sleep for a living, but I've been secretly locked in a losing battle against my doomscrolling habits. I'd constantly push bedtime later to watch a few more reels or reply to a couple more messages — and my nocturnal phone habit meant that getting out of bed each morning was becoming a chore. That was until I stumbled on a hidden feature in my Apple Health App. Now I'm far more disciplined when it comes to using my phone around bedtime, making a conscious effort to give myself time to truly relax in the evening and time to ease into the day come morning. Below, I dig into how I altered my iPhone settings to help me get to sleep on time and wake up with tons more energy. Plus, Dr. Shelby Harris , a board-certified behavioral sleep medicine specialist and psychologist, explains why enabling this feature works and why it's so important to restrict phone use around bedtime for better sleep. The iPhone feature that's helping me get my sleep schedule on track During my time as a sleep tech tester, I've tried my fair share of sleep gadgets. I'll forever rave about the top-rated sunrise alarm clocks and don't know where I'd be without by trusty Oura Ring to help track my rest. But, understandably, I'm yet to find anything that can physically restrain me from using my phone in bed. "The biggest problem with your phone at night isn’t the screen itself," explains Dr. Harris, who has over 20 years' experience in sleep medicine. "It’s what’s on it. Social media, videos, and games are designed to keep you hooked, with endless feeds and autoplay that make it easy to lose track of time. Before you know it, “just a few minutes” has turned into an hour of lost sleep." Our willpower is no match for Meta, basically. That's why it's so important nowadays to have measures and discipline in place to stop the endless scrolling when you should be sleeping. (Image credit: Future) I recommend everybody turns on Sleep Schedule in the Apple Health app. This feature allows you to set a recurring bedtime and wake-up routine. During sleep time, your phone will automatically shift into Sleep Focus mode where notifications and calls are silenced, your lock screen simplifies and phone screens dims. Without your phone constantly buzzing at your bedside, it's less tempting to pick up and even gives you the chance to forget about your constant notification feed while you drift off to sleep. (Image credit: Future) Depending on the Wind Down period you set, you'll get a notification telling you to prioritise your sleep. I get this 15 minutes before my desired bedtime, though I'm keen to push this earlier after hearing Dr. Harris' advice. The Diplomate in Behavioral Sleep Medicine says: "The best approach is to put your phone away, ideally outside the bedroom, 30 to 60 minutes before bed and replace scrolling with something calming, like reading a book or stretching ." How to set up your Apple Sleep Schedule "The iPhone’s sleep tools help turn good intentions into habits," says Dr. Harris. To set up your personalised sleep schedule, head to the Apple Health app (that pink heart in a white square). Find the Sleep section and scroll down to 'Your Schedule'. Open 'Full Schedule & Options'. Here you can toggle on Sleep Schedule and link it to your phone's Sleep Focus setting. There's the option to customise your schedule for different days of the week. However, experts recommend sticking to the same sleep and wake times seven nights a week as this helps sync your circadian rhythm (more on this below). (Image credit: Future) You can also set a Wind Down period between 15 minutes and three hours. During this time, your phone shifts into Sleep mode. Health will notify you when Wind Down begins, encouraging you to transition from scrolling to rest. For full peace of mind if you have caring responsibilities, you can select certain contacts to break through the notification block. This means you won't block out any important phone calls through the night. How…

articles.title: The Audiolab 6000CDT MKII is a new CD transport — further proof that the physical media revival is in full swing
articles.content: Audiolab unveils new 6000CDT MK II It's a CD transport, dedicated to processing a disc (not the full player) Requires a DAC and other separates to let you play the music I'm writing constantly about the physical media revival, and cover new CD players every week, but new disc buyers might not be aware of how frail these things can really be. One scratch can wipe whole songs off an album, and a cheap CD player might be putting undue risk on your collection. For that — and several other reasons — CD transports exist, and Audiolab has just unveiled a new model in the form of its 6000CDT MK II. No, I'm not talking about those wallets which you used to use to carry hundreds of discs around with you. These are, to a certain extent, CD players: they have disc drives and let you control your tunes. But they don't have Digital-to-Analog converters, or DACs, which are vital for converting the sound from your physical media into something your amplifier and speakers (also not included here) can understand. So why buy a CD device which can't play music from the box? Well firstly, housing the CD reading tech away from other electricals can ensure a clean and stable read, and it also lets audiophiles pick their favorite sound by choosing their own DAC, amp stage and speakers. Transport you to the (Audio)lab (Image credit: Audiolab) It also lets the CD transport focus on what it does best: reading discs. Everything in the Audiolab 6000CDT MKII is designed around the process; this lets you get the best from the medium, and ensures your little slivers of music are protected while they're in the machine. Audiolab has rebuilt the device from the original to make sure all the components like the laser, spindle and disc loader are stable, make no noise and are consistent. The laser correction, which counters any unpredictability in the spin of the disc, has been designed to avoid any unnecessary actions, again making sure no noise gets in the way of your playback. Looking at the technical specs, the 6000CDT MKII supports standard CDs as well as CD-R and CD-RWs (rewritable discs, basically, for which support can often be unreliable). The device is set to go on sale at the end of November, for a price of £399 (about $540, AU$800, and we're waiting on exact global pricing). Of course, if you buy it, you'll also need to pick up the other necessary accoutrements, but Audiolab would love to nudge you towards its very own similarly-styled 6000A MKII amplifier, which has a DAC built in — and judging by press pictures, the company is really hoping you'll pick up both. Fair warning though: it may sound very, very good . And his runs the risk of starting a bona-fide hi-fi collection, which can be quite a slippery slope. Obviously, you'll also need some pretty nice speakers to appreciate them with. Fortunately, I have listed a few below…

articles.title: Motorola Razr Fold gets a much-needed software update, but still no Android 17
articles.content: TL;DR The Motorola Razr Fold (2026) is receiving a new security update after being stuck on the August 2026 security patch. Android 17 remains unavailable in the stable channel, even though cheaper Motorola phones have already received the update. Motorola has attributed the delay to additional foldable-specific optimizations, with no confirmed stable rollout date. For a phone that costs nearly $2,000, the Motorola Razr Fold has been getting some rather budget-friendly treatment in the software department. Owners have watched cheaper and older Motorola handsets move to Android 17 while their newer, premium foldable remains on Android 16. A fresh update is finally arriving, but it isn’t the one they’ve been waiting for. A recent Reddit thread shows the Razr Fold receiving software version W3WBS36.36-123-2-1, while the carrier-locked Verizon model is receiving version W3WBS36.36-123-5-1 with the October 2026 security patch. However, instead of delivering Android 17, the update is another maintenance release based on Android 16, much to the disappointment of owners hoping for a major Android upgrade.

articles.title: How I freed up 4GB of storage to avoid paying for Google One
articles.content: Credit: Robert Triggs / Android Authority I’ve been cruising in Google’s free storage tier for as long as I can remember, backing up my Photos, emails, and even WhatsApp messages without ever spending a penny. But over the past few months, I’ve been creeping up to the 15GB cap (17GB in my case , as an old-timer who jumped through Google’s security hoops), leading to a barrage of Google One notifications urging me to upgrade to a paid storage tier. That’s never going to happen. The economics of starting out at just $1.99 a month for 100GB might not sound like much, but I know it won’t be many more years before I hit that limit, too. Then I’d be hooked: forking out $4.99 and then $9.99 every month, in perpetuity, for the luxury of having Google back up my odds and ends. Granted, Google One might be worth the cost if you want Gemini in your docs and double AI usage without forking out for yet another monthly plan. But for me, I’m happy just using the free allowance to keep the most recent things I need within quick reach. I could store everything else on a USB stick or external hard drive for cheap.

articles.title: I tested the Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series — and this superautomatic espresso machine is my biggest $2,000-shaped disappointment of 2026
articles.content: I have yet to find a fully automatic espresso machine good enough to earn a permanent place in my kitchen. I’ve tested upwards of twenty now, and they all leave a little to be desired. But nothing’s been quite as disappointing as the Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series… let me explain. The 8000 Series looks beautiful. It’s easily one of the prettiest superautomatic coffee machines I’ve ever tested. There’s a wood-veneer group head, a cup warmer, and two silver rails on top — just like a commercial espresso machine. My hopes were sky high. However, I’m not convinced it’s one of the best espresso machines . It’s outrageously expensive in the U.S. ($2k!), makes mid-tasting coffee, and can only make one type of milk texture. I’ll go through all the information in this Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series review. Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series review: Specs Price $1,999 / £895 Weight 20.5 pounds Dimensions 15.3 x 9.9 17.8 inches Grinder Yes Heating system Unspecified Pressure 15 bar Water tank capacity 64 fluid ounces Accessories Scoop, water filter Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series review: Price & availability (Image credit: Tom's Guide) The Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series is a high-end automatic espresso machine. It’ll set you back $1,999 at Amazon U.S. and £895 at Curry’s U.K. This is a premium price for a premium machine. Similar options would be the KitchenAid KF8 ($1,999) and the De’Longhi PrimaDonna Aromatic ($2,499). If $2k is a little too much for you, don’t worry. De’Longhi also makes the $1,499 Rivelia , my favorite superautomatic coffee machine to date. For the money-savvy, there’s also the $795 Terra Kafe Demi , which can’t froth milk, and the Smeg BCC13 , which is even cheaper at $749 but doesn’t have a full-color LED screen. Philips also makes the $394 2200 Series . What’s actually different between the two? Honestly, not as much as you might think. The 2200 Series still has a built-in milk frother, unlike the $795 Terra Kafe Demi, and has a bright screen, unlike the $749 Smeg BCC13. Sure, the 2200 only makes “espresso”, “coffee”, and “hot water”, but that’s the foundation of any coffee drink. While the 8000 Series is much easier thanks to its one-touch recipes, I’m not sure this justifies a whole $1,600 extra. Personally, I would get the $394 2200 Series, or a standalone milk frother, like the $139 Subminimal Nanofoamer Pro Gen 2 for more finesse. Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series review: Design (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Oh, the Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series is a sight to behold. It’s gorgeous . I’d go so far as to say it’s the most beautiful automatic coffee machine I’ve ever seen. Of course, it’s essentially a big plastic-and-metal box — it’s still an automatic coffee machine, after all — but there’s a sense of finesse missing from other machines (yes, even $2,000 ones). There’s a cup warmer on top of the machine, complete with two stainless steel rails on either side, and a low-profile grinder. The grinder holds a whole 250g bag of beans at once, even though it’s only rated for 200g. But my favorite part is the wood finish on the portafilter. Rather than plastic or metal — boring! — the 8000 Series has a gorgeous, glossy wood veneer, making the machine look more like an automatic version of the Lelit MaraX3 than something like the Casabrews Ultra Pro . You might be sensing a theme here, but it only gets better. Even though the water tank looks pretty small, it’s actually 64 fluid ounces (just under 2 liters). And it’s a slide-out tank, so you don’t need counter space with overhead clearance, unlike the KitchenAid KF3 ($999). At 15.3 x 9.9 17.8 inches, the 8000 isn’t the slimmest automatic coffee machine I’ve ever tested — that would go to the aforementioned KitchenAid KF3 — but it doesn’t look as bulky as its dimensions might suggest. I had this out in the office for a week (making around ten drinks a day) and it looked right at home. If you value a good-looking automatic coffee machine, the 8000 is surely for you. I…

articles.title: Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra is now just $949 ahead of Black Friday — save $450 right now
articles.content: This time of year is the perfect opportunity to buy a brand new phone. Sure some of the devices may be a little older, and set to be replaced in just a few months, but they're also experiencing some of the best discounts you're likely to see over the next 12 months. Case in point, the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, which is now $949 over at Best Buy . We have seen the flagship drop to this price before, but not since Samsung raised the MSRP to $1,399. This means you're saving $450 on one of the best phones money can buy right now. Galaxy S26 Ultra: was $1399 now $949 Save $450 on the best Android Phone, and get a device capable of excellent photos with strong battery life and the super-useful Privacy Display. There's also a built-in S Pen, the full suite of Galaxy AI features, and faster 60W wired charging. Price check: $949 @ Amazon | $979 @ Walmart View Deal The Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra is one of the best phones you can buy right now. While it's debatable as to whether it's better than an iPhone 18 Pro Max there's no doubt that it is the best Android phone currently on sale. Why? Well plenty of reasons. The main one is that it has one of the best cameras of any smartphone, complete with a 200MP main camera, which is teamed up with 50MP ultrawide and telephoto (5x zoom) lenses. There's also a secondary 10MP telephoto lens with 3x zoom, which isn't something you see on many phones. (Image credit: Tom's Guide) You also get a large 6.9-inch display with a built-in Privacy Display . When active, this feature cuts off the side viewing angles, and stops people from trying to subtly spy on your phone screen. It doesn't just do it to the whole screen either, and can operate on an app-by-app basis, censoring sensitive areas of your screen without blocking the whole thing. Other benefits to the S26 Ultra include the built-in S Pen, a large 5,000 mAh battery with 16 hours and 10 minutes of battery life (per our testing). Plus there's a whole suite of Galaxy AI features, including the upgraded Circle to Search, Automated App Actions, the Horizon Lock camera feature, and upgraded 60W wired charging. The Galaxy S27 Ultra may be coming in early 2027, with a bunch of upgrades, but rumor has it we may see another price hike . With that in mind, it's certainly worth taking the plunge now and swapping out your current handset for an S26 Ultra — and the (relatively) low price of $949. Because you likely won't see S27 Ultra deals like this until next November.

articles.title: Don’t mention the data center: OpenAI calls them ‘compute campuses’ instead
articles.content: OpenAI has responded to the data center culture war pitting communities against tech companies with a proposal to reduce its power demand during periods of grid strain. The company is also mindful of the bad publicity generated by talk of data centers and has renamed them “compute campuses” in an attempt to make them less scary. This is in line with the recent trend for renaming places like the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America, or rebranding artificial intelligence as super intelligence . The new name cropped up four times, and data centers just twice, in OpenAI’s announcement of its Grid Protectors Program , a proposal to dial back electricity consumption in its data centers when demand is high so that nearby homes can continue to run their air conditioning or heating. Data centers’ increasing power consumption is straining the grid , with AI servers accounting for an ever larger share of that consumption, with further increases forecast . These demands are leading to a growing number of protests against the development of data centers , which could lead to construction delays. OpenAI claims that its Grid Protectors Program will meet some of those issues head-on by taking into account future capacity needs and working to make power flexibility a key element in data center, sorry, compute campus, design. The company said that the approach would differ, region by region. It has yet to finalize all the details of the scheme, but it hopes to head off some of the protests. It remains to be seen whether it has this effect. Google recently took the opposite approach to the peak consumption problem, proposing to pay people to turn off their appliances at times of high demand so that it can continue to power its data centers. This article first appeared on Network World .

articles.title: Google is in trouble, deep
articles.content: Remember when Google’s motto was “Don’t be evil”? Boy, wasn’t that a long time ago! It was more than ten years ago, and they replaced it in 2015 with “Do the right thing.” That hasn’t aged well either. Today, we’re seeing how Google’s losing-its-way is finally catching up with the onetime darling of the no-longer-quite-so-magnificent Magnificent Seven . There are many reasons why big tech players are floundering in shrinking valuations AI infrastructure overspending and the political backlash against AI data centers . But Google, Google is special. For example, as any of you who rely on Google advertising to market your products and services — or media companies that rely on it for profit — have seen, Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode are sinking customers’ ad revenue . For businesses that rely on Google organic search, things are much worse. Oh sure, Google Search Ecosystem general manager Mrinalini Loew claims , “AI Overviews and AI Mode are designed to help people find and visit great websites, and to help publishers and websites strengthen their audiences.” That’s not what the websites are seeing. In fact, they’re seeing the opposite. Search Engine Land reports that three in four sites’ home pages have seen their traffic shrink in the past year. In the meantime, Ahrefs found that the “presence of an AI Overview now correlates with a 58% lower average clickthrough rate for the top-ranking page.” More specifically, Reddit CEO Steve Huffman said in the company’s latest earnings call that Google search referrals declined “meaningfully” because searchers didn’t go any farther than AI Mode and AI Overviews, instead of clicking onto Reddit. Now, where does Google make its money? Why, that would be ad sales, wouldn’t it? So what happens when publishers and advertisers start seeing less and less return? They stop spending money on Google ads, don’t they? As Forrester analysts pointed out last week, “The company’s advertising revenue growth slowed to 12% , its slowest rate in five quarters.” You’d think Google would have seen this coming, wouldn’t you? But its executives, too, are blinded by AI madness. Now it’s starting to sink Google’s own ad business. Oh sure, for now, Google’s internet search ad revenue rose to $63.35 billion, up 12%, vs. estimates of $64.87 billion, or 14.8% growth. So what? Spoiler alert: People don’t buy Google for its revenue. No, Google is still judged by its growth, and Google is no longer growing. The result? You’re getting less value from Google ads, and Google’s stock price has declined. As of November 6th, Alphabet’s GOOGL shares have fallen about 18% over the past 30 days. That includes a single-day drop last week that wiped out $500 billion in market value. Betting on Google, both in the market and as the foundation for your ads, seems like less and less of a good bet. Worse, Google seems to want to throw away whatever goodwill it has left by shoving AI down the throats of school systems . Google now insists that schools must turn on its AI tools in its K-12 student software. Otherwise, they won’t be able to use Google Search. Sure, there are search alternatives. DuckDuckGo says people are already moving to its service because they’re sick of Google forcing AI slop on them. But Google dominates the educational market. According to About Chromebooks , Chromebooks now run 60.1% of the global K-12 device market in 2026 … and 93% of US school districts are buying more this year. Google’s AI diktat is going over like a lead balloon in schools. As Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, told NBC News , “Instead of working with teachers and parents to uphold privacy and ensure their tools are safe and useful, it throws the baby out with the bathwater and bans access to the tools altogether.” Former FTC chair Lina Khan tweeted , “Google is using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI. This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an…

articles.title: ‘Life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness should be reflected in our computing systems’
articles.content: Is this our Golden Age? One where we are free of our labors and joined back to nature, returned to our mammal brothers and sisters, and all watched over by machines of loving grace (excerpt from a poem by Richard Brautigan) More than a decade ago, I began to engage in a series of wonderful philosophical discussions with Julio Frenk (then the president of the University of Miami, now the chancellor of UCLA). From our talks an idea emerged, a fusion of computing, technology, political systems, philosophy, economics, and governance. We manifested some of the thinking in Project Alexandria (2018) and with a Knight Foundation Grant (2022): Conversations on the Future of Democracy, Social Media, and Artificial Intelligence in the Americas. I was planning to go back to school and work on a PhD in Philosophy on this thesis—what we called “computational democracy”—and was greatly discouraged by a philosophy professor at one of the schools where I applied: “ Go build it, don’t be a philosopher; this is too important. ” So I did, and I founded SynthBee with the core idea that we would be the rebel alliance, the Jedi (not the Sith) and a north star in the ideals of computational democracy. What President Frenk and I conceived was more than a philosophy. It was architecture, system design, use, and operations of certain types of computing and intelligence systems manifested from the idea of personal freedoms. The idea of computational democracy in many ways reflected the ideals of liberty and the checks and balances of a well-run democracy. Looking back, the Bay Area of the late 1960s and 1970s was a hotbed of these ideals, in many ways birthing a mix of music, film, creativity, and technology. Stewart Brand’s DIY Whole Earth Catalog (which influenced the internet and the web), the Homebrew Computer Club, and the birth of personal computing with the Apple I were all markers of this fusion of freedom, democracy, and computing. The Grateful Dead played a key role, encouraging a blend of audience and band, fan participation, and the birth of open sharing. The ideals of life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness could, and should, be reflected in our computing system architectures and design. Distribution of power Today, the core philosophy of computational democracy includes the distribution of power and decentralization, strong protection of users and their IP and data, and systems designed to be safe and trustworthy by design (not by hopes and wishes). Of even higher importance is the ideal of empathy for humanity, and of placing people in the center. I look back at what we built at Mako Surgical, which helped to define the field of collaborative robotics, or Cobots, deployed in operating rooms around the world. And I see in those systems—their behavior, their connection to the surgical teams and patients—the emerging principles of computational democracy. I would argue and hope that Richard Brautigan would have seen the glow of a machine in true loving grace in the symbiosis between human and machine that exists with surgeons and the Mako robot, and the good they bring to patients. (Fun fact: The Mako robot was deeply influenced by R2-D2, and the love and good R2-D2 brought to the Star Wars world.) The alternative On the other end of the spectrum lies computational autocracy: massive, centrally controlled computing platforms run by a few techno-oligarchs who wish to amass and control all the world’s computing power, data, intelligence, and IP. The scaling and financial performance of these companies has created techno-monarchs. And in turn, actual monarchs, dictators, and autocrats have deeply immersed themselves in the creation, acquisition, and interweaving of these systems in how they govern, control, and suppress their populations. The cozy interplay between technology dictators and actual dictators has blurred the line between technology and government, with both sides fusing and enriching themselves. The ideals of absolute control,…

articles.title: UK ministers seek powers to investigate when AI agents are let off the leash
articles.content: The UK government is paving the way for rules requiring essential service operators and digital providers to guard against losing control of AI agents and report incidents when safeguards fail. An amendment to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, which is passing through Parliament , would give ministers powers to regulate the deployment and reporting of agentic AI in certain organizations. The new clause was introduced during the bill's third reading in the House of Lords this week. In an explanatory note , ministers outlined plans for safeguards, notification of affected organizations, preservation of evidence, and government-led incident reviews. The measures would require consultation and parliamentary approval through secondary legislation. The move follows a series of incidents. Last month, OpenAI revealed that its agents repeatedly strayed beyond their intended scope , prompting the company to notify more than 100 organizations about the issues. That came after July's incident, in which an OpenAI agent accessed the internet and breached machine learning platform Hugging Face . The episode, and the potential for more damage from poorly designed AI agent deployments, have prompted MPs to question whether UK law can deal with such threats. Speaking to The Register , Stuart Davey, a partner at law firm Pinsent Masons, described the clause as "quite novel." Rather than directly imposing new duties, it would allow ministers to introduce rules and investigatory powers covering regulated organizations. Davey said that could include powers "to look where there has been such an AI agentic compromise or issue, and do some things... appoint inspectors, enter and search premises, seize and retain documents." Under the proposals, the minister could confer certain powers on regulators, requiring action from targeted organizations. Potentially affected organizations include gas and electricity suppliers, managed service providers, and cloud providers deploying AI agents for customers. Foundation model developers would not automatically fall within scope simply because they build the underlying technology. "Where there's a security or operational compromise in relation to a relevant network or information system, that would seem to capture those managed service providers or cloud computing providers who are using AI, and there's that loss of control," said Davey. He advised cloud and managed service providers to track whether the proposed measures become law. Evin McMullen, CEO and co-founder of AI identity and control infrastructure company AmanTrue, said the amendment recognizes loss of oversight or control as a security risk but does not itself impose new duties. "The amendment allows future regulations to introduce investigatory and enforcement powers where an incident involves an AI agent, targeting organizations running essential digital services," he said. "The deployer of an AI agent chooses its permissions, connects it to systems, and gives it access to data. When something goes wrong, the deployer is the party that will be expected to explain what happened. "Accountability stays with the organization that put the agent into the system, and ultimately with executives and the board. Whether model builders are captured will depend on how the regulations are written and whether a builder sits in a regulated category or a regulated supply chain." ®

articles.title: Gelsinger-backed Nagare Labs’ Z2RAM promises SRAM speed at DRAM density
articles.content: A Pat Gelsinger-backed Georgia Tech spinout, Nagare Labs, says its Z2RAM can put SRAM-speed memory , at DRAM density, directly on top of AI chips. The founders’ own papers show a fast-improving cell that, tested up to 85 degrees Celsius, holds data for over 300 seconds. Gen 1 is projected to have 5x SRAM density with six stacked layers, 14x DRAM speed, and 3x less read energy than SRAM. AI chips require a lot of bandwidth, and it has been challenging to get sufficient yields of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) to feed them. Even when manufacturers can get it, some reportedly plan to settle for fewer layers for yield reasons, and heat is another. Heat is also why Samsung’s zHBM , which stacks DRAM directly on the processor, is planned at only about four layers. Alternatives include high-bandwidth flash , still in development, which stacks NAND like HBM and would sit beside the GPU, or SRAM stacked directly on the die, which is less dense and more expensive for the capacity, but also faster. DRAM, which is more capacious, can sit on top of the compute, but heat limits how hard the logic underneath can run. That limit is already shaping chipmakers’ design path for stacked memory. Micron’s vHBM plans, for example, include heat-spreading structures. With HBM stacked on a logic die, and DRAM needing to be kept at or below 95 degrees Celsius, the logic’s heat output is capped at 220 W/cm², or 300 W/cm² with better thermal vias, according to a 2025 simulation by co-founder Shimeng Yu’s group. Nagare Labs says peak compute has grown 70% a year over the past three decades, against 20% for memory bandwidth. (Image credit: J. Sharda et al., IEEE JxCDC (CC BY 4.0), cropped) The company describes its Z2RAM as “Two transistors and a shield. No capacitor,” where a write transistor places a charge on a storage node and the shield blocks noisy neighbors. The read transistor can sense without draining. In a gain cell like this, the read transistor’s gate capacitance holds the charge, so reads are non-destructive and the cell avoids DRAM’s write-back. Nagare aims for well under a picojoule per bit. Nagare builds Z2RAM by depositing its layers on top of the accelerator and patterning them “together on one die,” much as 3D NAND flash scales by adding layers. There’s no interposer and no bonds between the memory layers, which is part of the secret sauce. One lithography exposure covers several layers at once, and standard 300 mm tools with DUV do the job, with no EUV required. The current roadmap is aiming at over 100 layers with “hundreds of thousands” of vertical connections. Retaining data at higher temperatures is the challenge, and one the founders have probed repeatedly with their testing. A 2020 paper from co-founder Suman Datta’s group, on a tungsten-doped indium oxide two-transistor cell, had retention of 1 second at 25 degrees Celsius and just 300 milliseconds at 85°C. An update in 2025, which has Datta as a co-author, adds a third transistor and removes the gate overlap from its transistors, managing over 1,000 seconds at 25°C, up from 200 seconds with overlapped ones. It also simulated a GPU L2 at twice SRAM’s capacity but in the same area with 75–80% lower energy-delay-area product, a combined score that multiplies energy, delay and area. Six months later, both founders showed a “folded asymmetric boosted” three-transistor cell that held data for over 300 seconds at 85°C, as compared to only 100 milliseconds for a conventional three-transistor design. That’s still below the roughly 95°C that Nagare says DRAM must stay under, so neither the founders’ published cells nor Z2RAM have shown retention above that line yet. The boosted cell is also “refresh-free,” which means data in the GPU’s last-level cache, profiled from AI workloads, doesn’t have time to decay before it is overwritten. articles.title: Nintendo’s latest Zelda remake already circulating online as a Switch 2 ROM
articles.content: Nintendo’s remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has reportedly been dumped the same day it launched on the Switch 2. The game launched today, but ONE jailbreak says copies of the original 1.0.0 release and its 1.1.1 update are already circulating outside Nintendo's official distribution channels. The update reportedly weighs 23 GB. The leak is not entirely surprising. Physical copies had already started turning up at buyers' homes several days before the release date. Footage of the game was already appearing online by Nov. 1. Those early cartridges gave hackers access to the remake before most players could get their hands on it, with some gamers sharing videos of themselves playing the game on social media. However, the game still remains far from playable on PC, with emulators struggling to render its graphics correctly. Some users encountered washed-out visuals or black screens, while others saw terrain bleeding through objects or could not get past the title screen. 🚨 BIZARRO! ZELDA: OCARINA OF TIME RODANDO NO PC!O jogo já teve seu dump realizado e está sendo executado no PC através de emulação. Sim, estamos falando de um game que ainda não lançou oficialmente rodando fora do hardware original da Nintendo! https://t.co/giO956ssnI November 5, 2026 Notably, the game is identified by title ID 0400486024DEC000, with its report naming two tools involved in extracting the files: ‘ns2jb and OunceCake’. The first is a software jailbreak developed by security researcher Sammy ‘pepsipu’ Hajhamid. Last month, Hajhamid explained how he managed to get code running on Nintendo's latest console without installing a modchip, and also described what the exploit does: "This lets us run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod Switch 2 games, back up save files off the Switch, and access most of the Switch 2’s peripherals through MMIO. To my knowledge, it’s the first such exploit for the Switch 2." That opens up several possibilities for homebrew developers and researchers as well as pirates, but ns2jb has limitations. It is a tethered jailbreak, meaning it has to be activated again after the console restarts. The exploit also does not provide unrestricted kernel access. The same extraction method has reportedly been used with two other games: Deltarune Chapters 1-4 and Mario Kart World. This is not the first time hackers have found a way into Nintendo's hardware. Just a day after Switch 2 went on sale in June 2025, an exploit that allowed hackers to run custom code on the system popped up, although it did not provide root access or a full jailbreak. Cartridge-based backups have also caused headaches. In August this year, we reported that Nintendo had targeted more than 400 GitHub repositories , with 401 repos removed following seven Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) notices. Several Yuzu forks were among the affected projects. Nintendo has not publicly commented on the Ocarina of Time dump or the nsj2b exploit yet. However, SmileBASIC 4, the application used to launch the jailbreak, has disappeared from the Nintendo eShop following the exploit’s disclosure.

articles.title: Blue Origin Announces New Glenn Third Stage, New Booster Engine
articles.content: Blue Origin has unveiled a third stage called GS3 for its New Glenn rocket, designed to deliver satellite constellations directly to geostationary orbit and support heavy-lift missions to the Moon and deep space. The company also announced Northstar, a new methalox booster engine that it says produces 715,000 pounds of thrust while cutting mass by 30% and parts by 50% compared with the BE-4. Space.com reports: The new stage will be powered by one BE-7 engine, which the company developed for use on its Blue Moon spacecraft, one of the two private vehicles that NASA selected to be crewed lunar landers for its Artemis program. (The other is SpaceX's Starship.) Blue Moon landing missions won't need to launch on GS3-equipped New Glenn rockets, according to Blue Origin. But the third stage "can support sustained operations around the moon," the company wrote in today's blog post. "By delivering significant payload mass directly to trans-lunar injection (TLI), GS3 enables faster transit times while preserving propellant for on-orbit operations." And there's already demand for such services: Blue Origin also announced today that a government customer (which it did not name) has booked a GS3 mission to cislunar (Earth-moon) space, with launch targeted for 2028. And the company dropped yet more news today -- that it's working on a new first-stage engine, called Northstar. Like Blue Origin's other booster engine, the BE-4, Northstar burns liquid oxygen and liquid methane propellant, a combination known as methalox. But the new engine is more powerful and less complex. "Compared to the BE-4 engine, Northstar reduces mass by 30% and parts count by 50%, while increasing thrust from 640,000 to 715,000 pounds-force," Blue Origin said in a second blog post today. "Manufacturing advancements have also significantly shortened production timelines, enabling assembly in less than a day." Northstar went from program approval to development testing in just 11 months, according to the company. But today's update did not say when the new engine will fly for the first time. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: OLED iPad Mini, M6 iMac, and New MacBook Pros Available From Today
articles.content: From today, Apple's new iPad mini with an OLED display, M6 iMac, and its latest MacBook Pro models are available to buy from Apple's online store and in the Apple Store app, with the first pre-orders also arriving to customers today and both devices reaching Apple Store locations and Apple Authorized Resellers. OLED iPad Mini The eighth-generation iPad mini is Apple's smallest tablet with an OLED display. The 8.5-inch Super Retina XDR display offers up to 1,200 nits of peak brightness, a 2,000,000:1 contrast ratio, and a 1-nit minimum brightness, with a nano-texture glass option on 256GB and 512GB models for the first time. The device is powered by Apple's A20 Pro chip and the N1 wireless chip, enabling Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. At 5.4mm thin and 255 grams, it's the lightest iPad Apple has made. It's also the first iPad with an IP67 water and dust resistance rating, aided by a new Acoustic Display that produces sound through the screen itself, so there are no speaker holes in the enclosure. A 12MP Center Stage front camera is now located on the landscape side for video calls, and the device supports Apple Pencil Pro and Apple Pencil (USB-C). The display is limited to a 60Hz refresh rate with no ProMotion, which has been the main point of criticism in early reviews . In the United States, the new iPad mini starts at $699 for the 128GB Wi-Fi model. The 256GB and 512GB configurations are priced at $799 and $999, with nano-texture glass adding $100 on those models, while Wi-Fi + Cellular models start at $849. Education pricing starts at $649. M6 iMac Meanwhile, the new iMac is the first update to Apple's all-in-one since the M4 model. The M6 chip brings up to a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU, with Apple claiming up to 2x faster graphics than the previous generation, alongside Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and an optional 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet port on the power adapter. The iMac with M6 starts at $1,499 for the model with a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU, while the version with a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU starts at $1,699. Education pricing starts at $1,449. Latest MacBook Pro Models Also launching today are the new MacBook Pro models. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 starts at $1,999 and features a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU, alongside Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 via Apple's N1 wireless chip. The new 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro models with touchscreen PROLED XDR displays are also available, starting at $2,899 and $3,399, respectively. Powered by M5 Pro or M5 Max chips, the touchscreen models replace the notch with a Dynamic Island and offer up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness for both SDR and HDR content. Apple's online checkout system indicates many configurations of the 14-inch and 16-inch touchscreen MacBook Pro models in Space Black and Silver currently ship in 2-3 weeks, so anyone who wants one as soon as possible is likely to have more luck visiting their local Apple Store, where at least some base configurations are typically in stock. For a full rundown of everything new, see our iPad mini , iMac , and MacBook Pro roundups. articles.title: The $400 Aina smart ring comes with a tiny display to manage your AI agents
articles.content: Credit: Aina TL;DR Aina is a smart ring with a screen and a button. The bigger attraction is its context-aware cues, which interact with your phone and PC to control them or interact with your AI agents. The onboard AI is claimed to predict your next steps and take action automatically, such as ordering an Uber only after you finish breakfast. It’s available for pre-ordering and will start shipping early next year. Smart rings have lately been seen as viable alternatives to smartwatches because of their non-existent footprint, which makes them easier to wear all day. However, smart rings lack the interactive features of a smartwatch , or other abilities that make them an extension of your smartphone, not just another accessory. An AI company now plans to solve that by bringing together the best of both worlds, adding smartwatch-like controls to its first smart ring. Aina is a new smart ring with a tiny screen that wraps around your finger. Its maker, which shares the same name, does not share specifics about this display, except that it’s an OLED, but that’s possibly because it’s not being marketed as the main selling point for this smart ring. Instead, Aina is focusing on its context-aware operating system that digs information from your phone, PC, any AI agents, or other software you may use and establishes patterns to learn about your preferences.
articles.author: Tushar Mehta

articles.title: Google Pics: How to level up your visuals in Docs and Slides
articles.content: Simplicity and convenience are a tough combo to beat. That’s why basic features integrated into the productivity apps we’re already using almost always win out over more capable and complex third-party options, at least when it comes to most mainstream use — and why Google’s latest easily overlooked addition to its Workspace office suite is well worth your while to notice. The addition is called, rather confusingly, Google Pics. (If you ever mix up Google Pics with Google Photos or Google Images, don’t worry: Google Lens can help you sort it out.) Pics, unlike its similarly named Google app contemporaries, is meant to exist primarily within the Google Drive ecosystem as opposed to being its own standalone entity. The easiest way to think about it is as a newly souped-up, superpowered image editor and graphic creator that lives directly within Google Docs and Slides — and, eventually, also within Drive itself. It’s a fuss-free way to let you make new artwork and refine existing images in your documents and presentations, and it’s surprisingly powerful and effective in what it’s able to do. Critically, it’s also both simple and convenient, as an option within any document or deck you’re already working on. All you’ve gotta do is (a) realize it’s there and available to you and (b) learn how to best take advantage of the new powers it affords you. Here’s your start-to-finish guide. Part I: Google Pics for Docs and Slides image editing First things first, to find Pics, you’ll need to either have an individual Google account with a paid Google AI Pro or Ultra subscription or be part of a Google Workspace organization with the Business Standard, Business Plus, Enterprise Standard, or Enterprise Plus plan . Provided you fit the bill, just open up Docs or Slides like you normally would, then click on any image within your document or presentation and look for the “Edit” option beneath it. (Pics is a desktop-specific feature, at least for the moment, so you won’t find it in the Docs and Slides mobile apps.) The “Edit” button beneath an image in Docs or Slides is your entry point to Google Pics editing. JR Raphael / Foundry With Pics in the picture, hovering your mouse over that option should reveal text that says “Edit this image with Pics.” And that’s where the Pics magic begins. (If you don’t see that text, you’re either not on an account where Pics is available or the Pics update just hasn’t rolled out to you quite yet. Google says it’s in the midst of adding it onto all eligible accounts as we speak, so keep checking — it should show up soon.) The Google Pics image editor lets you select and edit specific elements of any image. JR Raphael / Foundry Once you’re inside the Pics editor, you’ll see the system taking a moment to process the image and identify all of its elements. Then, after a few seconds, you’ll be able to hover your mouse over any specific area of the image to see a description of it — and be able to click to edit it in any way you want. You can give Pics instructions for edits to different areas of your image. JR Raphael / Foundry From there, you can click onto any other areas to add instructions for additional edits — all using straightforward, plain-English language just describing what you want to see — then click the “Apply” button at the bottom to bring all your requests into action at the same time. So you might, for instance, ask the system to change the color of one specific element, change the text in another area of an image, and change the background. You can even ask it to translate text within an image into another language, if you want. And you can make up to five requests at once and then handle them all simultaneously. Pics will take a moment to process, with the length of that moment varying based on how many requests you made and how complex the edits within them were. articles.title: I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.
articles.content: I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons , even if just for an hour. I was also motivated by journalistic interest. In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up. Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists. As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants. Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round. Because this data is so valuable to Tau, the company charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product. At the time I booked, Tau was offering $30 for an hourlong cleaning with a single robot; now the charge is $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots, or $100 for a one-time visit. But even at the cheaper rate of $30 per hour, Tau’s robots aren’t a great bargain. They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself. But the robots are physically capable of cleaning, and they’re undeniably cute. Tau has armed each four-and-a-half-foot-tall robot with a 3D-printed “head” with antennae that allow it to communicate with Tau’s headquarters, as well as two 3D-printed claw “hands” (the more humanlike alternatives apparently aren’t durable enough, and claws do surprisingly well for most cleaning tasks). Mine was wearing a Tau Robotics shirt, and grippy socks so that it didn’t scratch hardwood floors. With all the human support they need, the robots are closer to radio-controlled cars than Waymos. Many tasks, such as making the bed and folding laundry, require what’s called kinematic guidance: The human pilot performs the necessary motions, and sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them. These kinematically guided tasks produce especially valuable training data. Tau’s AI models might not have solved laundry folding yet, but learning from the examples of robots that have completed the task in the real world is how they’ll get there. But according to Tau cofounder Cornelia Weinzierl, to whom I came clean as a journalist a few weeks after the cleaning, the robot can already complete some other tasks—such as vacuuming and mopping—without any human help. If Tau succeeds in using all the data it is collecting to train truly autonomous cleaning robots, they could even become San Francisco’s newest tech tourist attraction as Waymos become more commonplace countrywide. The cleaning robot that came to my building last month was already a bit of a spectacle. It arrived in a blue minivan, out of which it was helped by Weinzierl and another Tau employee. That’s when the robot encountered its first obstacle: the eight stairs leading up to the building’s front door. I’d come down to greet Weinzierl and the robot, so I had a front-row seat to its struggles with my steps. It climbed as if it were drunk. Each successful step was as likely as not to be followed by a stumbling backward stagger that erased all its progress—though, impressively, it never entirely lost its footing. articles.title: Why Robots Need Intelligence Built for the Physical World
articles.content: Robbyant’s LingBot 2.0 starts with the demands of perception and physical action to build intelligence across different robot bodies. A chatbot can wait for another prompt. A robot may already be moving by the time its surroundings change. That difference turns embodied AI into a distinct engineering problem, where intelligence has to account for physical space and predict how an action will affect what happens next. Robbyant , an embodied AI company under Ant Group , built LingBot 2.0 around those demands from the beginning. The system reflects a deceptively difficult question in robotics: What does an AI architecture need when its decisions have immediate physical consequences? Robbyant’s answer connects perception, environmental modeling, and execution through six models developed as parts of one embodied-native system. Physical Intelligence Begins With Perception A robot operating in a home or workplace receives a continuous stream of spatial information. Objects have depth and position, people move around, and the environment can change during a task. Understanding a verbal instruction covers only one piece of that process. LingBot-Vision and LingBot-Depth 2.0 form the perception side of LingBot 2.0. They give robots information about objects and three-dimensional space that can feed into later reasoning and action. Robbyant describes this layer as “See Clearer,” reflecting the need for physical agents to understand where things are before deciding how to interact with them. That spatial information also has to remain useful as conditions develop. A robot reaching toward an object needs intelligence capable of working with the environment it encounters at that moment. World Models Give Actions Consequences The next part of the system addresses prediction. LingBot-Video and LingBot-World 2.0 model physical environments and how they develop over time, creating Robbyant’s “Think Deeper” layer. This ability has particular significance for robots because movement changes the environment. Picking something up alters its position. Moving through a room creates a new spatial relationship with everything nearby. Effective reasoning involves anticipating what an action is likely to produce. The models give developers a way to study environmental interaction alongside the perception data that informs it. That relationship is central to Robbyant’s full-stack approach: seeing and predicting supply information that execution can use. Execution Has to Keep Pace Eventually, the robot has to move. LingBot-VLA 2.0 and LingBot-VA 2.0 handle the “Act Faster” portion of the architecture, translating information from earlier stages into physical behavior. LingBot-VA 2.0 serves as the capstone of the system. Rather than adapting a model trained for language or entertainment purposes, Robbyant built it from scratch around the demands of embodied AI, with dynamic modeling and causal prediction incorporated into an architecture intended for environmental interaction and real-time execution. Latency becomes especially consequential here. Software generating text can spend additional time producing an answer with few physical consequences. A robot responding to movement around it operates on a different clock. Its perception and reasoning have to reach the action system quickly enough for the response to remain relevant. One Brain Faces Many Bodies Hardware creates another complication: bodies differ. A model working on one physical configuration may eventually need to control machines with different dimensions or capabilities. Robbyant frames its goal as “building one brain for all robots.” LingBot-VLA 2.0 integrates data from 20 different configurations of robots from 17 different brands during the pre-training phase, enabling cross-embodiment capabilities. articles.title: NHS wants a second opinion on Palantir's glowing self-assessments
articles.content: NHS England CEO Sir Jim Mackey plans to tell Palantir to clear future claims about its Federated Data Platform's benefits with his team – although he admits that could be difficult to enforce. Speaking to the Health and Social Care Committee this week, Labour MP Ben Coleman noted that NHS England had cautioned against attributing improvements directly to the platform, but said newly appointed Palantir UK senior vice president Tom Watson "is making claims that [Palantir] is making a difference, and that it's due to Palantir that changes are taking place." Responding, Mackey said he would write to Palantir and "tell them that they have to share with us and clear with us any benefits claimed in the future." But getting Palantir to comply could be another matter. "They should share them with us, but contractually, it looks hard to enforce," Mackey said. The planned letter follows repeated questions about the evidence NHS England and Palantir have used to promote the Federated Data Platform (FDP). NHS England awarded the £330 million contract to a Palantir-led consortium in November 2023 to help improve planning and efficiency. In July, campaign group Foxglove wrote to the UK health minister questioning figures used in Parliament to justify the contract. The Office for Statistics Regulation (OSR) also began examining the evidence. NHS England had said that as of June, 139 trusts used the platform, with 137 reporting benefits. It said an Inpatient Care Coordination Solution tool based on the FDP had helped hospitals perform procedures on an additional 111,589 patients. However, a Freedom of Information request later found that nearly a third of NHS trusts using Palantir's health data platform were performing fewer patient procedures than before it went live. Later that month, the OSR said NHS England had accepted that it needed to communicate its claims about FDP performance more clearly. The regulator noted that NHS England had published on its website a caveat saying that it could not "draw conclusions about cause and effect as other variables have not been controlled for." Last month, Watson, the former deputy leader of the Labour Party, sought to rebut what he described as misinformation about the FDP, repeating the statement that 137 trusts were already reporting benefits without mentioning the caveats. In a statement on X, Watson said the OSR had pointed out that there had not yet been a study on the FDP that controls for other factors like staffing level changes or industrial action. "That's a fair note of caution." In a prepared video, he said Northampton General Hospital, University Hospitals of Derby and Burton, and Chelsea and Westminster Hospital had all produced figures showing they are benefiting from using the platform. "Can we prove that every one of those procedures happened because of our software? No. But does that mean we should ignore what the hospitals are telling us? Of course not," he said. In February 2026, NHS England awarded a contract to Imperial College Projects to independently evaluate the FDP. The findings are not expected until after ministers decide whether to extend the contract, which currently ends in March 2027. ®

articles.title: Britain's tech ambitions depend on minerals made in China, MPs warn
articles.content: Britain's ambitions for AI, advanced chips, and clean energy rest on mineral supply chains dominated by China, and MPs say they cannot establish whether ministers have a credible plan to reduce that dependence. The House of Commons Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee has set ministers ten tests for securing critical minerals. Its verdict is hardly glowing – it cannot be confident the government passes any of them. The tests cover whether ministers know which industries and technologies need protecting, what minerals they require, where supplies could be disrupted, and how domestic production, overseas partnerships, skills, and financing will close the gaps. In a report published today , the committee warns that diversifying supplies will take ten to 15 years, and will require sustained investment and cooperation with allies. Completely cutting China out is neither realistic nor desirable, it says. Leaving Beijing with so much leverage is another matter. Critical minerals underpin everything from batteries and semiconductors to datacenters and military equipment. The designation reflects their economic or security importance and vulnerability to supply disruption, rather than membership of an especially exclusive geological club. The UK – like pretty much all major industrialized economies including the US, the EU, Japan, and India – is almost entirely dependent on imports of these materials and mineral product s. But digging up more ore outside China would solve only part of the problem. The bigger bottleneck is processing. Citing International Energy Agency figures, the committee says China is the leading refiner for 19 of 20 strategic minerals, with an average market share of 70 percent. A different flag over the mine does not necessarily mean a different route through the refinery. The exposure extends beyond chips and batteries. As The Register reported in August , erbium is used to amplify signals in fiber-optic links, while yttrium goes into components including ceramic capacitors. IEEE Spectrum warned that China effectively monopolized the processing of both into the industrially usable materials manufacturers need. That concentration has already caused disruption. China's rare earth export controls in April 2025 , introduced following US tariffs, rippled through manufacturing supply chains and forced temporary automotive plant closures. British manufacturers can suffer even when Britain isn't the intended target. The committee also highlights gallium and germanium, used in advanced semiconductors for radar, communications, and electronic warfare. China accounts for 95 percent and 93 percent of their global production respectively, according to the report [PDF]. Beijing flexing its leverage over chip materials is not new. China announced export licensing requirements for gallium and germanium in July 2023 amid tightening Western restrictions on semiconductor technology. Yet MPs say the government has not clearly identified which domestic industrial and technological capabilities it wants to protect, making it difficult to determine which supply chains deserve priority. Nor do import statistics reveal the whole exposure. Minerals can arrive inside batteries, magnets, and other manufactured components, disappearing from view as individual materials. Businesses themselves may not know precisely what lies several layers down their supply chains. The committee wants confidential mapping and stress-testing with firms in critical sectors, followed by joint purchasing arrangements with allies to give new mining and refining projects dependable customers. Committee chair Liam Byrne said: "Critical minerals are the alpha of the new economy. We cannot re-arm Britain, build AI or deliver net zero unless we secure the minerals these technologies depend on. "Yet sixteen years after China first weaponised its chokehold over rare earths , Britain remains dangerously exposed. We don't know enough about what minerals we…

articles.title: Amazon controls its delivery drivers. NYC wants it to employ them, too
articles.content: Every workday, Luc Rene puts on a shirt and pants branded with Amazon’s logo and heads to a distribution center, where he climbs into a van that also carries Amazon’s logo across its side to deliver packages with the company’s swoosh smile emblazoned on them. When he rings customers’ doorbells, he yells out, “Amazon.” But Rene is not technically an Amazon employee. He’s employed by a delivery service provider (DSP) that contracts out his labor. That could soon change in New York City, where Rene lives and works, if the City Council passes the Delivery Protection Act. The bill would require companies like Amazon to directly employ the people who deliver their packages while also creating a licensing system that would hold the companies to new safety, training, and labor standards. It has the backing of Mayor Zohran Mamdani and 31 of the council’s 51 members—enough for it to pass if brought to a vote. Supporters of the bill say it would increase street safety while also providing better protection for the workers who deliver Amazon packages. Amazon has lobbied heavily against the bill. “We’re committed to creating good jobs and supporting our thousands of employees in New York City. We’re equally committed to the local small-business partners who work with us every day to provide fast, reliable delivery for New Yorkers,” Amazon spokesperson Steve Kelly tells Fast Company . “But as written, this legislation would directly undermine that commitment—threatening the small businesses that deliver to customers, putting the jobs of more than 5,000 of their employees at risk, and forcing us to consider relocating delivery operations outside of the city.” Safety on the job has been an issue for Rene ever since he started delivering Amazon packages in 2022. After completing a training on a computer, he was supposed to spend a day being trained by an experienced driver; the driver never showed up, so Rene drove by himself. Since he was never told how to avoid injury during his shifts, which stretch 10 or more hours, he’s come up with his own regimen, stretching before and after work. “No driver is ever required to complete a delivery if conditions aren’t safe—and neither they nor their DSP is penalized for making that call,” Amazon’s Kelly says. “Any allegation of unsafe working conditions would be taken seriously and we investigate accordingly.” In 2023, Rene slipped and injured his knees while delivering a package. Unsure whether he could access Amazon’s medical services, he called his employer, which asked only whether he could keep working. He did, despite the pain, taking painkillers to get through it. “If I can’t show up to work due to the pain, I won’t get paid,” he says. His experience appears to be common: A 2025 report from the New York City comptroller’s office found that last-mile facilities like the DSP that employs Rene reported an average of 678 injuries per year from 2022 to 2024, and 85% of them were severe enough to keep people from working or to need a reassignment. Amazon’s DSP program had the highest injury rates. In response to a request for comment, a spokesperson for the New York Delivers coalition, which represents DSPs and is bankrolled by $5 million in money from Amazon, says DSPs “provide flexible, good-paying jobs with strong workplace standards, opportunities for career advancement, and competitive benefits,” adding that the Delivery Protection Act “effectively eliminates the small businesses in the industry, and puts over 10,000 New York City jobs at risk.” Amazon also paid to bus in workers and DSP owners to oppose the bill in a city council hearing earlier this year. “On paper, Amazon’s not my employer” When Rene started driving, all he and his fellow drivers were given to haul packages, some of which weigh more than 40 pounds, were giant plastic bins called totes. He says it took a strike in 2024 and a march on their boss to get hand trucks. The effort of dragging totes across the ground…

articles.title: Inside the jagged era of AGI: 5 key takeaways
articles.content: Below, Kevin Roose shares five key insights from his new book, The AGI Chronicles: The Inside Story of the Race to Create an Artificial Superintelligence . Roose is an award-winning technology journalist, bestselling author, and cofounder of Machine Gods Media. He previously spent a decade as a technology columnist for The New York Times , where he co-created and cohosted the popular podcast Hard Fork . He now cohosts Machine Gods , an AI -focused podcast produced in partnership with NPR. What’s the Big Idea? For years, the world’s leading AI researchers have raced to build a technology that many of them fear. But the finish line keeps moving as AI becomes more capable. The truth is, we’re already living in the early, imperfect years of artificial general intelligence, and our institutions are dangerously unprepared for what comes next. Listen to the audio version of this Book Bite—read by Roose himself—in the Next Big Idea app , or buy the book . 1. The people most afraid of AI are the ones building it. This is, in some sense, the founding paradox of the whole AGI story. You’d assume the people building AI are true believers who expect it will do amazing things, like cure cancer and end poverty. And some of them are. But a surprising number of key figures in this race got into AI because they were terrified. They read the arguments about what a superintelligent machine might do to humanity, took them seriously, and concluded that if this thing was going to be built no matter what, it had better be built by people who were scared of it and would take the appropriate precautions. Ultimately, I came to think of the AI world as having three tribes. There are the scientists, who see AGI as the ultimate intellectual challenge and want to use it to discover new drugs and cure disease. There are the seekers, who see it as an evolutionary turning point for our species. And then there are the survivalists, who think that if this technology isn’t built by the good guys, then the bad guys will do it instead. The trouble is that getting there first is what everyone is trying to do. And they all end up concluding that the only way to move forward responsibly is to accelerate. Dario Amodei , the CEO of Anthropic , left OpenAI partly out of concern that it was moving too fast, and then went on to build a competitor that had to move just as fast to stay ahead. He’s living inside the paradox, and so are many of the people in this book. 2. The secret was a big blob of compute. For most of AI’s history, smart people assumed building an intelligent machine would require understanding the human brain, writing down the rules of reasoning, and encoding knowledge the way you teach a student. But what worked instead was almost embarrassingly simple. Amodei outlined it in a 2017 paper he called “Big Blob of Compute.” Essentially, you take a neural network, feed it enormous amounts of data, and then throw a huge computer at it. The model then learns to recognize the patterns in that data the same way a human toddler does, by looking at a lot of examples until it clicks. Amodei called this his Big Blob of Compute hypothesis, and it reoriented OpenAI’s research away from narrow applications and toward a more general approach. It’s what led to GPT-1, GPT-2, and ultimately to the large language models that we use today. This simple recipe is the engine of everything that follows. 3. Feeling the AGI is a key ingredient in AI progress. In San Francisco, people talk about “feeling the AGI” as a kind of spiritual awakening that comes from living on the technological frontier, internalizing the enormously fast pace of progress, and building up to something unimaginably vast. The people who work at these companies believe that they are building something closer to an alien species than a product, and they treat their work as a humanitarian mission: deliver AGI safely into the world before someone else screws it up. “Feeling the AGI” is what Ilya Sutskever, the…
