articles.title: The $50 Million Gamble That Made Red Bull Marketing History
articles.content: Imagine someone asks you, “Hey, do you want to jump from the edge of space?” Your first response would probably be, “What the hell is wrong with you?” Honestly? Same. But when that exact question was asked to Felix Baumgartner , he basically went, “Yeah, sure. Why not?” Now, you might be wondering who on Earth was crazy enough to ask that question in the first place. Enter our main protagonist: Red Bull Ladies and gentlemen, this is the story of the Red Bull Stratos mission: a man crazy enough to jump from the edge of space, a company crazy enough to fund it, and a PR gamble that somehow paid off spectacularly. Five Minutes of Marketing So the Rest Makes Sense Quick disclaimer: Everything you’re about to read comes from me spending the last few hours buried in articles, reports, and marketing resources because apparently that’s what I do for fun now. I tried reading an actual marketing textbook, but it made me question reality, so I fled to Wikipedia, reports, and other resources instead. If I get something wrong, please let me know! Constructive corrections are always welcome—I like learning more than pretending I’m right. Enough corporate jargon. Let's throw a man out of space. Earned Media Value (EMV) Yes, EMV. Now switch the M and the E, and you get Max Emilian Verstappen —okay, that’s not how names work. You get Max Verstappen . But let’s not get distracted. Earned Media Value (EMV) is the estimated dollar value of publicity a brand receives without paying for it directly. Wikipedia says: “The estimated dollar equivalent of unpaid public exposure.” Which is technically correct, but sounds like a corporate robot wrote it. So here’s the version my brain understands: You do something. People can’t stop talking about it. You didn’t pay them to talk about it. That’s EMV. Customer reviews? EMV. Influencers posting because they genuinely found something cool? EMV. News articles? EMV. People sending the campaign to their friends? EMV. Throwing a man out of the edge of space? Yeah... people are definitely going to talk about that. Spoiler alert: they did. A lot. So how is EMV calculated? A simplified formula looks something like this: EMV = (Total Impressions × Industry CPM) ÷ 1,000 Impressions = How many times people saw the content. CPM = Cost Per Mille (the cost of reaching one thousand people through advertising). Basically, it estimates how much money the brand would have had to spend on advertising to achieve the same amount of attention. Some companies also factor in engagement, audience quality, creator influence, and even audience sentiment. After all, ten million people saying, “This campaign is brilliant,” and ten million people saying, “This campaign is terrible,” are two very different outcomes. So why do brands care about EMV? Because it lets them estimate the value of all the buzz they generated without paying directly for every conversation. Imagine your campaign gets millions of people talking. If buying that same amount of attention through traditional advertising would’ve cost millions of dollars, that’s exactly what EMV is trying to estimate. One very important thing to remember: EMV is not real revenue. It isn’t money sitting in Red Bull’s bank account. It’s simply a way of estimating the advertising value of the attention they earned. Return on Investment (ROI) Compared to EMV, ROI is wonderfully straightforward. ROI simply measures how much profit (or loss) you made compared to how much you invested. The formula is: ROI = (Net Profit ÷ Cost of Investment) × 100 Where: Net Profit = Money earned − Money spent Cost of Investment = Everything you invested into the project Let’s use a simple example. Suppose you invest $1,000 into something. At the end, you make $1,500 Your net profit is: $1,500 − $1,000 = $500 Now calculate the ROI: ROI = (500 ÷ 1,000) × 100 = 50% That means your investment generated a 50% return. A positive ROI means your investment made money. A negative ROI means you lost money. (Or, as I…

articles.title: The Zero-Budget AI Launch Playbook: 80% of Your Launch Happens Before Launch Day
articles.content: Part 1 of 2: How to earn attention from Reddit, Hacker News and Product Hunt when you have no ad budget TL;DR In the AI era, ideas and even whole products get cloned in a weekend. Distribution is the part AI can't copy for you. A launch is not a day. By the time you hit "publish," about 80% of the work should already be done. One rule beats every tactic: give value before you take value. On Reddit, Hacker News and Product Hunt, patience and reputation beat polish and hype. Fast, promotional launches get removed, banned or ignored. You can build your first real audience for roughly zero dollars if you create something useful around your product before the product exists. Your idea is not the moat. Distribution is. Try this thought experiment. You have a good idea for an AI product. How long before someone else ships something nearly identical? A year ago the honest answer was a few months. Today, with Claude Code, Cursor and a dozen other tools, it's closer to a long weekend. You can polish the model, sand down the UX, tune the prompts. Competitors can do all of that too, and they'll do it faster than you'd like. What they can't copy overnight is who already knows you exist : the communities that trust you, the search results that surface you, the people who will say your name when someone asks "what should I use for this?" That's distribution, and it's still stubbornly human work. I come from a growth background and have worked on go-to-market for several AI products: a music generator, an AI companion app, a financial-data platform, and a few others. I've done launches with money and without it. Some of them worked. Some of them got my accounts banned. This two-part series is the playbook I wish I'd had at the start, with the failures left in. Part 1 is about the launch itself and the three communities most founders obsess over: Reddit, Hacker News and Product Hunt. Part 2 covers search, PR, creators and the art of making noise. Launch day is the last 20% When I picture "launching a product," my brain reaches for the standard toolkit: buy promotion, record a slick demo video, line up a wave of creators to post the same demo on the same day with the same script, and manufacture the feeling that this thing is blowing up. That's a valid playbook, and I'll get to it. But it hides the most important fact about launches: the visible event is the tip of the iceberg. Take Product Hunt. Whether your product climbs the daily ranking has very little to do with what you do that day. It depends on whether, months earlier, you quietly gathered people who care. We live in an attention economy where everyone is distracted by something else, so the traffic and noise you capture on launch day are a function of the groundwork underneath. The same goes for offline. A great launch is rarely purely online. It leans on the founder friends you met at a conference, the developers you traded favors with, the investor who happily retweets your news. These threads connect to each other, and none of them can be pulled out of thin air the week before. So the first reframe: stop asking "how do I launch?" and start asking "what can I build in the 90 days before the launch that makes launch day easy?" The one rule: give value before you take value If I could only give you one principle, it would be this: share the value, not your product. In marketing terms: give first, collect later. Put something genuinely useful in front of people before you ask for anything. Don't expect anyone to use your product in return. They have alternatives, they owe you nothing, and they can smell an agenda from the first sentence. I'll keep returning to this idea, because it shows up everywhere: in how you post on Reddit, how you write comments, how you build an audience, how you approach creators, even how you make friends at conferences. The tactics change by channel. The rule doesn't. It also changes how fast you should move. Value-first marketing is slow by design. If…

articles.title: Google's 2027 LSA Expansion Has an API Availability Problem
articles.content: Google's planned 2027 expansion of Local Services Ads (LSAs) creates an important technical question for agencies and software providers: will Google Ads API capabilities expand at the same pace as the advertiser migration? Google's migration roadmap says non-US accounts and remaining business categories will transition to Performance Max campaigns with pay-per-lead goals in 2027. Yet the current Google Ads API documentation still restricts the country_code field for these campaigns to US . This is not proof that international API support will arrive late. Google may update its API documentation and regional capabilities before the relevant migration phases begin. But it exposes an integration risk that agencies should address before international accounts move into the new campaign architecture. The issue is bigger than campaign creation. It affects account provisioning, location validation, campaign automation, conversion-goal configuration, reporting, and the ability to manage multiple markets through a single software layer. The migration roadmap and API documentation are not at the same stage Google is moving LSAs into a specialized Performance Max campaign structure while retaining the pay-per-lead model and local placements on Search and Maps. Its published migration schedule has three broad phases: Migration phase Expected rollout Phase 1 August 2026: selected US home and storefront services Phase 2 Late 2026: broader advertiser groups, including service-area businesses and professional services Phase 3 2027: non-US accounts and remaining supported categories Source: Google's LSA migration roadmap . The API documentation describes a more limited geographic capability at present. The Performance Max for pay-per-lead setup requires a two-letter country code in local_services_pmax_campaign_settings.country_code , and the documented supported value is US . The documentation also states that location criteria must belong to the campaign's home country. That creates a distinction between two forms of availability: Product availability: An advertiser can use the pay-per-lead campaign experience in a particular market. API availability: A developer or agency can create, configure, and manage that campaign programmatically in that market. These capabilities are related, but they are not interchangeable. A campaign becoming available in the Google Ads interface does not automatically establish that every API workflow, field, validation rule, or regional dependency is available too. Sources: Google Ads API: Performance Max for pay-per-lead goals and supported business verticals . The country code is a provisioning constraint, not a cosmetic field Consider an agency managing campaigns for plumbing businesses in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia. A conventional campaign-management platform might represent each account using a shared configuration: { "business_id": "client_104", "market": "GB", "country_code": "GB", "business_profile_id": "123456789", "campaign_type": "LOCAL_SERVICES_PMAX", "lead_goal": "PHONE_CALL_LEAD" } This is a simplified internal representation, not a Google API request. The problem emerges when the provisioning service translates that configuration into Google's campaign resource. If the API validates the country code against the currently supported value of US , an international campaign cannot simply be created by substituting GB or AU . The integration must distinguish between a market supported by the advertising product and one supported by the API provisioning workflow. A robust system should therefore maintain a capability registry rather than assuming that every market supports every operation. For example: { "market": "GB", "product_available": false, "api_campaign_creation": false, "api_campaign_updates": false, "location_targeting": "UNCONFIRMED", "last_verified": "2026-11-05" } The values above are illustrative. They should be populated from verified Google documentation and…

articles.title: “Move Fast and Break Things” Is Dead. What Counts in Enterprise AI Now?
articles.content: The invoices are ending Silicon Valley’s favorite motto that built the AI boom. Right before Facebook went public, Mark Zuckerberg shared the “move fast and break things” motto in his 2012 letter to investors. The idea was to build and launch quickly, fix problems later, and learn from mistakes. Startups across Silicon Valley embraced this approach. During the web and mobile boom, the focus was on gaining users first, with monetization, compliance, and governance left for later. When ChatGPT entered the market, the industry repeated this strategy on a larger scale. Companies scrambled for computing power and began spending heavily on licenses, pilots, and APIs, treating AI as a land grab. At Facebook’s developer conference in April 2014, Zuckerberg joked about a new motto: “move fast with stable infra.” With 1.28 billion users, breaking things had become expensive. Why the Era Is Over The motto worked until mistakes became more expensive because of the token costs, and the results stopped matching expectations. In a PwC survey of 4,454 CEOs, 56% said they had seen no significant financial benefit from AI so far. Costs have also been harder to predict than anyone planned. A Harness study found that 72% of organizations had had an unexpected AI cost spike, and more than half said no one clearly owns AI spending. Harness sells AI cost-management software, so it has a stake in how big the problem looks. Cloudera’s research points to another problem: segmented data systems and silos make it hard for companies to measure what AI really costs them to run. Then the CFOs Reached for the Cap In April, Uber’s CTO Praveen Neppalli Naga said the company had used up its entire 2026 AI budget after just four months of Claude Code. Teams had been ranked on an internal leaderboard by how much AI they used. By June, the company limited each employee to $1,500 a month per AI coding tool. In August, Naga wrote that Uber was coming to the end of the so-called “tokenmaxxing era,” when burning tokens meant productivity. Gartner's advice to CFOs is to treat AI cost as an architecture issue rather than a budget line item. One unmonitored prompt library alone can "risk running up millions of dollars in additional expense". That’s the new rule. Finance asks the question nobody asked loudly in 2023: what did we get? How the Ledger Rewrites the Stack Finance teams can't parse a transformer model, but they can easily understand a unit price. Unit price is now the driver of architecture decisions. So how do you deal with that? Route tasks wisely. Don’t just send every job to the largest model. In his annual letter on October 21, 2026, Satya Nadella introduced the “cost-to-outcome” frontier: “After all, Super Intelligence is changing every organization’s inputs (how they work) as well as their outputs (the products and services they sell). At the same time, inference is making marginal cost an important factor in software economics as usage scales. As a result, customers will increasingly measure the cost of tokens against the outcomes they produce. We call this the “cost-to-outcome” frontier, and we are focused on optimizing it.” For engineers, that means sending classification, extraction, and summarisation to a smaller, cheaper model, caching repeated prompts, and using the frontier model only for the work that needs it. Count everything. FinOps for AI is the top priority in the State of FinOps 2026 Report, and AI expense management is a skill teams currently need to build. In practice, that means tagging every model call by team and feature and giving each agent its own budget and alert, so a runaway loop triggers an alarm before it reaches the invoice. A new software market is emerging to meet this demand. Max Gontar, CEO of the AI-powered finance software company Kairos, explains: The first wave of enterprise AI was all about wild spending on experiments in the hope of seeing what the models could write/generate. The current state is that CFOs are…

articles.title: Learjet Crash Has Brought The Conspiracy Crowd Out of The Woodwork
articles.content: Apparently, it was a missile, the government was involved, and the lack of easily recognisable aircraft parts on the ground proves something sinister happened. Then came the YouTubers comparing the wreckage to the September 11 attack on the Pentagon and the lack of visible aircraft parts, as though putting two crash videos beside each other amounts to an investigation. These are the kinds of statements I’ve been reading on social media following the Learjet crash in Florida, and the confidence behind them is extraordinary. Fly-by-night conspiracy theorists have been announcing their conclusions while investigators are still recovering evidence. People who appear to have little understanding of aviation are presenting themselves as authorities on aircraft structures, impact damage and the circumstances of the crash. I’ve been around aviation my entire life, and watching this nonsense circulate is infuriating. Someone sees footage they don’t understand, decides the wreckage looks wrong and immeditely starts suggesting a government opration. The Pentagon comparisons are particularly tiresome. Comparing the appearance of two crash sites cannot establish what happened at either one without examining the aircraft, impact conditions, structures and physical evidence. Yet these videos invite viewers to treat their own unfamiliarity with aircraft accidents as proof that something has been concealed. What makes this behaviour so callous is that real people died. They had families and futures, including a 20-year-old pilot whose aviation career had barely begun. Imagine losing someone you love, then opening social media to find strangers using their final moments to promote an unsupported missile theory. The aircraft was a Learjet 60, registered N722BD , flying from Austin towards the Bahamas. Flight tracking information and cockpit transmissions document a weather encounter followed by a catastrophic descent near West Palm Beach on 1 November. The crew reported icing, turbulence and precipitation before reporting an overspeed condition during the descent. There is meaningful information to examine, but apparently that requires more effort than typing “government cover-up” beneath a video. My own assessment, based on the information available, is that this looks like poor navigation and possible pilot error during a dangerous weather encounter. That remains my interpretation, subject to the investigation establishing what happened. The sequence I consider plausible is that icing contributed to an aerodynamic stall and loss of control, followed by a rapidly accelerating descent and structural damage. Ice forming on the wings, including around their leading edges, can disrupt airflow, reduce lift and increase stall speed. The FAA describes these effects in its guidance on airframe icing. If sufficient ice accumulated on this aircraft, it could have contributed to a stall and the subsequent nose-down descent. Investigators will need to establish whether that occurred, how the ice protection systems were operating and what other factors affected the aircraft. At the reported altitude, temperatures around minus 40 degrees Celsius are conceivable, although altitude alone cannot establish the actual outside air temperature. Extreme cold also needs to be understood properly : conventional airframe icing depends on supercooled liquid water, which approaches its theoretical freezing limit around minus 40 degrees Celsius. The crew’s reported icing encounter deserves serious examination. It doesn’t give any of us permission to declare the complete accident sequence proven. During the extreme descent, increasing speed and aerodynamic loads may have caused part of the tail to separate. Losing an essential pitch control surface would make recovery impossible, depending on the damage and the aircraft’s condition. Investigators recovered three pieces of the left elevator between 1.3 and 3.8 miles from the impact site. They have yet to establish whether…

articles.title: Why SSH Still Matters After More Than 30 Years
articles.content: Introduction Imagine managing a server located thousands of miles away. You need to update its software, investigate an application failure, or change a configuration file. You cannot physically access the machine, but you still need to work with it almost as if it were sitting on your desk. Today, this is a completely ordinary task. Engineers connect to remote servers, execute commands, transfer files, and maintain infrastructure from practically anywhere in the world. Much of this is possible because of a technology called SSH, or Secure Shell . SSH is one of those technologies that most people outside the IT industry have probably never heard of, even though it plays an important role in the systems they use every day. Websites, banking platforms, cloud applications, and enterprise services all depend on infrastructure that is frequently managed through SSH. What makes SSH particularly interesting is its longevity. The protocol was introduced in 1995, when the internet was a very different place. Yet, more than three decades later, SSH remains an essential tool for software developers, system administrators, DevOps engineers, and security professionals. To understand why it has survived for so long, it is worth looking at the problem it was originally designed to solve, how its security mechanisms work, and how its role has changed as computing has evolved. What Is SSH, and Why Is It Important? At its simplest, SSH is a network protocol that allows two computers to communicate securely over a potentially untrusted network. The most familiar use case is remote terminal access. A user opens a terminal, connects to another computer, and begins executing commands. For example: ssh admin@192.168.1.100 This command asks the SSH client to connect to a remote machine at the specified IP address using the username admin . If authentication succeeds, the user can work with the remote system through a command-line session. But SSH is much more than a remote terminal protocol. It can also transfer files, execute individual commands, carry application traffic through encrypted tunnels, and provide secure authentication for automated processes. The importance of SSH comes from three fundamental security properties: Confidentiality means that network traffic is encrypted so that someone intercepting the communication cannot easily read its contents. Integrity means that the receiving system can detect unauthorized changes to transmitted data. An attacker should not be able to modify commands or responses without the modification being detected. Authentication helps establish that the client is communicating with the intended server and that the user attempting to access the server has appropriate credentials. These properties work together. Encryption alone would not be enough if an attacker could impersonate the destination server. Similarly, verifying a user's identity would provide limited protection if commands and passwords were transmitted openly. How SSH Works: From Connection to Secure Session One of the most interesting aspects of SSH is how much happens before the user sees a command prompt. Typing a simple SSH command starts a sequence involving network communication, cryptographic negotiation, identity verification, session-key generation, and user authentication. Understanding these steps helps explain why SSH is considered secure and where configuration mistakes can introduce risks. Step 1: Establishing the network connection SSH normally operates over TCP, using port 22 by default. The client first establishes a TCP connection with the server. TCP provides a reliable communication stream, ensuring that data is delivered in order and that lost segments can be retransmitted. At this point, the connection itself is not yet protected by SSH encryption. articles.title: Decentralized AI Inference Needs a Boring Job Queue
articles.content: Whenever people talk about decentralized AI, the conversation usually revolves around GPUs, tokens, and governance. But there's another problem that doesn't get nearly as much attention. How do you get an AI request from an application to a remote GPU and back without things falling apart along the way? Imagine sending a request to a GPU on a decentralized network. The GPU finishes the job, but the worker responsible for saving the result crashes. Your backend gets a timeout. Now you're left wondering: Did the GPU finish the job? Should I try again? And if I do, will I end up paying twice for the same work? These might sound like small problems, but anyone who has worked with backend systems knows how messy things can get when different services depend on one another. I'm a backend engineer, and I work with things like APIs, job queues, retries, and idempotency. So when I look at decentralized AI, I don't just think about how to access GPUs. I also think about what happens when things go wrong. This article is my proposal for making decentralized GPU inference feel more like a regular backend service that developers can actually rely on. It's an architecture I'm proposing, not a finished product. A little about me I'm a self-taught backend engineer from Nigeria. I work with TypeScript, Node.js, MongoDB, Redis, RabbitMQ, BullMQ, and Docker. I also build web and mobile products for Nigerian SMEs. One thing that makes AI infrastructure interesting to me is the cost. GPU compute is often priced in dollars, while many of the businesses around me earn in naira. As a product grows and starts making more AI requests, those costs can become harder to manage. Depending entirely on one provider also comes with risks. Prices can change, services can become unavailable, and your application can become too dependent on a single company. Decentralized GPU networks offer another option by connecting users with computing resources operated by different providers. That's promising, but getting access to a GPU is only part of the story. Developers still need a reliable way to send jobs, recover from failures, retrieve results, and keep track of what they're paying for. That's the part I want to work on. Having access to GPUs isn't enough Let's say you're building an application that uses AI. A user submits a request, and your backend sends it to a remote GPU to process. What happens if the request takes longer than expected? What if the GPU goes offline? What if the computation finishes but your backend never receives the result? You also have to think about duplicate requests and billing. If your system retries a job after a timeout, how do you know the original job isn't still running? These aren't problems unique to decentralized AI. They're challenges developers already face when building systems that depend on multiple services. Thankfully, we already have tools that can help. Job queues, databases, retries, and idempotency are all useful building blocks. They won't magically prevent every failure, but they can help us handle failures in a more controlled way. And that's where I'd start. How I'd build it I'd build the system around four main components. 1. An API that accepts the request The first component would be a simple API built with Express.js and TypeScript. Its job would be to receive the request, check that it's valid, authenticate the user, and create a record for the job. Instead of making the user wait for the entire AI computation to finish, the API would return a job ID immediately. For example, a client could send a request to: POST /v1/inference And receive something like this: json { "jobId": "job_123", "status": "queued", "statusUrl": "/v1/jobs/job_123" } The user could then check the job's status or retrieve the result later. The important thing is that the application wouldn't need to know which specific GPU provider is handling the request. 2. A queue that keeps track of the work Next, I'd use BullMQ and Redis to…

articles.title: A New Community For In-House UX People
articles.content: You might have already read my name every now and then here at Smashing Magazine. I’m Paul Boag. I’ve written three books with Smashing and 77 articles (yes, I counted), and I sit on Smashing’s advisory board. So when Vitaly and the Smashing team offered me this slot in your inbox, I didn’t take it lightly. I want to tell you about something I’m launching in January with Smashing as my partner , and why I think it matters right now. The Bit Of The Job Nobody Talks About Every year I talk to hundreds of people working in digital. Some work in-house, some run agencies, and some freelance. And the same thing comes up again and again. The hardest part of the job usually isn’t the design work. It’s everything around it . The stakeholder who redesigns things in the review meeting. The business case sitting in someone’s inbox. The project that has been “about to start” since last spring. And now, the senior manager who has read that AI can do user research in an afternoon. What makes it harder is that a lot of us deal with all this on our own . Many are a team of one, or a team of a few. Their colleagues are great, but they work in the same organization with the same blind spots. Nobody down the corridor has dealt with this before. What’s missing is an outside view . Someone who has dealt with the same awful stakeholder and can tell you how they handled it. Most of us rarely get that conversation, and the job is changing faster than ever. There’s very little established best practice for working with AI yet. Everyone is figuring it out at once, mostly alone. So I’m Starting UX Insiders UX Insiders is a small, paid community for people doing UX inside organizations . Designers, researchers, UX leads, and anyone championing UX where they work, whatever their job title. UX Insiders Agency Academy UX Insiders $ 65/mo Join in-house UX community For in-house UX teams. Founder rate for as long as you stay. Launches Jan 5, 2027. Agency Academy $ 65/mo$ 105/mo Join Agency community For freelancers and agency owners. With the Smashing price until the end of November. Here’s what you get: 📞 Weekly call every Tuesday from 3:30 to 4:30pm UK time (10:30am ET, 7:30am PT). Bring a problem, a question, or a win. 💬 Private Slack for the questions that can’t wait until Tuesday, and a second opinion on that email before you send it. 🎥 Every call recorded with a summary, so you can catch up when a meeting gets in the way. 📚 A shared library of the business cases, templates, and research plans that have actually worked for other members. I run every call myself, and I’m in Slack most days. But the best advice usually comes from other members . I’ve seen that first-hand running Agency Academy, my community for agency owners, every week since July 2024. It’s For In-House People Only That’s deliberate. It means people can talk openly about their organization without wondering who’s listening. And it keeps out agencies and freelancers who’d join just to sell you their services. So you apply first . It takes about a minute, and I only check that you work in-house. If you do, the answer is almost always yes. Founder Pricing And How The Launch Works The first 25 members get founder pricing : £49 a month billed annually (£588 a year) + VAT, or £59 a month + VAT paid monthly. You keep that rate for as long as you stay. Your employer can pay by invoice too, so it can often come out of a training budget. Nobody is charged until we launch on Tue, 5 January 2027 . If fewer than 15 people have joined by Friday 11 December , it doesn’t go ahead and nobody pays a penny. Apply for a founder spot → Run An Agency Or Freelance? UX Insiders is just for in-house people. But if you run an agency or freelance, Agency Academy works the same way: a weekly call every Thursday and a Slack full of people who get it. Members even pass work to each other. Until the end of November , Smashing readers can join for £59 a month + VAT , or £49 a month + VAT billed annually (£588 a…

articles.title: Safari's Autofill feature may be distorting time
articles.content: The autofill feature of Apple's Safari browser appears to be suffering from a date handling error that occasionally leads it to supply an incorrect credit card expiration date when filling out forms. The supposed issue has been a sore spot for Apple customers dating back at least to 2017, when the author of an Apple Community forum post complained about changes to the month field in the Autofill credit card expiration date when moving between time zones. "I've noticed for the last year or so, whenever I travel from Eastern time zone (my home) to Central time zone or even Pacific time zone that my credit card expiration date month changes in Safari Autofill," the Safari user wrote. Another post in 2021 raised similar concerns. "I don't know how to reproduce this," the author wrote. "Every few months Safari on any of my devices changes the expiration month of all of my stored credit cards by decreasing the month by 1, for example instead of 10/2029 it changes it to 09/2029." Three years later, another person posting to Apple's Community forum reported the same issue. "For a few years now every time I use Autofill on my computer my credit cards (ALL of them) always have their expiration dates change one month earlier," the 2024 post says. "I thought it was just a glitch on my computer but I bought a new computer and didn't transfer anything from my old one and it is still doing it." An unrelated Autofill bug report from 2024 suggests that if there is an issue, it resides in Apple-owned Safari code rather than Safari's open source WebKit engine. Wherever the bug may reside, Safari's unreliable handling of credit card dates has kept a complaint-filled Reddit thread going for four years. And the reported month-shifting has been noted in other threads, too. The Register was unable to reproduce the described behavior, but a reader insists it's still a problem. "The Safari AutoFill feature sometimes fills in the credit card expiration date wrong," the reader explained. "My credit card expires in December, but sometimes Apple helpfully enters November." "To be clear, the card is stored correctly when inspected in Settings," our tipster added. "The off-by-one error only happens when filling out a form in Safari, and not consistently." One possible way this might happen is if the Safari Autofill code implemented the expiration date using Swift's DateComponent type and stored it as a Calendar object with UTC as the TimeZone identifier. Doing so would anchor the date to a specific time. If the date components were extracted in Pacific Time, the value would be represented as eight hours ahead (PST). So 9/1/2027 at 00:00 would appear as 8/31/2027 at 16:00. Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but we're told Apple's Help Desk – or "Helpless Desk" as our source put it – advised clearing the browser cache and re-entering details of the affected credit card. If that works, it suggests Safari's handling of cached data in the context of Autofill dates may need to be revisited. Apple does not maintain a public bug database and the community-maintained OpenRadar sheds no light on these reports. ®
articles.author: Thomas Claburn

articles.title: FAA Phases Out Floppy Disks From Air Traffic Control
articles.content: The FAA announced today that it is finally phasing out floppy disks from air traffic control systems at more than 400 facilities. Engadget reports: They'll be replaced by a more modern system called Enterprise -- Information Display System (E-IDS), which is comprised of a digital display for relaying status information, updates and other alerts to air traffic teams. The FAA plans to have E-IDS installed in 435 sites by the end of 2028; the first five locations to receive the upgrades are the Atlantic City International Airport, Nashville International Airport and Greater Rochester International Airport, as well as data processing hubs in Atlanta and Salt Lake City. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Hospital gave very sick doctor a special PC for his personal, erm, pleasure
articles.content: Welcome to Friday and therefore to a fresh edition of On Call, The Register 's weekly tale of tech support trials and tribulations that readers kindly share. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Mason," who told us he once worked at a hospital doing tech support for its research labs. "One of the labs was for a doctor who was one of the world's top organ transplant researchers" Mason told On Call. The doctor was also a voracious consumer of – ahem – adult entertainment, a habit that saw his PC and other machines around the lab often come down with a nasty case of malware. Mason got to clean that up, sometimes multiple times in a single week. The doctor's foibles were widely known around the hospital, as was the fact that his activities violated several workplace policies. Mason pointed this out to his boss every time he cleaned up a fresh malware outbreak but such was the doctor's status that management never intervened. And then the hospital was hit by a nasty cyber-worm that did a lot of damage. During the cleanup, Mason's colleagues found logs that showed the doctor's PC was the source of the infection, and that he had been indulging in his online hobby at the time the worm arrived. Mason assumed this would be the moment at which the doctor would finally be held accountable and face disciplinary action. Instead the doctor made a bargain with the IT department to henceforth use only a designated PC when pursuing – ahem – personal and/or intimate matters. And he would only use office PCs for actual work. The hospital's tech team rescued a PC from its e-waste pile for this job. "Get this thing going and deliver it to Doctor Pervert," Mason's boss ordered. By this stage, Mason had had enough. He escalated his protests, telling his boss that indulging this doctor was unprofessional, likely exposed the hospital to lawsuits, wasted IT department resources, and was just wrong. "What do you want to hear?" his boss replied. "The CIO told me do this or get another job." After Mason prepped that PC, he only needed to clean up malware about once a year – after the poor machine was so overrun with malware that it no longer served the doctor's purposes. Mason left the hospital while this PC was still in place. "You'll be shocked, no doubt, to learn that years later the doctor's graduate students filed a lawsuit," he told On Call. "And that the separate fun-time computer was one of the pieces of evidence that the hospital knew about his – ahem – proclivities and not just ignored them but facilitated them." Have you been asked to cover up revolting behavior? Or ignore policy? Click here to share your story with On Call. It's our policy to tell a great tech support story week, so we appreciate every contribution. ®
articles.author: Simon Sharwood

Installing it takes root access, so the attackers must already control the server.

articles.title: The midterm elections’ blue wave could throw a wrench in SpaceX’s mobile ambitions
articles.content: Elon Musk has made no secret of his hopes of turning SpaceX into a viable competitor to mobile companies like Verizon and AT&T. But with the Democrats’ resounding victory in the 2026 midterm elections, that plan is suddenly thrown into question. SpaceX has been busy over the past month making deals and positioning itself to step into the mobile space. In October, it bought an 800 MHz spectrum portfolio from private equity firm Grain Management, which had acquired it from T-Mobile following its 2020 merger with Sprint. And earlier this week, SpaceX struck a deal with Qualcomm to build out base stations for its planned mobile carrier. Taken together, those moves bring the company closer to entering the market. But to launch the new division, SpaceX will also have to jump through legislative hoops, something that could be significantly more challenging with the Democrats in charge. Several Democratic candidates made it clear they planned to target Musk —who spent $500 million trying to stop the blue wave —should the party gain a majority in the midterms. Some lawmakers want to explore potential conflicts of interest in the billions of dollars Musk’s companies receive in federal contracts and subsidies. Others have questions about his possible role in throttling internet access to Ukraine’s army . And several want to do a deep dive into Musk’s role at DOGE (the Department of Government Efficiency that he spearheaded)—which accessed tremendous amounts of sensitive data . Last December, Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Democratic Representative Greg Casar of Texas began warning about SpaceX’s possible entry into the mobile market amid a proposed deal to acquire some wireless spectrum licenses from EchoStar. That deal, they wrote at the time, “would help Musk expand SpaceX’s Starlink capacity and provide an opportunity for the company to gain ‘firepower’ in the satellite communications industry that competitors will struggle to compete with. . . . The close relationship of Mr. Musk to the Trump administration and to key Trump administration officials make it particularly important that the FCC and DOJ engage in a robust, independent, and impartial review.” The deal, valued at $17 billion, ultimately went through . Building a network SpaceX didn’t stop there. Last month’s purchase of the 800 MHz spectrum portfolio seemed mundane at first glance. That frequency was used by Sprint to power its push-to-talk/walkie-talkie-like features in 2004. SpaceX, though, saw it as a way to bypass building an expensive, complex network of repeaters across the U.S. and the globe, when used in conjunction with its Starlink satellites. “Starlink’s satellite signal at 2 GHz can reach your phone outdoors, but it dies at the first wall,” wrote Aakash Gupta, a product management leader, creator, and educator in a post on X. “800 MHz penetrates buildings. Most phones already have the band built in. So satellites handle the open sky, this low-band layer handles indoors, and suddenly Starlink Mobile covers everywhere a normal carrier does without the tower network.” Musk was similarly upbeat, writing on X that the portfolio is “the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America.” The deal with Qualcomm will enhance the cellular infrastructure and enable high-capacity coverage for Starlink Mobile. There are even reports SpaceX is in talks to buy Boost Mobile or use its network, which would give Musk another entry into the mobile market. Allies and advantages Come January, Musk will have significantly fewer friends on Capitol Hill—and many more enemies. “We must get big money out of our politics, so no billionaire or trillionaire can buy our elections,” James Talarico , the Democratic Senator-elect from Texas, said in his victory speech. “We must unrig this economic system that only benefits the top 1%.”…

articles.title: Thinking Machines Releases Inkling 2 Small, a 594B MoE With 17B Active
articles.content: Thinking Machines Lab has released Inkling 2 Small , the first model of its second Inkling generation. The Inkling 2 Small model is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) with 594B total and 17B active parameters. It accepts text and images, and supports variable reasoning effort. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , it scores 31. Its predecessor, Inkling Small , scores 13 on the same index. The model is live on Tinker for fine-tuning and inference. TL;DR Size: 594B total, 17B active MoE; 1M-token context. Runs on: Tinker API only for now. Self-hosting hardware is not disclosed. Weights support MXFP8 and NVFP4. Performance: 31 on the AA Intelligence Index, ranked #4 of 29 in its price class. Best: 86.3% on SWE-Bench Pro v2 (Hard), second only to Kimi K3 in the lab’s table. Worst: 13.1% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, versus 32.8% for GLM-5.3-Flash. What is Inkling 2 Small? Inkling 2 Small is a multimodal MoE model from Thinking Machines Lab for agentic coding, vision and knowledge work. It takes text and image input and returns text. It is important to note that it does not support audio as of now. Weights are closed at launch. The Thinking Machines Lab plans an Apache 2.0 release next week, after external safety testing and red-teaming. This follows its safe path to open weights policy. How is Inkling 2 Small built? It includes a 48-layer decoder-only transformer. Each token routes to 8 of 384 experts. Attention mixes local and global layers. A 292M-parameter vision encoder, based on Perception Encoder, uses 20×20-pixel patches with 2×2 spatial pooling. Image patches are interleaved with text tokens. Pretraining ran in 4 phases: H1: 8.4T tokens over 68 hours on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 racks, trained natively in NVFP4. H2: 3.8T tokens of newer, higher-quality data at 512K context. H3: about 320B tokens of reasoning and agent trajectories at 1M context. H4: about 34B tokens of the highest-quality agent trajectories. A single joint RL run followed. It took 1,075 steps, 17M+ rollouts and 9 days on 2,048 GPUs. Compute exceeded 4 × 10²³ FLOPs. Coding made up 65.0% of RL tokens. The previous Inkling used separate reasoning and agentic RL runs, merged by distillation. Alignment got explicit attention. Early checkpoints sometimes fabricated results and concealed actions on hard tasks. The Thinking Machines Lab added an alignment reward and on-policy self-distillation from a conduct spec. Its internal misbehavior score fell from 66.8 on Inkling to 14.9. How does Inkling 2 Small perform on benchmarks? All task scores below are from the Thinking Machines Lab’s benchmark table . They run at effort 0.99 (xhigh) and temperature 1.0. Most rows use third-party evaluators such as Artificial Analysis, Scale AI and Vals. Where it scores highest: SWE-Bench Pro v2 (Hard): 86.3%. PerceptionBench: 64.7%, versus 58.5% for Kimi K3. EnterpriseBench-CoreCraft: 71.8%, versus 46.7% for GLM-5.3-Flash. JobBench: 70.5%. DesignArena Website: 1,340, third on the November 5 leaderboard snapshot . Where it trails: Terminal-Bench 4.0: 13.1%, versus 33.8% for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017. DeepSWE v1.1: 72.1%, versus 77.0% for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017. GDPVal-AA v2.1: 1,630, versus 1,746 for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017. On the PMPP-Hard GPU kernel benchmark, it solved 54.25 of 69 tasks on average. In an autoresearch demo, it fine-tuned Qwen3.5-4B for time-series forecasting. It spent $426 of a $500 Tinker budget. The release post cites both 4.5 hours and 4 h 17 min for the run. How does Inkling 2 Small compare with DeepSeek and GLM? articles.title: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch Is Changing the Color of the Ocean
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Scientific American: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch, an area in the Pacific Ocean where debris naturally accumulates, is full of tiny bits of plastic -- so full, in fact, that it seems to be changing the color of the ocean. [...] To better understand how microplastics may have influenced the ocean's color, [Daniel Koestner, a postdoctoral fellow at the University of Bergen in Norway] and his colleagues looked at 20 years of satellite data from the spot in the ocean with perhaps the most of plastic -- the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, a zone between Hawaii and California where trash trapped by ocean currents accumulates. Between 2002 and 2022, the researchers found, waters near the garbage patch have gotten brighter in both blue and green wavelengths compared with surrounding areas. The results, published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment on Thursday, don't yet prove that microplastics have directly brightened the ocean, the researchers emphasize, though their findings are backed up by lab experiments with microplastics. But without taking direct ocean samples, it's hard to know for sure what's causing the ocean's color to change. "We're still one step away from proving definitively that microplastics are causing the shift in color that that we're seeing," adds study co-author Shea Cheatham, a Ph.D. student also at the University of Bergen. "We just have to get in there [to the garbage patch] to verify." The hope is that detecting these color shifts could help identify other areas around the world where microplastics have accumulated. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Agility Robotics co-founder on its Nasdaq debut, lessons from Amazon, and the future of work
articles.content: Agility Robotics co-founder and Chief Robot Officer Jonathan Hurst and the company’s Digit 5 humanoid robot, which was designed to work alongside people without a safety barrier. Agility began trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday. (Agility Robotics Photos) Agility Robotics of Salem, Ore., made its Nasdaq debut Thursday as the first publicly traded U.S. company devoted solely to humanoid robots — offering an ambitious vision for how the technology will change work, and a cautious view of how long it will take. “Maybe we’ll never have faster-than-light travel. Maybe we’ll never have transporters from Star Trek,” said Jonathan Hurst, the company’s co-founder and chief robot officer. “But we absolutely will have machines that can do all of the physical work that a person can do.” However, he cautioned, “It’s not going to be next year or five years from now. It’s really a grand challenge.” Agility went public through a merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a special purpose acquisition company, or SPAC, led by financier Michael Klein. The deal valued Agility at $2.5 billion before the new investment and brought in about $465 million in gross proceeds. Its shares trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker AGLT. After initially dipping below its opening price, the stock closed Thursday at $11.51, up 2.2%, bucking the trend on a day when the Nasdaq fell 5.5%, its worst day in 18 months. Agility’s robot: The company’s main character is Digit, a two-legged robot with two arms mounted near the top of its torso that let it lift bins high and recover from falls. It moves totes and containers in warehouses and factories. Digit 5, the latest version, was unveiled in September. Standing 5-foot-11 and weighing 284 pounds, it’s covered in sensors, with cameras and antennas in its head and safety-rated sensors in protective housings around its body. Agility says it can lift 50 pounds, reach 7.2 feet high and work more than 20 hours in a 24-hour day. Agility’s Digit 5 robot, which stands 5-foot-11 and weighs 284 pounds. (Agility Robotics Photos) But the big advance is that Digit 5 was designed to work alongside people without a barrier. Earlier versions had to be fenced off from workers, which limited where customers could use them. Agility learned how much that mattered at Amazon, an early investor in the company, which tested prior versions of Digit for moving and stacking bins in its warehouses. Digit did useful work in tests there, Hurst said, but when Agility asked about scaling up, Amazon said it couldn’t deploy the robots. It showed Agility what it had taken to get its own wheeled robot through three to four years of safety certification, and said it didn’t know how a balancing robot would ever get there. “The safety case to do this is unbelievably hard,” Hurst said. “Nobody has ever deployed a dynamically stable balancing machine, and it brings new risks.” Getting a robot out from behind the barrier took years of engineering and standards work. Agility has been co-authoring ISO safety standards for the category and making its case to insurance companies and warehouse operators who want proof in numbers before putting a balancing machine next to a person. Digit 5 uses AI and multiple sensors to watch for nearby people . Depending on the situation, it steers around them, stops or sits down. Visual and audio cues signal what it’s about to do, and a safety controller triggers its responses when someone gets too close. Hurst credits the lessons from Amazon, along with ones from GXO, Toyota and Schaeffler, with shaping the design of Digit 5. “Amazon was a huge, huge part of getting us to that point,” he said. Amazon made an initial deposit in 2024 toward a $1.05 million purchase of five robots, according to Agility’s filings. Agility recorded about $1.04 million in net sales from Amazon in 2025,…

articles.title: Apple Surveys iPhone Duo Buyers About Crease and Camera
articles.content: Apple is sending email surveys to some iPhone Duo buyers to get feedback on display size, crease, under-display camera, and other features. The first question asks why the buyer chose the ‌iPhone Duo‌ now, with answers like "I wanted to try Apple's first foldable," "It was an impulse purchase," and "I expect smartphone prices to increase." Other questions ask about the size of the ‌iPhone Duo‌'s display when it's closed, how visible the crease is, whether the under-display camera is distracting, and the camera's image quality. The final question is open-ended and asks what the buyer would add or change about the ‌iPhone Duo‌. View all 6 photos in the full article → It's been about two weeks since the ‌iPhone Duo‌ launched, and it's not too unusual for Apple to conduct surveys following a new product's debut. Some of the questions are about ‌iPhone Duo‌ compromises compared to standard iPhone models. The Duo's outer display is 5.4 inches, making it about the same size as the discontinued iPhone mini line. The inner display's under-screen camera is limited to 4MP, and it was one of the main complaints in reviews . The survey does not ask about Touch ID , the experience of using unoptimized apps, or the display cracks some users have reported, all of which are also top Duo complaints, (Thanks, Willy!) articles.title: Applebee's Exposed Customers' Personal Data After Leaving Database Password In App
articles.content: Joe_Dragon shares a report from TechCrunch: Applebee's has fixed a security flaw that allowed anyone to access the personal information of its registered customers, after a researcher found a password for an internal database inside Applebee's mobile app, TechCrunch has learned. The popular restaurant chain confirmed [last Thursday] that it had taken action to address the security issue to prevent any unauthorized access to its customer database. [...] The exposed database contained customer names, email addresses (including whether or not the customer verified their email), dates of birth, phone numbers, and ZIP codes. The data also included veteran status, the number of times customers had logged in, when their accounts were created, and the IP addresses of their most recent log-ins, which can be used to reveal the person's approximate location. [...] When asked by TechCrunch, the spokesperson would not say if the company has server logs that it can review to determine whether anyone accessed the database, or if it has any logs at all. "Our investigation is ongoing, and we will take appropriate steps based on our findings," the company added. It's unclear how many customers were affected by the data exposure. [...] Applebee's had at least 8.5 million customers enrolled in its rewards program as of last year, though the company would not provide a number of how many customers had their personal information exposed by this security flaw. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.author: BeauHD
articles.fingerprint: after app applebee customers data database exposed leaving password personal

articles.title: Apple's First Touchscreen Mac is Now Arriving to Customers
articles.content: It's Friday, November 6 in Australia and New Zealand, which means customers who preordered a PROLED touchscreen MacBook Pro , OLED iPad mini , M6 ‌MacBook Pro‌, or M6 iMac are now starting to receive their devices. People will soon be sharing photos and first impressions of the new products on the MacRumors forums, Reddit, Instagram, and other platforms, giving us a first look at what real-world users think of the ‌OLED‌ upgrade for the ‌iPad mini‌ and the PROLED and touchscreen update for the ‌MacBook Pro‌. Apple's new high-end ‌MacBook Pro‌ models come with M5 Pro or M5 Max, and the major change is the display. It's touch-enabled and is the first Mac with an ‌OLED‌ display. The design has been updated, so the new machines are thinner and lighter than the mini-LED models, which Apple is still selling. Apple also brought back the glowing Apple logo, and replaced the notch with a Dynamic Island . Pricing on the PROLED ‌MacBook Pro‌ starts at $2,899 for the 14-inch model and $3,399 for the 16-inch model. The ‌OLED‌ ‌iPad mini‌ is Apple's first smaller-screened iPad to get ‌OLED‌, and it's also the most affordable ‌OLED‌ ‌iPad‌. It's almost a millimeter thinner than the prior version and has an Acoustic Display that does away with speaker holes. Without them, the enclosure is sealed, making it the first ‌iPad‌ with a water and dust resistance rating (IP67). It uses Apple's A20 Pro chip. The ‌OLED‌ ‌iPad mini‌ starts at $699. The 14-inch entry-level ‌MacBook Pro‌ and 24-inch ‌iMac‌ got little in the way of updates beyond an M6 chip. The ‌MacBook Pro‌ is priced starting at $1,999, and the ‌iMac‌ starts at $1,499. Australia is the first country where customers can buy one of the new products in an Apple retail location. Online orders of the PROLED ‌MacBook Pro‌ don't ship until late November or early December, so it's possible in-store stock will be limited. The ‌OLED‌ ‌iPad mini‌, 14-inch ‌MacBook Pro‌, and ‌iMac‌ should be readily available. After Australia and New Zealand, sales and deliveries of the new Macs and ‌iPad mini‌ will begin in Asia, the Middle East, Europe, and finally, North America. articles.title: Meet *sshole, the vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices
articles.content: Devices running some configurations of Alpine Linux, and possibly other distributions, are affected by a decade-old vulnerability that allows attackers to log into devices with no password. The vulnerability exists in the interaction between OpenSSH, the code library implementing SSH connections, and musl, a lightweight alternative to the libc library that, unlike most other Linux distributions, is used in Alpine. Further, OpenSSH using musl (pronounced muscle) must not use PAM (pluggable authentication modules), a framework that handles user authentication and account-access checks. Alpine is a lightweight, widely used Linux distribution. Other platforms may be affected if they use the same configurations. One connection, works every time, needs no retries There are two other conditions necessary for successful exploitation. First, a system must have at least one user account that’s accessible using a password that is hashed using the SHA256 or SHA512 functions. Second, the target system account must be configured to be passwordless, by way of specifying a "*" in the password field in /etc/shadow, the Linux file where password hashes are stored. Passwordless accounts are commonly used for accounts that use certificate-based authentication. This setting is common for certain types of accounts. Read full article Comments

articles.title: OpenAI Responds to US Midterm Elections With New Commitment to Communities
articles.content: "OpenAI has published a new National Community Compact and Compute Campus Policy Blueprint, apparently in response to the Blue Wave Midterm Elections," writes ancient Slashdot reader Gilmoure. "Instead of moving into communities like a juggernaut, they say they will be dangling friendly carrots going forward." Here's an excerpt from OpenAI's article: Every future compute campus OpenAI owns and operates will have its own local compact. We'll engage residents early enough to ensure their input shapes project plans, give them a local point of contact throughout the life of the campus, and report publicly each year on how we're doing. Each compact will reflect local priorities and include a common set of commitments: - Pay our own way on energy and infrastructure. We'll pay the full cost of the electricity we use and the infrastructure needed to serve us. Before major spending begins, we'll provide financial assurances so other customers are protected if a project is delayed, reduced, or canceled. - Protect local resources and report on our impact. We'll develop a water plan for each campus, prioritize closed-loop or low-water cooling, and publish site-level water and electricity use. We'll publish construction plans and independent noise studies before operations begin and annually afterward. And we will not use non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with public officials, allowing only narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information. - Create opportunities for local workers and businesses. We'll publish the jobs we expect to create, work with unions and training providers to help residents prepare for them, and report annually on hiring and apprenticeships. We'll also make sustained investments in priorities residents help select. [...] The investments that help America compete globally can also help communities prosper locally. That starts with giving residents a say while plans can still change and a way to hold developers accountable for delivering on their commitments. That's what we're committing to at the campuses we own and operate, and what we believe people should be able to count on wherever AI infrastructure is built across the country. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Google Releases Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash: 15-Second AI Video at $0.07 per Second
articles.content: Google has released Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash , the newest version of its video generation and editing model. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates and edits clips up to 15 seconds natively. It also cuts the price by 30% compared with Omni 1.1 Flash. The model is generally available on Google Cloud and the Gemini API . For developers, the takeaways are longer clips, fewer re-renders and a lower bill per second. TL;DR Runs on: Google-hosted only (Gemini API, Google Cloud). No open weights, no local deployment. Performance: Google reports better reference adherence and less drift. No 1.2 benchmark scores are published. Best: Native 15-second clips at $0.07 per second of 720p video, about $1.05 per 15-second clip. Worst: Google says fast sports action, rapid script changes and complex physics still need work. What is Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash? Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is a multimodal video model from Google DeepMind. It takes text, images, short video clips and audio as input. It outputs video with audio. Google’s developer docs describe the Omni line as natively multimodal, with editing handled through the Interactions API. What changed from Omni 1.1 Flash? The launch lists 6 upgrades: Longer clips: Generation and editing now reach 15 seconds, up from 10 seconds in Omni 1.1. Duration control: You set length in 1-second steps from 3 to 15 seconds. Reference adherence: You can combine character, product or style images with motion clips up to 3 seconds. Consistency: Faces, garments, packaging text and brand colors hold across camera angles with less morphing. Speech: Dialogue sounds more natural, with clearer lip-sync and distinct multi-speaker conditioning. Camera control: FPV flythroughs, zoom-outs and orbits show fewer unwanted jump cuts. How does the draft, edit, upscale workflow work? Google frames cost control as a workflow, not just a price. You draft at 360p or 720p. You fix a detail with a follow-up edit instead of regenerating the whole clip. Then you upscale the best result to 1080p or 4K. Multi-turn conversational editing now works across full 15-second clips. In practice, you can swap a product, background, lighting or aspect ratio turn by turn. The docs show this through a previous_interaction_id , so the prior video is not re-uploaded. How much does Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash cost? Google prices Omni 1.2 Flash at $0.07 per second of 720p video . Savings are similar at other resolutions . For context, the pricing page bills Omni 1.1 Flash at roughly $0.10 per second of 720p video. A full 15-second 720p clip on 1.2 works out to about $1.05. Google Vids users can generate 15-second clips at no additional cost. Provisioned Throughput is available, and outputs carry a SynthID watermark. How does it compare with other video models? Feature Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash Veo 3.1 Seedance 2.0 Developer Google DeepMind Google DeepMind Google ByteDance Parameters Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Max single clip 15 s 10 s 8 s 15 s Duration options 3 to 15 s, 1 s steps Not disclosed 4, 6 or 8 s 4 to 15 s Output resolution 360p, 720p; 1080p and 4K upscaled 360p, 720p; 1080p and 4K upscaled 720p, 1080p, 4K 480p, 720p native Native audio Yes Yes Yes Yes Multi-turn editing Yes, up to 15 s Yes Not listed Not disclosed 720p price $0.07/s About $0.10/s Not listed on source page Token-based, varies Weights Closed, API only Closed, API only Closed, API only Closed, API only --> How does it perform on benchmarks? articles.title: NASA unveils mysterious X-70 experimental aircraft using AI-generated image
articles.content: NASA has announced a new experimental aircraft, the X-70 Fractal, that will supposedly feature reconfigurable flight-control technology and a modular design for swapping in different payloads. But much remains unknown about the aircraft’s design and development timeline, even as NASA administrator Jared Isaacman said the X-plane could take flight within two years. The mystery surrounding NASA’s newest X-plane was exemplified by the agency’s press release, including an apparently AI-generated image of the X-70, showing a dark silhouette vaguely resembling a military fighter jet obscured by smoke. The news was announced by Isaacman during the UP.Summit held at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on November 4. “The X-70 Fractal gives NASA a crewed, high-performance platform to test advanced flight-control, maneuverability, and other cutting-edge technologies in real flight,” Isaacman said. “Its modular design and ability to rapidly swap internal and external payloads will keep our teams flying, learning, and moving quickly from one experiment to the next.” Read full article Comments

articles.title: Claude Gets Personal Finance Feature With Bank Account Linking
articles.content: Anthropic today added Personal Finance to Claude, allowing users to connect their bank and card accounts for analysis. Claude has read-only access to accounts, and there is no option for it to move, manage, or invest money. Anthropic says Claude gives answers in everyday language and can explain unfamiliar financial terms. The feature can track spending across categories, upcoming bills, and out-of-the-ordinary purchases. It can look for unexpected fees, increasing bills, and subscriptions, plus it can create charts, calendars, and dashboards. Financial accounts are connected to Claude through the Plaid service, so Claude does not see bank passwords. Claude has access to the bank name, account name and type, balances and credit limits, and up to two years of transactions for bank accounts. Personal Finance chats are not used for model training and are not added to Claude's shared memory. OpenAI added a similar finance feature to ChatGPT back in May. Personal Finance is rolling out in beta on the Pro, Max, and Ultra plans in the United States. articles.title: Apple Arcade Adds Crossy Road Rush and NBA 2K27
articles.content: Apple today added several new games to Apple Arcade , including Crossy Road Rush, NBA 2K27 Arcade Edition, Kami 2+, and Food Stylist - Design Game+. Crossy Road Rush is the latest game in the popular Crossy Road series. Players will make their way across an island obstacle course and unlock fun characters. The game supports up to four players in local or online multiplayer, as well as solo play. NBA 2K27 adds the WNBA, which is a first for the Arcade Edition. The game has all 15 WNBA teams and 180 active players, though they're limited to Quick Match and Blacktop modes. The new edition also has faster, deeper progression for the MyCAREER journey and a refreshed Neighborhood. Kami 2+ is a puzzle game where players fold colorful paper patterns, and Food Stylist lets players create virtual dishes and tablescapes inspired by cuisines around the world. Apple Arcade is Apple's subscription gaming service, priced at $6.99 per month. Up to six family members can share a subscription, and there are no ads or in-app purchases. articles.title: Seattle startup OneCourt brings tactile tablets for blind and low-vision fans to NHL games
articles.content: A hockey fan uses OneCourt’s tactile device during the NHL Heritage Classic, an outdoor game between the Montreal Canadiens and the Winnipeg Jets at Princess Auto Stadium in Winnipeg, Manitoba, on Oct. 25. (Ticketmaster Photo) Seattle startup OneCourt is bringing its haptic devices for blind and low-vision sports fans to hockey, with the NHL and Ticketmaster making the tablets available free at the league’s marquee events this season and at all home games for four teams. The device turns real-time game data into vibrations that users follow with their fingertips. For hockey, OneCourt draws on the NHL’s EDGE puck and player tracking data. Related Seattle startup wants to bring vision-impaired sports fans closer to the action with tactile device The tablets debuted at the Heritage Classic on Oct. 25, and the Washington Capitals, Colorado Avalanche, Chicago Blackhawks and Detroit Red Wings are the first clubs to offer them at every home game. “Our community has been asking us for hockey since day one, and launching it with Ticketmaster and the NHL is a milestone for OneCourt,” CEO Jerred Mace said in a news release. The hockey launch builds on OneCourt’s work in other leagues, starting with the NBA’s Portland Trail Blazers. Since 2025, Ticketmaster has offered the tablets at every home game for nine NBA teams, and it backed an NFL pilot during the 2025 season with four clubs, including the Seattle Seahawks , along with Super Bowl LX. Mace started OneCourt as a University of Washington student studying industrial and product design. His co-founders are three fellow UW grads: COO Antyush Bollini, CTO Andrew Buckingham and CIO Nick Durand. Time named OneCourt’s tablet to its Best Inventions of 2026 list last month, in the accessibility category. It was one of several Seattle-area innovations on the list.

articles.title: Google: Schools can keep search while skipping Gemini, but AI search is non-negotiable
articles.content: Google faced the ire of educators and parents earlier this week when it announced a new AI policy for K–12 schools . Google said that it developed its new approach to give schools more control, but early reporting also suggested Google would block search access for schools that didn't want to use AI. Google didn't see the backlash coming, but now that it's here, the search giant is clarifying what exactly its new policy means and what's changing. The gist of the new policy, according to Google's blog post, is that schools using Google apps will have to opt into its AI products going forward. Since the company considers search part of its AI portfolio (Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Search), schools have to specifically turn that on for logged-in student accounts. When Google revealed its new policy, the company's VP for education spoke exclusively to The New York Times , which interpreted the situation as Google will "turn off search" if schools reject AI. This has a nefarious vibe, but it's probably not the most accurate way to describe how Google's educational AI system will operate. Google's approach may not be entirely altruistic, but it technically offers schools more choice and control than they have now. Instead of Google turning off search, it will let schools make that decision based on their internal AI policies. Read full article Comments

articles.title: Lawsuit: Man introduced his wife to ChatGPT. She used it to plan his murder.
articles.content: ChatGPT allegedly helped a North Carolina woman, Cheryl Gates, craft a “personalized plan” to poison her husband, James, after fueling her delusions that he planned to divorce her and leave her with nothing. A grand jury indicted Cheryl Gates on charges of attempted first-degree murder and food contamination in October. About a week prior, the accusations that ChatGPT was a co-conspirator in the attempted murder came in a lawsuit filed in San Francisco County Superior Court that was made public this week. In it, James Gates alleged that OpenAI and Sam Altman failed to employ technical safeguards to shut down Cheryl’s chats even after her queries became “obviously suspicious” and sought advice on how to execute and conceal a homicide. At first, Cheryl told ChatGPT that she was researching poisoning out of fear that her husband might possibly try to kill her—framing her queries as “self-protection.” Coming to the rescue, ChatGPT did not terminate the conversation. Instead, it helped her “with specific instructions for the preparation, dosage, and administration of Oleander, including whether anti-nausea medicine would accelerate or inhibit death, whether it would show on an autopsy report, and whether it could be injected into a vein or muscle instead of being ingested in tea and have the same lethal effect,” the lawsuit said. articles.title: Baidu Releases ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base: A 280B MoE Base Model With 14B Active Parameters
articles.content: Baidu has released ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base , the raw pre-training checkpoint of its new sparse Mixture-of-Experts language model. ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base is a 280B-parameter text model from Baidu that activates 14B parameters per token. The weights stop at the end of pre-training, with no mid- or post-training applied. This as a clean starting point for teams that want to compare fine-tuning, instruction tuning or RL methods from one checkpoint. TL;DR Size: 280B total, 14B active per token; 128K training context, 1M for fine-tuning and inference. Runs on: Multi-GPU servers. Baidu’s reference configs use 4-way parallelism in SGLang and vLLM. GPU model and VRAM not disclosed. FP8 and BF16 weights. Performance: Best score on 24 of 30 base-model benchmarks in Baidu’s unified pipeline (self-reported). Best: MMLU-Pro 78.4, ahead of DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base at 69.2. Worst: HELMET-Rerank 56.2, behind DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base at 60.0. What is ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base? It is a text-only MoE base model with 43 layers and a 4096 hidden size . It was pre-trained from scratch on 33.5T tokens with the Muon optimizer. The tokenizer has 201,216 entries and groups numbers right-to-left in chunks of up to 3 digits. Activated compute, KV cache and long-context cost were treated as one budget. Pre-training data leaned on repository-scale code and long-context material, since those are hard to add later. How does the ERNIE 5.5 Flash architecture work? Hybrid attention : 37 layers use Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA), which caches 1 entry per 128 tokens. The other 6 layers use Multi-head Latent Attention with sparse attention (MLA + DSA). That means 1 in 7 layers keeps full-context access. HCA layers use 512-dim heads; MLA layers use 256-dim heads. Gated and mixed heads : The attention output gate comes from the low-rank query latent, cutting gate-projection parameters by 75%. Virtual Head Attention adds a lightweight low-rank mix across heads. Multi-Router Latent MoE. Each MoE layer has 512 routed experts (top-10) plus 1 shared expert. Several independent sigmoid routers replace a single router, per Baidu’s Multi-Router paper . Expert FLOPs and communication volume stay unchanged. Experts run in a 2048-d latent space, half the hidden width. ECHO instead of MTP. : ECHO reuses the backbone’s final layer to predict future tokens. The same layer doubles as a built-in draft model for speculative decoding. ECHO adds 0.36B parameters, excluded from the headline counts. Other pieces : The model uses Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections with expansion rate 4 and a MultiMax output head. How does ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base perform on benchmarks? Baidu team evaluated all 4 models with the same pipeline, prompts and few-shot settings. All figures below are self-reported by Baidu. Exams: MMLU 93.3, MMLU-Redux 94.1, MMLU-Pro 78.4. Knowledge: SimpleQA 34.1, versus 29.1 for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base. STEM and reasoning: GPQA 60.2, MGSM 87.0, BBH direct 77.1. Code: HumanEval+ 82.3, MBPP+ 81.5, LiveCodeBench 40.1. Long context: RepoQA 91.7, LongBench-v2 48.7, HELMET-ICL 85.9. It loses on 6 tasks. DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base leads on ChineseSimpleQA, INCLUDE-lite, HELMET-Rerank and InfiniteBench. Hy3-preview-Base leads on BBH CoT and FullStackBench. Competitor numbers in Baidu’s pipeline differ slightly from each vendor’s own report. DeepSeek lists MMLU-Pro 68.3; Baidu measures 69.2. Tencent lists Hy3 MMLU-Pro at 65.76; Baidu AI measures 66.9. How does it compare with DeepSeek, Tencent and Xiaomi base models?
