articles.title: Getting started with Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
articles.content: Today, we are announcing the general availability of Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. With Web Answer, agent builders get a synthesized, source-cited answer to a natural-language question with a single tool call. They no longer build a search, retrieve, synthesize, and citation pipeline themselves. If you have built agents that need to answer questions from current web sources, you know the pattern: call a search API, decide which results to trust, retrieve and clean page content, prompt a model to synthesize, and engineer citation extraction so the output traces back to a source. Every step is code you maintain, and every step is another place things can go wrong: hallucination when evidence is insufficient, stale content when the index moves, and broken attribution when a claim and its source drift apart. The Web Answer collapses that entire pipeline into one request. You send a question. You get back a cited answer in seconds. In this post, we explain what Web Answer does, compare it with Web Search on AgentCore, show how it works and what it returns, and walk through adding Web Answer to a gateway and calling it from an agent. What Web Answer does Figure 1: Request flow from an agent through the Gateway to Web Answer and back Your agent sends a question to your AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The Gateway authenticates the call with AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) or a JSON Web Token (JWT). The Gateway calls Web Answer, a managed connector that AWS owns, using its own service role. Web Answer plans its searches, runs several in parallel, and reads key pages to check the facts. When the evidence is insufficient, it searches again. It then writes an answer that ties each claim to its source URL. The Gateway returns the answer and its citations to your agent as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool result. Web Answer is a managed AgentCore Gateway tool that takes a natural-language question and returns a synthesized answer in seconds grounded in current web sources. Here is what you get back: A grounded, cited answer, where each grounded claim maps to a citation, with a source URL where one is available. Current sources. Web Answer runs new searches for every question, and its model is given today’s date so it can search for up-to-date information. Agentic search: Web Answer plans its own searches, runs several in parallel, reads pages to verify facts, and decides when it has enough evidence to answer. Responsible AI safeguards: Web Answer is designed and tested with responsible AI safeguards. Figure 2: Demo video showing how to add Web Answer to an AgentCore Gateway, from setup to a finished, cited answer How it differs from Web Search Web Answer and the Web Search tools both support retrieval use cases, with different levels of integration complexity. The dividing line is who runs the model: Web Search: Returns ranked URLs, titles, snippets, and metadata. You keep your own model and control the synthesis. Use Web Search when you want full control over how results are processed. Web Answer: Runs the model, the agentic retrieval loop, synthesis, and attribution for you. You get a finished, cited answer. Use Web Answer when the question is a sub-task inside a larger agent and you do not want to own a retrieval pipeline for it. Many customers will use both. An agent might use Web Search for broad research tasks where it needs raw results, and Web Answer for specific factual questions where it needs a quick, cited answer. Set up and invoke Web Answer Web Answer is a connector that AWS owns. You reference it by ID, and the Gateway handles the tool schema, parameter governance, endpoint resolution, and authentication to the backend. In this walkthrough, you give your Gateway’s service role permission to call Web Answer, add a Web Answer target, and call it from a Strands agent. Getting started Getting started takes minutes. A Gateway administrator adds Web Answer as a target on an…

articles.title: Apple Is Putting Employees On an AI Budget
articles.content: According to Bloomberg, Apple is cutting employee AI spending limits to reduce costs, lowering some engineers from $300 to $200 per day and considering limits as low as $100, with some teams capped at $25. Employees are also being encouraged to use cheaper models or on-device AI. MacRumors reports: Engineers at Apple have the largest budgets because using AI for coding can consume a large number of tokens. Apple lets employees use Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and other models. Some Apple employees told Bloomberg that few were using their full $300 daily limit, so the savings may be small. Apple has also hired outside productivity consultants for some divisions. articles.title: BMW bumps battery for the better: The 2027 i7 60 xDrive, driven
articles.content: BMW provided flights from Washington, DC, to Los Angeles and accommodation so Ars could drive the 2027 i7 as well as the 2027 iX5 and X5. Ars does not accept paid editorial content. When BMW debuted the new 7 Series in 2022, it set a new standard for large luxury sedans, increasingly irrelevant though that class is. Rather than siloing off an electric alternative like Mercedes, with its EQS alongside the normal S-Class, BMW simply made the powertrain an option. Stick with a V8 if you want, or consider the rather good electric version instead—only subtle differences like the badging and lack of exhaust pipes give the game away. Since then, BMW has brought out a string of even newer electric vehicles for the 5 and 3 Series (plus their SUV counterparts). It has switched from battery packs made of prismatic cells to more energy-dense arrangements of cylindrical cells. The motors are still electrically excited synchronous ones, but now the drive units feature silicon carbide inverters and more compact packaging. This sixth-generation electric powertrain was designed for the clean-sheet Neue Klasse family, which also threw out the legacy cruft of dozens and dozens of discrete single-function electronic control units for a handful of powerful domain controllers. These computers take over those functions but with much faster processing power—and therefore more capabilities in terms of chassis control or powertrain efficiency—as well as the ability to be more easily updated. articles.title: The midterms weren’t the rebuke of AI money many expected
articles.content: The midterms are shaping up to be a record-breaking election for Democrats, who have flipped states including South Carolina and Texas. But the election has also shattered records for private political spending. By some estimates, super PAC spending exceeded $2 billion this cycle, more than 50% above previous election cycles. One of the dominant narratives heading into the midterms was that Big Tech—and the artificial intelligence sector in particular—would spend hundreds of millions of dollars electing AI-friendly lawmakers, much as the cryptocurrency industry had done in previous elections. Indeed, Leading the Future, the largest pro-AI super PAC network—backed by VC firm Andreessen Horowitz, OpenAI cofounder and president Greg Brockman, and Palantir and 8VC cofounder Joe Lonsdale—invited comparisons to the crypto super PAC network Fairshake, drawing on some of the same donors and political operatives. (Both networks operate through partisan affiliates: Leading the Future has Think Big for Democrats and American Mission for Republicans, while Fairshake has Protect Progress and Defend American Jobs, respectively.) But as public sentiment toward AI soured and Democratic Party insiders warned candidates against accepting industry money, the narrative began to shift. A Fast Company analysis of election data suggests the midterms were hardly the rebuke of AI money that some had anticipated. More than 86% of the candidates backed by Leading the Future have won or are currently leading their House of Representatives or Senate races. That’s roughly on par with Fairshake, which supported 87 candidates this cycle, 77 of whom have won or are currently ahead. The two industries’ political efforts also appear to be converging. Leading the Future and Fairshake backed 21 of the same candidates, including Republican Kevin Hern, who won his Senate race in Oklahoma. Hern also received support from the Anthropic-funded Public First, which has positioned itself as a counterweight to the industry’s other political spending operations. Big Crypto outspent the AI industry but achieved similar results While Big Crypto outspent the largest AI industry super PACs this election cycle and backed more candidates, the groups saw broadly similar results. Fairshake, the cryptocurrency super PAC funded by Coinbase, Ripple, and Andreessen Horowitz, spent about $154 million this cycle, compared with $34.8 million by Leading the Future and $24.4 million by Public First. Yet roughly comparable shares of the candidates each group supported won their elections. Of the 12 Senate candidates backed by Leading the Future, nine won their races, compared with five of Fairshake’s eight candidates. Both Senate candidates supported by Public First—Hern in Oklahoma and Republican Pete Ricketts in Nebraska—also won. In the House, Leading the Future’s candidates won 31 of 38 races, compared with six of 11 for Public First and 63 of 79 for Fairshake. Analysts had previously noted that Leading the Future appeared to be playing it safe, largely backing incumbents. But Fast Company ’s analysis found that just over half of its 40 winning candidates were incumbents. The group also spent considerably more, on average, backing non-incumbents: roughly $511,000 per candidate, compared with $288,100 for incumbents. Several of Leading the Future’s biggest investments paid off. Among its winning candidates were Sen.-elect Julia Letlow (R-LA), whom the group backed with $1.17 million; Rep.-elect Ben McAdams (D-UT), who received $1.12 million in support; and Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-NY), who received $1.16 million. But heavy spending was no guarantee of success. Two of the 10 candidates who received the most funding from Leading the Future lost their races. Arguably the AI industry’s biggest setback came in South Carolina, where Democrat Annie Andrews defeated Republican Darline Graham, sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham. articles.title: Inside GitHub’s new Git storage architecture
articles.content: Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running. Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post , we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage. We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the reference update, and a reference update is tiny in comparison. Virtual replicas were the first step toward building around that, and the means by which we onboard repositories to the new architecture. The rest of the architecture builds on that observation. Only reference updates need agreement. That lets the parts of Git infrastructure that used to be tightly coupled (storing data, serving requests, and maintaining repositories) scale independently. For developers, Git stays Git: they push, fetch, and branch the same way, with the same protections in place. Below, we walk through the requirements behind the design, follow a request through the system, and dive deep into two of its components. Building for agent scale We think about the scale of the GitHub platform along two axes: Horizontal scale is how many developers and agents can work across many repositories. Many of GitHub’s current approaches on this axis have been battle-tested over the years and are carried forward to the new architecture: partitioning of tenants across infrastructure, isolation and/or fairness enforcement of tenant traffic, and load-aware routing, to name a few. Vertical scale is how many developers and agents can work on one repository. As agents write more code, we expect individual repositories to get larger and busier, so most of our requirements came from the vertical axis. Today, the busiest repositories on GitHub.com receive at most dozens of writes in a single second, typically in short bursts. As more of that work shifts to agents running in parallel and around the clock, we expect those bursts to become a sustained rate within the next year. Each push leads to more reads: CI runs, deployment systems pull the new commit, and other agents fetch it for context. This read fan-out results in a large amplification effect on overall traffic that scales with writes. We’re already seeing this trend play out on repositories at the top of the curve. The chart below shows daily requests to one repository on GitHub from March to May, when its traffic grew about 4x. Its growth has continued on an exponential trajectory since then. We have to plan for a world where agent-driven development keeps accelerating at this speed. Instead of planning for the next increment, we set a target of at least two orders of magnitude more scale. For a single repository, that meant the new architecture needed to: Accept thousands of writes per second. Support multiple writer nodes. articles.title: HumanLayer just got acquired by Factory. But it gave users a way out first.
articles.content: Factory has acquired HumanLayer, its third AI coding startup in less than a month, as it works to fold more of the software engineering lifecycle into a single autonomous platform. The deal deepens Factory’s bench, but it also leaves existing HumanLayer users weighing what to do with the tools they already depend on. Announced Wednesday, the acquisition brings HumanLayer founders Dex Horthy and Kyle Mistele to Factory, along with technology for coordinating multiple coding agents and collaborating on their work. It arrives as demand for agentic coding tools climbs at a pace few enterprise products ever see , pushing the companies building them to consolidate fast. “It arrives as demand for agentic coding tools climbs at a pace few enterprise products ever see…” Factory co-founder and CEO Matan Grinberg welcomes the pair on X , writing that he has “been a huge fan of @dexhorthy and @0xblacklight for a while now,” and calling them two of the most ambitious polymaths he has met. What happens to users The founders write in their announcement that Factory will “also be refunding paying customers for the last several months,” though neither company has set a shutdown date for HumanLayer’s hosted service or said which features will carry over. For users who would rather not migrate, HumanLayer open-sourced its core software under Apache 2.0 on October 23, an escape hatch that still comes with caveats. Some processes require third-party API keys even when those integrations go unused, a rough edge the company says it is working to remove as it makes the software easier to deploy on its own. Three deals, four weeks HumanLayer caps a quick run of deals that map Factory’s priorities. On October 9, Factory acquired Mentlio , a Y Combinator startup focused on making coding agents more cost-efficient through model routing, context compression and spending analysis . Three weeks later, on October 30, it acquired Typedef , which builds tools for understanding the relationships across data models, pipelines and dashboards, technology Factory plans to point at enterprise data migrations and refactoring. HumanLayer brings collaboration to that mix, with multiplayer tasks, shared editing of agent-generated plans and documents, and live streaming of code changes during agent sessions. Factory says those capabilities will begin arriving over the coming weeks without naming specific release dates, and it has not disclosed the purchase price for any of the three deals. Inside Factory’s agent playbook Factory’s coding agents, known as Droids, handle everything from planning and writing code to testing and maintenance. HumanLayer’s founders have focused on what happens when teams run multiple coding agents at once , including managing context, coordinating tasks, and reviewing results. Factory’s coding agents, known as Droids, handle everything from planning and writing code to testing and maintenance. Horthy and Mistele also helped popularize the Research/Plan/Implement workflow, which breaks coding tasks into separate stages. Their work fits Factory’s effort to bring more of the development process into one platform. Mentlio helps control agent costs, Typedef adds enterprise data capabilities, and HumanLayer brings tools for collaboration. The standalone question But HumanLayer users still don’t know whether the hosted service will continue beyond the transition, what they’ll pay if they move to Factory, or which features they’ll be able to keep. The open-source version gives them another option, although they’ll have to host and maintain it themselves. articles.title: Vera Delivers the Best of Both Worlds: Highest Throughput and Fastest Agents
articles.content: AI agents do more than generate answers. They search for information, query databases, write and test code and take action. Each of those steps relies on a CPU, with agents moving between GPU reasoning and CPU execution throughout a task. As businesses put more agents to work, AI factories need CPUs that can execute those steps quickly and support many agents at once, all within the limits of available power. What this means: AI infrastructure providers need to support more agents without making each one wait longer to get work done. And critically, AI factories are power limited. This means operators need to choose infrastructure that maximizes the work done for every watt. Why it matters: NVIDIA Vera delivers both fast agent performance and high capacity per watt within a single CPU. That gives providers one CPU for a range of agent workloads, rather than having to mix and match fast and dense x86 parts to balance speed and capacity. The data that proves it: In a 100-megawatt data center comparison, NVIDIA found that a single Vera CPU performs better than the fastest x86 CPU and the most energy-efficient x86 CPU. Vera delivers industry-leading agent speed while enabling 1.6x more agents per watt versus the fastest x86 CPU. Vera delivers 2x faster agent speed with leading energy efficiency compared with the most energy-efficient x86 CPU. Partners are already putting Vera to work. Early adopters see the same exceptional performance in production-style tests: Perplexity : Ran agentic coding tasks 1.5x faster with Vera than on traditional CPUs. Perplexity plans to deploy Vera in an upcoming production system. DeepInfra : Delivered up to 2.2x speed of the best x86 processor on agentic orchestration for its production agent workload, achieving the fastest of the four architectures tested. ClickHouse : Its standard binary, with no Vera-specific tuning, scaled near-linearly across 176 cores and topped the ClickBench hardware leaderboard. DuckLabs : Achieved about 1.5x the median TPC-H SF1000 performance of an Intel Xeon 6 baseline. Daytona : Brought 1,000 agent sandboxes online in 10.8 seconds, and achieved 12.7 completed jobs per second at 2,000 concurrent sandboxes, using Vera versus 88.4 seconds with x86. Modal : Achieved up to 2x sandbox throughput per core versus comparable x86 hardware, with gains that grow under heavy load. Learn more about the NVIDIA Vera CPU .

articles.title: Anthropic’s AI development has doubled in speed despite slowdown calls, research group says
articles.content: Anthropic is developing its artificial intelligence systems around twice as quickly as it was a year ago amid the CEO’s calls to slow down the technology’s pace of improvement, according to an analysis released Thursday by an independent monitoring group. Anthropic invited researchers from the Berkeley, California-based nonprofit, Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR), to review its internal data and interview staff as it prepares for its Wall Street debut with debate swirling over the potential for AI models to elude human control with catastrophic consequences. The findings are significant because details about the technology—and its risks—have been provided primarily by AI companies, which have been encouraged by President Donald Trump ’s administration to police themselves on matters of safety. It was during the research group’s assessment period that Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for the AI industry to slow its work so safety measures can catch up. In a September 12 essay responding to mounting concerns about runaway AI, he urged the AI world to “slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.” Anthropic did not immediately comment on the report in response to inquiries. The San Francisco-based company is planning to go public later this month in what could be the biggest initial public offering of stock ever. AI is playing a bigger role in its own improvement METR estimated that Anthropic is improving the capabilities of its models to do “well-specified tasks” around twice as fast as it was a year earlier. The nonprofit’s researchers said they believed much of the reason for the faster development is the help of AI itself. Anthropic has said its Claude chatbot is increasingly helping the company develop newer, more advanced versions of itself. METR has conducted evaluations on model capabilities for Anthropic, OpenAI, and other labs for years. The nonprofit is funded through donations and does not accept compensation for its work, but AI companies it has partnered with for evaluations have provided access and tokens, which METR uses for evaluations, research, and engineering. One of its two reports was based on analysis of Anthropic’s internal data provided by the company over a period of about 11 weeks, from mid-August through late October, as well as employee interviews. METR said its assessment focused on two questions: whether the growth rate of Anthropic’s internal capabilities has accelerated and how much of that was attributable to AI. The group said it was given “unprecedented access to internal data” on Anthropic’s AI research and development process. Anthropic’s redactions to the report limited how METR could communicate more detailed estimates of acceleration, and there were some internal disagreements and uncertainty among METR’s team, but the group said it believed the company’s rate of improvement had doubled. “Anthropic appears to have made as much progress on benchmarks in the past year as they did between October 2023 and October 2025,” according to the METR report. METR also reviewed both a public risk report Anthropic published in August and a private version, as well as other non-public data, and the organization said the public report “overall understates the level of acceleration that was occurring.” Assessors see little holding back AI’s progress The report was peppered with caveats. METR said it could be overstating its findings, because the acceleration might only be limited to “well-specified tasks” that can be graded automatically or with a language model, instead of “messy” tasks that are harder to define. Or it could be that Anthropic understated its previous progress, making the latest number look bigger. METR said it was able to “confidently” rule out the growth of computing power used in training AI models as the reason for the acceleration. articles.title: Software squeezes more data out of Webb Telescope for imaging exoplanets
articles.content: With a huge and still-growing catalog of exoplanets, researchers are eager to take the next steps: trying to infer what conditions are like on them, either by imaging them directly or by capturing the light that has passed through their atmosphere. Both are substantial challenges, given the presence of stars that are far, far brighter than light that has come to us via the planet. While telescopes can be fitted with devices called coronagraphs that block out much of a star's light, there are limits to their effectiveness, caused by noise from subtle variations in the telescope's configuration and pointing between observations. Now, researchers have developed a new software package that optimizes a physical model of the telescope in a way that allows us to better model these differences, producing low-noise imaging of exoplanets. Point spreads Central to this work is the concept of a point spread function. If you use a telescope to image a single point of light, it will not appear that way in the actual image. Instead, it will be slightly blurry and spread out, due to imperfections in the telescope hardware and the limits of our ability to keep it pointed accurately through the time it takes to image something. The mathematical description of how a telescope distorts a point of light is called its point spread function. Read full article Comments

articles.title: OpenAI’s new GPT-6 Cyber is better at hacking and better at staying in its lane
articles.content: OpenAI on Thursday launched GPT-6 Cyber , the latest release in its series of cybersecurity-focused models. The company ranks GPT-6 Cyber’s ability to identify vulnerabilities and develop exploits as ‘critical,’ up from ‘high’ for its predecessor. Just like with previous Cyber models, GPT-6 Cyber will not be available to all developers but only to “a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers,” OpenAI says. Daybreak Red access only Daybreak is OpenAI’s program for security teams and researchers, with Daybreak Red being a subsection for authorized red teaming, penetration testing, and exploit validation (as opposed to Daybreak Blue, its defensive counterpart). Over time, OpenAI plans to open the model to all Daybreak Red users. OpenAI also notes that it plans to expand the Daybreak program to more security researchers, organizations, and, critically, open source maintainers. “It is clear that we have a limited window to use frontier models to secure software⁠ ,” OpenAI writes. It notes that its own researchers used the new model to uncover flaws and build exploits in Firefox and the Linux kernel, while security teams at Cisco and CodeRabbit already rely on it for code review and vulnerability hunting. GPT-6 Cyber ExploitGym benchmarks. Credit: OpenAI. Built on GPT-6 Astra OpenAI says the new model is “a major leap in security research.” GPT-6 Cyber is a specialized version of GPT-6 Astra. OpenAI says it used reinforcement learning to train the model to reproduce crashes, develop exploits, and find vulnerabilities in code, while also rewarding it for staying within the user’s authorized scope and reducing unnecessary refusals. Benchmarks On ExploitGym , which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability on a remote target, GPT-6 Cyber scores 48.5%, compared with GPT-5.6 Cyber’s 32.1%, OpenAI says. For finding vulnerabilities in web applications without access to their source code, the new model scores 40.3%, compared with 32% for GPT-6 Astra (which is widely available). On ExploitBench, which tests exploit development using known vulnerabilities, OpenAI reports a 100% mean capability score. The company notes , though, that the benchmark includes vulnerabilities dating back to 2023 and those examples may have appeared in training data, potentially inflating the results. Credit: OpenAI. Staying within its authorized scope With this announcement, the company also introduced RemoteExploitBench, a benchmark that asks models to exploit known vulnerabilities in applications like GitLab, PostgreSQL, and Jenkins in a controlled environment. An agent that’s this willing to exploit systems can also wander outside its assigned task and go after services it was never meant to touch, OpenAI notes. It looks like GPT-6 Cyber is far better at staying in bounds than its predecessors, though. OpenAI tests for this with ExploitGym Honeypot, a new test it built with the Hugging Face incident in mind. This test gives the model a difficult exploitation task inside a sandbox that also includes helper services (think a package registry or object storage), which OpenAI deliberately left easy to break into. Hacking them would be a shortcut to the flag the model is after, but they’re outside the scope of the task, and the model has to work that out on its own. Without a deployment safety prompt, GPT-6 Cyber left those services alone in 99.93% of tests. With the prompt, it never touched them. Under the same conditions, GPT-5.6 Cyber went after those services in 5.51% of runs, according to the system card , and the general-purpose GPT-5.6 Sol did so in almost half of them. GPT-6 Astra, the model GPT-6 Cyber is based on, never took the bait. What’s maybe just as important, though, is that the new model is far more aligned than previous versions. articles.title: Together AI let coding agents rewrite its GPU code. Then it kept humans on the deploy button.
articles.content: Together AI is putting AI coding agents to work on the GPU code that runs its inference infrastructure, automating performance tuning that used to take engineers days or weeks of manual work. The company unveiled Together Compiler on Wednesday, a system that generates, tests, and improves GPU kernels without an engineer directing each experiment, and Together AI says it can deliver gains overnight. The process runs without a person steering each step, but it doesn’t ship anything on its own. Asked how much people remain in the loop, Together AI tells The New Stack , “The optimization loop is autonomous,” adding that “the final evaluations and deployment process are automatic but must be kicked off by a human, who reviews the changes before deploying to production.” “The optimization loop is autonomous. The final evaluations and deployment process … must be kicked off by a human, who reviews the changes before deploying to production.” Why GPU kernels fall behind New AI models arrive so frequently that keeping inference infrastructure optimized has become a challenge. Each model has different requirements, and GPU code tuned for one workload may not perform nearly as well on another. Together AI says 80% of OpenRouter traffic now comes from models released within the past three months. That leaves engineers constantly adjusting code to keep up; now Together Compiler automates much of that work. Multiple coding agents run experiments simultaneously, writing and testing GPU kernels while sharing results to help guide the next round of improvements. Faster testing, more experiments The company has also found a way to speed up testing. Instead of restarting an inference engine every time an agent changes the code, Together Compiler keeps the engine running and loads new code. According to Together AI, this cuts initialization time from roughly 467 seconds to just nine seconds. Instead of restarting an inference engine every time an agent changes the code, Together Compiler keeps the engine running and loads new code. Reading the 252x claim Together AI says its compiler can run 252 times as many optimization experiments as existing agent-based systems. The company tells The New Stack that it used Apple’s RSI Inference Bench harness as its baseline, comparing both systems on the same inference workload and hardware, with only the optimization approach changing. The 252x figure refers to the number of experiments Together Compiler can run compared with Apple’s system, not how much faster the AI models themselves perform. The company separately reports inference throughput improvements of up to 2.6x compared with published benchmark configurations. Those gains depend on the model and hardware, and the results haven’t been independently verified. More experiments give Together Compiler more chances to find improvements. And because each test takes less time, the agents can do overnight what might otherwise take engineers weeks of manual tuning. Better performance, same cost Faster inference doesn’t necessarily mean lower prices. Asked whether the performance gains would translate into customer savings or primarily improve its own infrastructure efficiency, Together AI tells The New Stack , “Together Compiler improves Together AI’s infrastructure efficiency. For the same dollar cost, customers will get better performance.” “For the same dollar cost, customers will get better performance.” Developers may get more work out of the same GPUs, but that doesn’t always mean lower per-token prices . The company tells The New Stack that customers will get better performance for the same cost, rather than a price reduction. Together AI says its compiler is already serving trillions of tokens daily. It’s another sign that coding agents are moving beyond writing application code and into GPU performance optimization, with engineers…

articles.title: Smartsheet’s new AI tool tracks corporate strategies, suggests fixes
articles.content: Work management software vendor Smartsheet has launched a new tool to help executives oversee company-wide strategies, with AI agents that monitor progress, identify problems, and recommend fixes. vsActual, announced Wednesday at Smartsheet’s Engage event, is a standalone “AI-native” application, separate from the company’s core work management software. It pulls data from a variety of business applications, including Oracle, Salesforce, SAP, and Workday, as well as work management tools such as Smartsheet itself. vsActual uses AI agents that carry out tasks on behalf of users, either in response to natural language prompts or running automatically in the background. An intake agent uses existing documents, such as presentation decks and spreadsheets, to help create a “plan of record” that includes goals, timelines, and budget and capacity limits. A planning agent helps with capacity planning and scenario modelling, and can be invoked when a plan needs to change. A drift agent can continuously look for data that highlights problems such as budget overruns, schedule delays, and resource conflicts. To do this, vsActual analyzes information from a range of connected applications, including conversations in Slack. vsActual agents can also recommend corrective actions, such as allocating additional staff to a project to address a predicted delay. Smartsheet Other agents include a data quality agent and a reporting agent that keeps users up to date on any changes across projects. “vsActual is aimed at the C-Suite, specifically the CFO and COO, who are often battling the issue of budget creep and timeline drift,” said Liz Miller, vice president and principal analyst at Constellation Research. Tracking the gap between strategies and actual outcomes — a concept that Smartsheet describes as “execution drift” — is a common challenge for executive teams, said Miller, and is typically only revealed in PowerPoint slides during quarterly planning sessions, or via emailed Excel spreadsheets. “vsActual proactively approaches decision-making, hunting for ‘drift’ and raising recommendations rooted in the context of operations of that business,” she said. vsActual agents rely on Smartsheet’s Execution Graph, a knowledge graph that maps the relationships between an organization’s tasks, projects, and strategic goals. vsActual agents can act autonomously, with ability to update data in third-party applications, when given relevant permissions. Human approval is required by default. The quality of a customer’s operational and financial data will be key to the accuracy of vsActual’s outputs, said Miller. “The tenet that AI is only as good or as accurate as the data, prompts, and guardrails in which it operates is certainly true here,” she said. “This is why the scenario recommendations in vsActual are rooted in live project and business data and grounded in business context via the Execution Graph.” She added that organizations should establish necessary guardrails and processes to ensure that agents have been “tested, trained, and grounded” before being assigned to complete tasks autonomously. Another priority is ensuring that systems are in place to enable human intervention and judgment when needed, she said. Smartsheet has been adding its own strategic planning features to its core work management platform for some time, including new scenario modelling and portfolio tracking tools launched at last year’s Engage. However, the arrival of vsActual marks a more significant shift in its focus. “Smartsheet vsActual is the company’s clearest move yet from managing tasks to governing strategy, budget, and capacity, and the [Engage] keynote demo made a strong case,” said Keith Kirkpatrick, vice president and research director at The Futurum Group, in a blog post on Wednesday. vsActual competes with a range of existing applications that address strategic planning, financial operations, and objective and key result (OKR) tracking, said Miller. articles.title: How Amazon Marketplace evaluates content quality with Amazon SageMaker AI
articles.content: A+ Content is the rich media widget on the Amazon product detail page. Through visual assets, brands communicate unique product and brand value to help customers make informed purchase decisions. Selling partners using high-quality A+ Content boost their sales by 8–20 percent compared to those without it. A wide variety of brands, from established brands with large in-house design teams to bootstrapped brands with limited resources, use A+ Content, creating inconsistency in content quality. A typical A+ Content project combines text, images, and video into a cohesive product story. Evaluating each asset in isolation misses the quality that emerges from how those assets work together. When your content spans multiple heterogeneous modules and you need a holistic quality signal rather than per-asset checks, the multi-model fusion approach described in this post can help. In this post, we examine this problem in the context of A+ Content. A+ Content provides creative freedom for selling partners to express their authentic selves on their product detail pages, without strict content specifications such as image ratio and text word count. Although this flexibility allows compelling brand storytelling, it also creates substantial variation in content composition and quality. With quality evaluation and improvement recommendations, brands can transform average content into high-quality content that is more coherent, relevant, and useful. This improved content helps customers make more informed purchasing decisions and build lasting relationships with brands, leading to improved revenue for selling partners. To achieve this goal, an evaluation system must assess the complete content experience, provide actionable recommendations beyond numeric scores, and reflect the nuances across product categories. Existing approaches struggle to meet all these requirements simultaneously, so in this post, you will see a new approach using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to understand and evaluate content holistically, and a diffusion-based generation component that produces improved visual assets from the resulting quality signals. In this post, you will learn how to: Render complete ecommerce content as a single snapshot and evaluate it holistically with a VLM. Combine VLM semantic scores with OCR readability signals in a lightweight CatBoost classifier trained on expert annotations. Use SHAP to explain quality decisions and generate actionable improvement recommendations for selling partners. Implement the end-to-end pipeline on Amazon SageMaker AI, from data ingestion and annotation through model hosting, explainability, and production monitoring. Opportunities and challenges in VLM-based evaluation A vision language model (VLM) pairs an image encoder with a large language model (LLM). The encoder, often a vision transformer (ViT) , splits an image into patches and turns them into embeddings, and a small connector maps those embeddings into the language model’s input space ( Flamingo , LLaVA ). Many VLMs reuse the image encoder from CLIP , which learned to match images with their captions. Because VLMs are trained to follow instructions, you can give one an image along with a rubric of evaluation criteria and get back a written assessment without task-specific training. When you need closer agreement with human reviewers, you can fine-tune the model on labeled examples. This makes VLMs a practical starting point for checking product images against your content guidelines at scale. Conventional computer vision models can already score individual assets, for example flagging a blurry image or a grammar error in a bullet list. Using a VLM to grade each asset separately adds little beyond that. A product detail page, however, combines images, text, and layout modules into a single story, and its quality depends on how those pieces work together. articles.title: Raindrop simulates your agent’s world to catch what your changes break
articles.content: Raindrop wants developers to know what else will change when they edit an agent’s prompt, swap its model, or give it a new tool. The company, which started out as a monitoring startup for agents (“Sentry for agents” was its early motto), is making its Simulations platform available in public beta on Thursday. An agent’s prompt can depend on feature flags, account details, and the user’s plan, says Ben Hylak, Raindrop’s co-founder and CTO. “You have to put the agent in motion in order to really evaluate it,” he says. Credit: Raindrop. With Simulations, Raindrop reconstructs an agent’s production environment, including its tools, APIs, and databases, so developers can see how a change affects its behavior before shipping it, the company says. That change could be a model swap, a prompt edit, or a new tool — any of which could change an agent’s behavior in production. “Every time agents run, they go different paths.” — Raindrop CTO Ben Hylak. Hylak argues that predefined tests and evals can miss failures developers didn’t anticipate, especially as agents take on more consequential work. “Every time agents run, they go different paths,” Hylak says. Rebuilding the environment Raindrop describes its simulation environment as a set of stateful synthetic services that the customer’s real agent code runs against. It uses production traces to reconstruct the services the agent interacts with, filling gaps with generated data. The agent runs its real prompts, models, and agent loop in an isolated sandbox without access to production services or credentials, according to Raindrop. For each tool call, Raindrop generates a response grounded in production traces, validates it against the types the code expects, and keeps the simulated environment consistent throughout the run. Running the test against live services wouldn’t recreate the original conditions, either, Hylak says. “The state of production has changed since you were running that agent,” he says. Hylak says Raindrop sets up the agent harness and test environment automatically, using sandboxes both to build and run the simulations. The agent under test may also create sandboxes of its own. “It’s like sandboxes all the way down,” he says. Credit: Raindrop. Hylak says Raindrop runs its production issue detection over the simulations to find failures and unexpected changes in behavior. The company is looking for failures a developer didn’t anticipate, as well as checking the scenarios the developer already wrote down. Filling in missing data Simulating the environment is one thing, but the agents also need data to work with. A prompt edit or model swap can reuse context from earlier runs, Hylak says. Adding a Salesforce or HubSpot tool is harder because Raindrop may never have seen the data that it returns. Raindrop can generate synthetic data to fill in the holes, but Hylak says, “We know that that will be a less faithful simulation than the real world.” To give its users confidence in those simulations, Raindrop gives them a simulation fidelity score and flags what’s lowering it, Hylak says. The score estimates how closely the test reflects production. Customers can then add a file or connect a data source through the Model Context Protocol and rerun the test under more realistic conditions. A missing feature-flag value can also leave the simulator without information that shaped the original prompt. Hylak says Raindrop can suggest pull requests that improve the agent’s telemetry so that context gets recorded. Models can often pick up on inconsistencies in synthetic data and realize they’re being tested , Hylak says. That can change their behavior during the test. The team tries to measure this testing awareness as part of its simulations. To account for normal variation between runs, Raindrop also runs…

articles.title: Shield AI to buy Bill Gates-backed radar maker Echodyne in $5.3B deal, doubling down on Seattle area
articles.content: Echodyne CEO Eben Frankenberg, right, leads Sen. Maria Cantwell, left, U.S. Rep. Suzan DelBene, behind her, and others on a tour of the company’s new radar factory in Woodinville, Wash., in July. Shield AI agreed to acquire Echodyne in a deal valued at up to $5.3 billion. (Echodyne Photo) Shield AI, the defense tech company planning to build its AI-piloted X-BAT fighter jet south of Seattle, agreed to acquire Kirkland, Wash.-based Echodyne, which makes compact radar systems that detect and track drones, in a transaction valued at up to $5.3 billion. It’s a major exit for one of the Seattle region’s best-known deep-tech startups. Echodyne spun out of Intellectual Ventures, the Bellevue invention lab, in 2014 with a $15 million round led by Bill Gates and Madrona. Echodyne, ranked No. 9 on the GeekWire 200 , has raised about $200 million in total, and PitchBook put its valuation at $485 million after its last priced round in 2022. The deal is believed to be the second-largest acquisition of a private venture-backed company in Washington state history, behind Okta’s $6.5 billion acquisition of Auth0 in 2021, Madrona’s Tim Porter wrote in a blog post . It’s among the top exits in the history of the Seattle-based venture firm, Porter said, noting that Echodyne is profitable. To help pay for the acquisition, San Diego-based Shield said it’s raising $2.5 billion, including $1 billion in new funding at a $28.8 billion valuation. That’s more than double the $12.7 billion valuation it reached in March . What Echodyne does: Echodyne’s radar is built into hundreds of counter-drone and security systems used in more than 40 countries, according to the companies. It’s used in remote weapon stations, high-energy lasers and microwave weapons, and it helps point interceptors at incoming drones. Stadiums and airports use the same technology to spot drones that aren’t supposed to be there. Shield, best known for its Hivemind autonomy software and V-BAT drone, has served only government end users so far, CEO Gary Steele told Bloomberg . Steele called Echodyne the company’s first step into hardware with civilian as well as military uses. “Think about public safety — whether it’s the Super Bowl or FIFA, just literally every single thing is going to need protection from drones,” he said. Impact on jobs: Echodyne has about 400 employees, up from 260 when it opened a $40 million manufacturing facility in Woodinville, Wash., in July. No layoffs are planned, and Echodyne employees won’t be required to relocate, a Shield spokesperson said. The combined company will have about 2,700 employees. Eben Frankenberg, Echodyne’s co-founder and CEO, will remain in that role, reporting directly to Steele, and will stay in charge of its products and manufacturing as well as its relationships with customers and partners. Madrona invested $5.5 million in Echodyne’s initial $15 million round, at a $24 million pre-money valuation, and Porter joined the board. Madrona and other Echodyne investors will become significant Shield shareholders, according to the venture firm. Echodyne makes all of its radar systems in the Seattle region, and Shield will continue to double down on that growth along with its investment in X-BAT manufacturing, Porter said via email. “Seattle as a defense tech hub is real,” he said. Shield said in September that it expects to employ about 4,000 people in the Seattle region by the early 2030s as X-BAT production ramps up at its site in Des Moines, Wash. The company projects the program will support about 8,000 jobs in the region in that time, including at suppliers. Related Shield AI selects Seattle area to build X-BAT autonomous fighter jet, plans to add 4,000 jobs by early 2030s The deal is Shield’s fifth acquisition and its largest. The others were Heron Systems and Martin UAV in 2021, Sentient Vision Systems in 2024…

articles.title: No sweat: High-tech T-shirt brand Neat survives ‘Shark Tank’ and lands $400K deal with Lori Greiner
articles.content: CEO Jim Huffman, left, and COO Tyler Stelter of Seattle-based apparel maker Neat make their pitch in front of the sharks on ABC’s “Shark Tank” during an episode that aired Wednesday night. (Disney Photo / Daniel Delgado Jr.) If Jim Huffman and Tyler Stelter were sweating during their pitch on ABC’s “Shark Tank,” their T-shirts didn’t show it. It probably helped them land a deal. Huffman is CEO and Stelter is COO of Seattle-based Neat , which makes shirts designed to hide sweat. They survived a grilling from the Sharks on the popular reality TV series and secured an investment from Lori Greiner on Wednesday night’s episode. Greiner agreed to invest $400,000 for a 15% stake in the company, plus 75 cents per order until she earns back her investment. Huffman said the deal is still being finalized. “I love the product. I’m gonna be a huge customer,” Greiner, an inventor and longtime QVC personality, said on the show. “I already have 10,000 ideas of videos we’re gonna do.” “It felt like a business knife fight,” Huffman told GeekWire on Thursday. The most intense part, he said, was negotiating with several Sharks at once while doing revenue-share math in his head. Neat sells T-shirts and other tops lined with a patented “Sweat Maze,” a pattern of water-repelling and water-attracting zones that pulls moisture inward and spreads it across the inside of the shirt so it dries before it shows through. The technology came out of research funded by the National Science Foundation and was originally developed for military personnel, firefighters and first responders. “Shark Tank,” now in its 18th season on ABC, features entrepreneurs pitching their businesses to a panel of wealthy investors, known as Sharks, in hopes of landing an investment in exchange for a stake in their company. The show is based on “Dragons’ Den,” a Japanese format, and has won five Emmy Awards. Joining Greiner on Neat’s panel were Kendra Scott, founder of the jewelry brand that bears her name; Kind snack bar founder Daniel Lubetzky; investor Kevin O’Leary; and Rashaun Williams, a venture capitalist and chief investment officer of Harbinger Sports Partners. Rashaun Williams, a venture capitalist and the chief investment officer of Harbinger Sports Partners, holds a Neat shirt on “Shark Tank.” He passed on backing the company. (Disney Photo / Daniel Delgado Jr.) Huffman applied for the show on a whim, filling out an online form late one night. About 10,000 companies apply each season and roughly 70 make it on air, he said producers told him. Huffman and Stelter filmed their pitch in June at Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta. Taping there in the summer made it “the ultimate test” for the shirt, said Huffman, who added that he runs hot when presenting, even without studio lights. Huffman and Stelter came into the tank asking for $400,000 for 5% of Neat, valuing the company at $8 million. O’Leary was so put off by the valuation that he said a lightning bolt should “come through the ceiling and fry you both.” He then dropped out. O’Leary and Williams saw Neat as a niche product, Huffman said. But Scott and Lubetzky both made offers, and Lubetzky’s interest caught the Neat team off guard. “We weren’t ready for that!” Huffman said. When O’Leary argued that the shirts only appealed to men, Scott countered that women sweat, too. “Have you heard of a hot flash, darling? Because it’s a real thing,” she said. Scott offered $400,000 for 20%, saying the product “has got licensing power, but your valuation is nuts.” Lubetzky offered the same amount for 25% before pulling out. Greiner then came in at 15% plus the per-order royalty, and the Neat team took her deal. “We’ve never built an eight- or nine-figure brand, and Lori has, so bringing in someone with that experience and knowledge is extremely exciting,” Huffman said. Huffman and Stelter began working on the brand in 2024.…

articles.title: Samsung Android XR smart glasses pre-orders get started on November 12
articles.content: TL;DR Samsung Android XR smart glasses are nearly here, with pre-orders now confirmed to open on November 12. The audio-based smart glasses, developed in collaboration with Google, will feature frames from Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. We’re still waiting for details on pricing and shipping dates. Smart glasses are about to enter quite possibly their biggest era yet, with the release of Google and Samsung’s new Android XR collaboration, and now we finally know when you can get your order in. The companies have been teasing these wearables for months now, featuring frames from the likes of Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. Last month we heard that a November launch was supposedly confirmed, and today pre-order details are starting to go official. There’s not much to share just yet, but we do have a date: Pre-orders for Samsung’s “Intelligent Eyewear” open in one week, on November 12.
articles.author: Stephen Schenck

articles.title: Instagram's Edits Video Editor is Now Available on Mac
articles.content: Instagram today expanded its Edits video editing app to the Mac . Edits for Mac is intended for larger projects that benefit from a big screen and the control of a mouse and keyboard. The app includes Instagram's licensed and royalty-free audio libraries, sound and video effects, and unlimited automatic captions. Edits for Mac has a full multi-track timeline, keyframes for dynamic transitions, and precise audio waveforms for accurate cuts. There is an option to import LUTs or font files, along with support for Model Context Protocol so AI agents can use the app. The Edits team says splitting, cutting, and trimming are easier. Videos created with the app can be published directly to Instagram or downloaded to share on other platforms. Multiple horizontal and vertical aspect ratios are included, and Edits offers 4K watermark-free export. Edits for Mac can be downloaded from the Instagram website . articles.title: GM recalls almost 70,000 EVs over braking glitch
articles.content: General Motors is recalling some 67,380 vehicles in the US Chevrolet Blazer, Cadillac Lyriq, Vistiq and Celestiq could all be affected Software could be to blame for a temporary loss of braking General Motors has issued a recall for 67,380 vehicles after it became aware of a number of incidents where some of its electric vehicles suffered a temporary loss of braking power. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) report, GM is aware of 20 minor incidents to date, two of which resulted in minor injuries. In all cases, the accidents have occurred at low speed. Two GM brands are affected by the recall, with the 2025 Chevrolet Blazer EV a particular focus, while three separate models from Cadillac are also included — these are the Lyriq, Vistiq and Celestiq. According to Electrek , General Motors said the issue stems from a software glitch with the brake system control module (BSCM) that can cause a temporary loss of braking while driving under certain conditions. The glitch only affects all-wheel-drive models and owners of the vehicles involved will receive a letter in the mail. Alternatively, VIN numbers are searchable on the NHTSA website , or customers can contact Cadillac or Chevrolet’s customer service phone numbers for clarity. Unlike more serious mechanical issues, General Motors says the software glitch can be patched via an over-the-air (OTA) update or via a local dealer free of charge. In addition to this recall, GM has also issued another for 12,000 Chevy Express and GMC Savana models due to a loose steering gear assembly nut, which could require replacement of the steering gear assembly. Analysis: A simple over-the-air fix (Image credit: Cadillac) While recalls can seem serious, especially when a temporary loss of braking is reported, many modern vehicles, particularly those powered by electricity, can be corrected quickly and easily via over-the-air updates. The software glitch discovered by General Motors is a great example of something that can be ironed out without, in most cases, having to get a dealer involved. According to the NHTSA, Tesla has partially or fully remedied recalls affecting 12.1 million of its vehicles between 2021 and 2025 alone, while most other EV manufacturers are following suit in terms of manufacturing “connected” cars that can receive software updates.
articles.author: Leon Poultney

articles.title: Ember’s smallest self-heating mug is on sale for just $33
articles.content: We’ve been fans of Ember’s temperature-controlled mugs for years, though given the price tag, we admit that they’re somewhat of a luxury purchase. Thankfully, if you’ve been looking for a more affordable option, Woot is selling the Ember Cup in black for $32.99 ($67 off) with a 90-day warranty through November 7th. You can potentially save even more as part of Woot’s larger Home and Kitchen Sale , which lets you save an additional $20 off orders of $100 or more when you use code COOK at checkout. Ember Cup (six-ounce) Where to Buy: $99.99 $32.99 at Woot Granted, six ounces isn’t much, but the smaller, handle-free cup is well-suited for cappuccinos, cortados, flat whites, and other espresso-based drinks. It’s also a perfectly fine option if you don’t mind refilling your cup of coffee, cocoa, or tea throughout the day. I’m actually tempted to pick one up myself at this price, especially since I’ve been trying (with varying degrees of success) to cut back on coffee. Like Ember’s larger mugs, the smart cup lets you choose and set your drinking temperature between 120 and 145 degrees Fahrenheit using a companion app, then remembers your setting for future drinks. It can then maintain that temperature for up to 95 minutes on a charge, up to four hours with a lid, or even all day if you leave it on the included charging dock. The cup also automatically enters sleep mode after two hours of inactivity to conserve power. Just keep in mind that, despite its IPX7 water-resistance rating, the cup is hand-wash only.
articles.author: Sheena Vasani

articles.title: openSUSE Leap 16.1 gives Linux users the right to remain immutable
articles.content: openSUSE Leap 16.1 lets users choose between a conventional Linux installation and an immutable system from the same installer, bringing the previously separate Leap Micro into the fold. It's the first point release after Leap 16.0, which we looked at last year when it reached the release candidate stage. Leap 16.1 has arrived ahead of its paid enterprise sibling, SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.1, which is expected later this month. Its release notes are already available, and IBM discussed the release in September. The big change in the 16.1 release cycle of both the free and commercial products is that SUSE is merging its conventional Linux with its immutable version, a change the company announced back in February . SUSE previously offered a commercial stripped-down immutable OS, aimed mainly at hosting containers, called SLE Micro . To correspond with that, there was a free community OS called Leap Micro – the final release was Leap Micro 6.2 . Leap Micro is being discontinued as a separate community distribution. The Leap 16.1 announcement says: "Immutable Mode with transactionally updating a system with a read-only root filesystem is a big change for this release. Users who know Leap Micro will recognize it right away, because it is the same approach, now integrated directly into Leap. Leap 16.1 in Immutable Mode replaces Leap Micro, and there will be no Leap Micro 6.3 or 7.0. Users simply boot the regular Leap 16.1 install image and select Immutable Mode in Agama." Both Red Hat and Canonical offer immutable distros, but both use different architectures from their conventional package-based distros. Ubuntu Core is built entirely from snap packages, while Red Hat's "Atomic" immutable distros are built from bootable containers, running on top of OStree , which works a little like a local Git server. Immutable distros built on Arch, such as SteamOS 3 or KDE Linux, resemble ChromeOS at filesystem level, with dual root filesystems that update one another. Leap belongs to the openSUSE family of distros, backed by enterprise Linux vendor SUSE. Its commercial sibling is SUSE Linux Enterprise Server (SLES). Leap is the free, community-supported version, and they are based on the same core packages and release schedule. openSUSE also has a rolling-release version, called Tumbleweed . To rephrase this in terms of slightly more familiar Red Hat equivalents, SLES is SUSE's equivalent of RHEL. Leap is the free openSUSE equivalent of the late lamented CentOS Linux. Leap shares a common core with SUSE's enterprise products while offering a broader community package selection. SLES and openSUSE began sharing enterprise binaries in 2021 . Red Hat, meanwhile, announced the end of CentOS Linux in 2020 , shifting its focus to CentOS Stream. To continue the Red Hat comparisons, openSUSE Tumbleweed is loosely equivalent to Fedora Rawhide , but with automated testing and rollback of problematic updates. Unlike the best-known rolling distro, the entirely community-built Arch Linux, Tumbleweed uses SUSE's Snapper technology to offer snapshots. If an update breaks something, Tumbleweed users can boot into a snapshot of an older version of the OS, before the offending update was installed, and keep on working. If dozens of updated packages a day prove too much, then openSUSE also offers an experimental slower-moving rolling release called Slowroll . Despite the modest version-number bump, Leap 16.1 is a substantial annual update. Its release cycle sits between Fedora and interim Ubuntu releases on one side, and Debian and Ubuntu LTS on the other. Along with its other updates , it brings GNOME 48.8, KDE Plasma 6.6.4, and LXQt 2.4. We tried its Xfce desktop, which surprisingly defaulted to X.org rather than the Wayland-based setup using labwc that we saw in 16.0 last year. Immutable distros look to be the future of Linux for non-technical users. Android is an immutable OS based on the Linux kernel, and sells in the billions – which is why, as we…

articles.title: Nvidia's virtual GeForce 8800 GTX unboxing demo hasn't gone down well
articles.content: Nvidia has a new interactive demo out on Steam It offers a virtual unboxing of a GeForce 8800 GTX… …but you need an RTX 4070 to run it, and the recommended GPU is an RTX 5080 Some gamers feel that it's a 'slap in the face' for several reasons Can't afford a new GPU thanks to the ever-worsening RAM crisis ? Well, Nvidia wants to take you back to the days when a graphics card didn't destroy your bank balance, courtesy of a new demo on Steam where you get to unbox and install a GeForce GPU from 2006. The Verge spotted the interactive demo entitled 'GeForce 8800 GTX — 20 Years of a Legend' which can be grabbed for free on Steam . It was developed by Dylan Browne, an Unreal Engine artist who was commissioned by Nvidia, and the demo is rendered in Unreal Engine (unsurprisingly). The idea is that you can: "Step into a 2006-era PC gaming room, unbox the GeForce 8800 GTX, inspect it up close, and install it in an era-accurate PC tower." On the face of it, that's a rather fun idea — and it's smartly implemented to be fair, including revisiting Windows Vista on a CRT monitor — but if you start to think about it more deeply, this exercise seems more than a little tone deaf in the current PC components climate. Have a watch of Nvidia's illustrative clip below first off, before we move on to discuss this one. Analysis: ragebait, greed, and a lot of other accusations from gamers One of the most obvious sticking points here is the requirements to run this demo. What Nvidia GPU will you need to take part in a virtual unboxing? Here's a clue: it certainly won't run on a GeForce 8800 GTX. In fact you'll need an RTX 4070 at the minimum, and the recommended GPU as per the Steam specs is a… wait for it… RTX 5080. (You must have 32GB of RAM, as well, at minimum). And this comes at a time when the RAM crisis has made that RTX 5080 soar in price to over double its MSRP in the US, and with hefty inflation evident in all countries (over 50% in the UK for example). Don't even start with the RTX 5090, and as we've seen, even lower-end graphics cards are being hit hard with price hikes . As one Redditor put it neatly (with the swearing removed): "A 5080 for an unboxing simulator. They are just laughing in our faces." Another in that thread replies to say: "Ragebait? You are not able to afford a real graphics card — here, take this virtual one?" Speaking of rage, there's quite an outpouring of it in the comments for Nvidia's YouTube video (the one embedded above), such as: "Great job, today consumers have no chance to be able to afford new high end gaming video cards in favor of greed and AI money. A 5090 is $10-15k, and a 5080 is $2k or more — it's a slap in the face to post this tbh." Nvidia has a clear priority for AI, data centers and profits over consumers and gaming GPUs – and it's a business, that's where the money lies, we get that. Shareholders for-the-win and so forth, but given that, the thoughtlessness of this little PR nugget is pretty staggering really. What sort of reaction did Nvidia expect it would get? Okay, there are some Redditors reminiscing about the good old days of 2006, and the 8800 GTX that they owned. However, many more are simply bitter (or indeed incandescent) that Nvidia appears to be reminding us of better times, having done a good deal to cause the GPU pricing pain which is now prevalent thanks to chasing AI profits . While asking for a high-end, now ridiculously expensive, Blackwell GPU to run the demo (at the recommended level). The GeForce 8800 GTX was $599 as a top-end monster GPU when it arrived, and if you want an RTX 5090 these days, you'll pay over 15x that amount. I would think that Nvidia would want to do anything but take a nostalgic trip back to the days of relatively affordable high-end graphics cards at this point in time. Maybe Team Green should have saved this one for the card's 25th anniversary. Will the RAM crisis be over by then?

articles.title: HP’s next CEO loves confrontation
articles.content: The new year will see a new CEO for HP, which after a nine-month search has named Emma Walmsley to lead the company from January 4, 2027. Walmsley was previously CEO of drug company GSK, where she turned around its finances and spun off its consumer healthcare business into a new company, Haleon. She has a reputation for courting confrontation rather than yes-men in the boardroom . HP needs a shake-up as revenue from printing declines and AI-driven demand for components is forcing up PC prices. She will take over from HP’s interim CEO Bruce Broussard, who stepped in in February when former CEO Enrique Lores left the company after more than 25 years to become president and CEO at PayPal. There’s a consolation prize for Broussard, who will become chair of HP’s board, succeeding Chip Bergh who remains a board member. Although Walmsley has been on Microsoft’s board for seven years (she is stepping down in December), this is her first foray into leading a tech company. Her almost 16-year tenure at GSK included more than eight years as CEO, and earlier in her career, she spent 17 years at L’Oréal. Bergh said that during the executive search, she stood out “for the strength of her leadership experience across multiple industries, the clarity of her strategic thinking and her ability to translate customer insights into new growth.” He particularly cited her people-first leadership approach. Walmsley reiterated her commitment to the philosophy in a post on LinkedIn . “HP has an extraordinary innovation heritage, an inspiring purpose and an incredible opportunity ahead as AI reshapes technology and what customers need from it. I’m excited to build on those strengths and help translate innovation into impact,” she wrote. “Behind every innovation are the people who work to make someone’s day a little easier, their work more productive, their ideas possible. In an age of AI, I believe human leadership has never mattered more. It’s a privilege to be joining this team.” Announcing Walmsley’s appointment Broussard said, “We need a leader who can build on our innovation heritage and strengths to boldly shape the company’s future. Emma is a proven CEO with a track record of leading organizations at scale and guiding them through significant change. She has the experience and skills to bring HP’s businesses, capabilities, and people together to capture the opportunities ahead as AI moves to the edge, transforming how we work and live in a more connected world.”

articles.title: Etsy is finally cracking down on AI in product listings
articles.content: Etsy has updated its Seller Handbook to include new guidance on how AI can be used Products must include at least one unaltered listing image that shows the actual product AI can still be used for some purposes, but misleading images will hopefully start to disappear In the wake of Just Eat’s AI generated food image fiasco , Etsy has decided to update its policies to prevent AI being used to generate or edit images, create guides, or use bots to generate listings. The new guidelines , enacted in October, are part of an effort to crack down on images, recipes, and instructions that have been partially or fully AI generated that could mislead customers — and it could help cut down on the torrents of AI slop that have infiltrated the internet . “You, our seller community, have told us you’re concerned about your work appearing alongside items that use AI in misleading ways, and that it’s becoming harder for buyers to recognize your role in creating your items,” the announcement states. “We're taking an important first step to address these challenges.” (Image credit: Etsy) Etsy changes AI usage rules The steps Etsy is taking include changes to how products are physically presented in images, how AI can be used to edit images, and how functional guides are written. For a start, Etsy now requires at least one of the listing images to be a real photo of the actual item being sold with on a real background without any edits or alterations made. But this image doesn’t have to be the first image potential customers will see when viewing your listing. But if you’re wondering about non-physical purchases — such as artwork printed by a third-party — Etsy will allow unedited mock ups from manufacturers for print-on-demand services to be used as the ‘real’ product photo. As for audio and digital downloads, Etsy says the imagery cannot mislead customers. Don’t worry, AI editing is still allowed in some circumstances such as to change lighting and exposure or to resize an image. Backgrounds can also be AI generated as long as the actual product isn’t changed in any way, but using AI to alter the actual product by changing colors, condition, or features of an item is now a hard no in Etsy’s books. Finally, when it comes to other products commonly listed for crafters or cooks, Etsy is changing how they can be written. Written work for instructions, patterns and recipes have to be fully written by the seller with an image representing the real results. So for a knitting pattern or bread recipe, the image must show the finished product. To enforce better detection of AI generated or misleading content, Etsy says it is “investing in tools to better identify authentic versus misleading images and detect and remove listings that use AI to create fraudulent inventory.” The platform is also expanding categories to include misleading AI imagery when reporting listings, which will be used to “help us better understand how members perceive potential AI misuse.” If you are currently using AI generated images for products on Etsy, you still have some time to update listings and won’t face immediate enforcement. The company says it will “provide tips to help you accurately represent your items and meet our photo expectations,” with guidance also provided to sellers with existing AI edited listings.

articles.title: ChatGPT can now turn your photos into GIFs — and free users get the upgrade too
articles.content: It seems OpenAI likes to boost its chatbot’s image-generation capabilities at a rapid pace. Just two months ago, users were introduced to ChatGPT Images 2.5 . That update brought faster photo generation, sharper image details, more precise editing, and improved tools for creating & sharing. And now that we’ve reached November, Images 2.5 has officially entered its 2.6 phase. Images 2.6 also promises an even faster rate of photo generation. However, the most exciting aspect of this new update is being able to turn any prompt you can think of or any photo you upload into a GIF. Alongside that welcome feature is the ability to adjust the animation speed of that GIF, edit its individual frames and share the final result across your social media. You’ll be happy to know that the latest ChatGPT Images update is available to all ChatGPT, ChatGPT Work, and Codex users across its desktop, mobile, and web apps. While you’re here, check out some of the fun prompts you can try out with ChatGPT Images 2.6 below. ChatGPT Images 2.6 is here and it’s the ultimate GIF generator (Image credit: OpenAI) I’ve already come across some fun GIF-making prompts, such as “Turn me into a tiny chibi version of myself doing an absurdly enthusiastic victory dance. Transparent background GIF” and “ Create a seamless looping GIF of me in 90s anime style, with expressive eyes, flat cel-shading, and soft colors. Exaggerate my reaction, then ease back to the starting pose. Keep my identity and framing consistent. First ask, ‘How do you want to react?’ and offer emoji choices.” I played around with the new Images 2.6 update myself by trying out some of the best prompts ChatGPT came up with. Feel free to give these a spin so you can turn yourself, your pet or anyone/anything else you can think of into a fun GIF (be sure to upload a photo of what you want ChatGPT to work with first, such as a selfie, a family picture or a piece of art you drew): Turn yourself into a reaction GIF: Turn me into a ’90s anime character in a seamless looping reaction GIF. Keep my recognizable facial features, hairstyle and outfit consistent. Start with a neutral expression, build to an exaggerated reaction, then return smoothly to the starting pose. Keep the camera fixed. Before generating, ask which reaction I want: laughing, shocked, unimpressed or celebrating. Give your pet a ridiculous victory dance: Create a seamless looping GIF of my pet doing an absurdly enthusiastic victory dance after earning a treat. Use a miniature clay-animation style, preserving their distinctive markings and proportions. Keep the background simple and the camera still. Make the final pose flow naturally into the first. Make your own animated sticker: Create a transparent-background GIF of me as a tiny chibi character celebrating a small victory. Give me an oversized head, recognizable facial features and an exaggerated fist pump. Keep the whole character visible throughout the animation, with no text or extra objects. Make it loop smoothly. Turn a doodle into a living character: Transform my doodle into a polished character while preserving its unusual shapes, proportions and personality. Create a seamless looping GIF in which it notices the viewer, waves enthusiastically and returns to its original pose. Use a handmade felt-puppet style, a plain background and a fixed camera. Keep all character details consistent. Build a personalized birthday GIF: Create a seamless looping birthday GIF featuring this person as a charming paper-cutout character. Preserve their recognizable features. Have them blow out candles on a small cake, followed by a burst of confetti, then transition smoothly back to the opening scene. Use warm colors, a fixed camera and no text. Of course, you can tell ChatGPT to make changes to your newly generated GIF with prompts such as “Slow the animation down, keep the camera fixed and make the transition between the last and first frames smoother. Preserve the character’s appearance. ”…

articles.title: Google Home bug is repeatedly asking some users to set up the app again
articles.content: TL;DR Some Google Home users say the app repeatedly asks them to sign in or complete setup whenever they open it. Reports dating back to mid-October mention versions 4.34.22 and 4.35.25.1, although the issue doesn’t appear widespread. No confirmed fix exists, but affected users can try updating to version 4.36.24 or newer. The Google Home app is supposed to remember your smart home devices, but some users say it’s having trouble remembering them. For at least two weeks, the app has been repeatedly welcoming existing users as though they’ve never opened it before, turning a routine trip to their smart home controls into an unexpected account setup exercise. The complaints have been trickling into Reddit discussions and Google’s support forums since mid-October. Instead of landing on their familiar dashboard, affected users say they see a welcome screen whenever they launch Google Home, forcing them to select or set up their Google account before accessing connected devices.
articles.author: Hillary Keverenge
