articles.title: Groundcover automates Kubernetes sizing. Engineers set the bounds.
articles.content: On Tuesday, groundcover launched Autonomous Infrastructure in beta to continuously adjust CPU and memory requests for Kubernetes (K8s) Deployments based on production data. Built on technology from Wand, the K8s resource optimization platform groundcover acquired in September , the beta uses data already collected from groundcover’s eBPF sensor to inform resource allocation decisions, while giving engineers a direct view into how those decisions could affect infrastructure costs and workload performance. Shahar Azulay , CEO and co-founder of groundcover, tells The New Stack about the balance the company is trying to get right: “The goal isn’t simply to reduce resource requests as much as possible. It’s to find the right balance between efficiency and stability across the entire environment.” That can mean reducing requests for workloads consuming far less than they’ve been allocated, but it can also mean increasing requests when a workload needs additional resources to operate reliably. The objective is not simply a smaller infrastructure footprint. It’s an environment that continuously receives the resources it needs, without paying for capacity it doesn’t. How to get there? Azulay says teams need “a continuous feedback loop that uses real production telemetry to identify when workloads are over- or under-provisioned and safely adjust them.” Does nobody know a good way to right-size K8s workloads? It’s not for lack of trying. There are already a lot of different ways to tackle the burden of right-sizing K8s workloads. For example, scheduled rightsizing applies changes at chosen intervals, so it may not respond between scheduled updates. In-place resizing can change resources on running pods, although some changes require container restarts. Automated tools can also generate and apply recommendations within policies engineers set. When asked why he thinks K8s rightsizing continues to trip people up, Azulay tells The New Stack the challenge lies in striking the right balance between cost efficiency and application stability: “Resource requests are typically set at deployment time, when teams are making their best estimates before a workload has experienced real-world production traffic,” he explains. “The challenge is that workloads are constantly changing, but resource configurations often aren’t.” “The challenge is that workloads are constantly changing, but resource configurations often aren’t.” After initial deployment, teams may simply let sleeping workloads lie, i.e., they don’t revisit original resource requests for reconfiguration. While workloads may keep spinning along just fine, this approach means teams risk unknowingly leaving them over- or under-provisioned—with costly consequences. For organizations running hundreds or thousands of workloads, keeping those configurations accurate becomes an ongoing engineering task. Teams must analyze utilization, identify opportunities, test new settings, and revisit them as traffic and application behavior change. Even with the expertise, they may not have the time to do it continuously. Azulay describes over-provisioning as “the safer choice because nobody wants to risk performance issues or outages.” But that extra peace of mind can come with unnecessary infrastructure costs; in a 2025 study published in Applied Sciences , researchers found that optimizing K8s resource allocation improved a combined performance-and-cost score by approximately 50% compared to the conventional maximum resource allocation approach. Under-provisioning carries different risks. Requests help Kubernetes schedule pods, and CPU requests influence how CPU time is shared under contention; setting them too low can leave workloads short of CPU time. Limits work differently: CPU limits cause throttling, while exceeding a memory limit can trigger an out-of-memory (OOM)…

articles.title: YouTube bug makes the app appear in half dark mode, half light
articles.content: Credit: Joe Maring / Android Authority TL;DR YouTube viewers are reporting an issue with using the app in light mode and dark mode. The issue causes the playback area and comments section to be displayed in dark mode, while the rest of the screen is in light mode. Both Android and iOS users are experiencing the bug. Some YouTube viewers are reporting a display issue with the mobile app. The top half of the screen, where the player and comments section are located, is displayed in dark mode. Meanwhile, the rest of the UI is displayed in light mode. According to the reports ( 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ), the bug happens regardless of whether you have dark mode or light mode enabled. Switching Ambient mode on or off reportedly doesn’t have an effect either. Users have tried restarting the app, restarting their phones, clearing cache, uninstalling and reinstalling the app, and adjusting accessibility settings. Despite taking these measures, the effected users claim that the issue persists.
articles.author: Ryan McNeal

articles.title: Siri AI's Biggest Upgrade Yet + John Ternus's First Apple Earnings Call
articles.content: Apple is finally bringing some of Siri's most ambitious AI capabilities to the iPhone. In this episode of Power On, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman and Vlad Savov break down the major changes coming with iOS 27.3, including Siri's new ability to control apps, carry out complex tasks and coordinate actions across multiple applications. They discuss how these improvements compare with AI agents from OpenAI and Meta, and why Apple still has a long way to go. Plus, Mark and Vlad analyze John Ternus's first earnings call as Apple's CEO, the company's strong iPhone sales, concerns about slowing growth and profit margins, and why more price increases could be coming. They also examine Apple's AI rollout in China and the privacy implications of new always-listening Apple Watch features. Have a question for Mark? Email us at poweron@bloomberg.net or join the Power On Discord Subscribe to the Power On Newsletter at https://www.bloomberg.com/poweron (Source: Bloomberg)

articles.title: The FAA is finally ditching floppy disks
articles.content: The air traffic control tower is seen San Diego International Airport on May 27th in San Diego, California. | Photo by Kevin Carter / Getty Images It's the year 2026 and the Federal Aviation Administration is still running critical pieces of American airspace on 3.5-inch magnetic floppy disks. But those technology artifacts could be headed for the dustbin after Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced an effort to ditch floppy disks in favor of a new digital system. Duffy announced Thursday that the FAA is rolling out the Enterprise - Information Display System (E-IDS) to replace four legacy setups across more than 400 air traffic control facilities. articles.title: AmneziaVPN's latest update rolls out location sorting to streamline server selection alongside several technical improvements — here's what you need to know
articles.content: AmneziaVPN's latest update adds location sorting, favorites, and a browser proxy for desktop At a more technical level, the update brings log separation, server patching, and design tweaks Roadmap hints at seamless location switching and domain-based split tunneling Amnezia VPN version 5.1.0.6 is now available, bringing location sorting to the forefront of its Premium service. For users comparing it against the best VPN options, this update addresses one of the most frequent user requests as the number of available server locations continues to grow. With over 50 Premium locations now active, the previous flat list had become difficult to navigate. The new version introduces filtering options that let users organize countries by geographic region or alphabetically. Navigation features The latest update places a “Filters” button to the right of the search field, offering two organization modes. Users can group countries by world region – with alphabetical ordering within each section – or maintain a single alphabetical list spanning all locations. A search bar enables quick lookup by country name. Users may also mark up to 15 frequently used locations as favorites by tapping a star icon. This feature works across both the main location screen and the Config Files section. However, favorites are stored locally on each device and tied to the subscription key. This means favorite selections made on a phone will not sync to a desktop computer, though the settings persist through app updates and device restarts. Browser proxy for desktop users Amnezia has also introduced a local proxy option for Premium subscribers using Windows, macOS, or Linux. The Xray proxy runs at 127.0.0.1 on port 10808 by default, routing browser traffic through Premium servers without establishing a full system-wide VPN tunnel. The feature requires the CensorTracker browser extension to function. It operates for a single subscription at a time and automatically stops when the main VPN connection activates. This suits users seeking selective browser routing without affecting other applications on their machine. Additional improvements The update also separates app logs from tunnel logs, giving users clearer visibility before sending diagnostic data to support. Connection handling for Self-hosted servers using XHTTP and XMUX protocols has been refined, alongside fixes for mobile operator connectivity. The Switzerland P2P location now supports bidirectional traffic, with Universal Plug and Play (UPnP) protocols enabled there – handy for hosting game servers , for example. Self-hosted users also gain a one-click button for updating server packages, and some interface tweaks lay groundwork for a redesign due in the next release. What comes next Users can check for updates within the app under Settings > About Amnezia VPN. Desktop installations apply the update automatically, while mobile users can download from the App Store or Google Play. Looking ahead, Amnezia has outlined several planned improvements. These include seamless location switching without disconnection, domain-based split tunneling for desktop users, better stability when managing large domain lists, and more transparent Self-hosted server management. As internet restrictions evolve around the world, tools like Amnezia VPN continue iterating to remain effective. This update signals a focus on usability alongside security – a balance that’s particularly important for users relying on these services for daily access to information.

articles.title: Prevent Siri and Search From Accessing Specific iPhone Apps
articles.content: In iOS 27.2, Apple has a new settings menu that lets you choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access, all from one list. Here's what's changed and how to use the new menu. With iOS 27.2, Apple has replaced the old App Access controls with a redesigned Excluded Apps feature that makes it a lot simpler to keep specific apps away from Siri, Search, and suggestions. It's actually a bigger change than it might sound. Previously, excluding an app in iOS meant opening Settings ➝ Apple Intelligence & Siri ➝ Apps and adjusting each app's toggles individually. This included a switch that let Siri "Learn from this App," and several suggestion options that appeared in Search and widgets. What was confusing is that some of these switches controlled on-device personalization, rather than access to an app's contents. Moreover, fully keeping an app's content out of search results also required toggling off a separate "Show Content in Search" switch that was buried in each app menu in Settings ➝ Apps. Thankfully, in iOS 27.2, Excluded Apps consolidates all of this into a single multi-select list, where you can add an app once and make it unavailable to Siri, Search, and suggestions. Here's where to find it. How to Exclude Apps From Siri and Search Open the Settings app on your iPhone. Tap Siri . Tap Excluded Apps . Tap Add Apps , select the apps you want to exclude, then confirm your selection. Bear in mind that excluding an app can disable some Siri features for it. For example, the Electronic Freedom Foundation found that excluding Messages stops Siri AI from reading or replying to messages. Also, onscreen awareness – where you invoke Siri and ask it for information about what you're currently looking at – will no longer work in any app you exclude. Let an App Back Into Siri and Search To return individual app access to Siri and Search, simply tap the Edit button in the Excluded Apps menu, then tap the minus button next to the app in question and hit the checkmark at the top to confirm. articles.title: A device in the White House is apparently using an unsafe proxy — which attackers could use it 'to reach internal systems'
articles.content: Researchers spot White House network traffic being routed through dozens of residential proxy services Findings suggest a device on government infrastructure may have been enrolled in a proxy network Security experts warn proxy services on sensitive networks could enable abuse, anonymity, and potential lateral movement The IT network at the White House was seen routing traffic for at least 28 residential proxy services, meaning there is a strong chance government infrastructure is being abused by (malicious) third parties, cybersecurity experts are warning. Security researchers at Layer3 Intel published a new report , saying they saw 236 instances of residential proxy traffic originating from AS2650. That is the name of an autonomous system registered to the Executive Office of the President, the federal agency that hosts the White House network. The researchers observed the traffic between October 5 and November 3 2026, and said that in 26 of the 30 days of observation, six IP addresses kept appearing. Dozens of proxies “This is public access,” the researchers said. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it.” Residential proxy is a service with a self-explanatory name: paying customers can route their internet traffic through devices connected to residential internet connections (households, essentially), making it appear as though their requests originate from those connections rather than their own. They are not malicious per se, and have legitimate uses, but they’ve become popular among cybercriminals looking to hide their identities, evade security controls, and distribute malicious traffic. Now, according to Layer 3 intel, 28 different residential proxy providers were able to route traffic through the White House network. The researchers cross-checked the IP addresses against public databases maintained by residential proxy detection companies Spur and Synthient, and both identified them as proxy exits. Apparently, the researchers did not set out to analyze the White House’s network. Instead, they said they were testing a newly launched platform that “gives researchers a global view of residential proxy and anonymized internet activity,” and stumbled upon the activity while requesting rotating access through residential proxy services. The cybersecurity community did not seem all too surprised with the news. In a Reddit discussion , IT experts shared their experience with senior leadership, both in public and private sector organizations, saying many were happily sacrificing security for convenience, opting not to install 2FA, or leaving their devices and email inboxes wide open. One reader suspected someone in the White House “probably installed a sketchy free app on their phone, and now strangers are browsing the internet through the building's connection.” The timing of the activity is also worth a mention. Around half of the observed connections happened between 5pm and midnight, Eastern time, with almost no activity recorded during the early morning. Layer3 Intel surmised that a device was regularly connecting to the White House network during evening hours, potentially one compromised by a residential proxy SDK. Reaching internal systems “That pattern suggests a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device is infected with a proxy SDK,” the researchers explained. The researchers also pointed out that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow internal network access and lateral movement. “This is how past botnets have spread,” they said. “If an SDK on this network has the same kind of flaw, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems.” There are plenty of other unanswered questions, too. articles.title: Agents aren’t humans (but they kinda are)
articles.content: AI Agents now act on the web for millions of people. To a Site, an Agent can take many forms. It may be indistinguishable from a human user carrying out a task, or it might look like one visitor carrying many Users. This removes the ability for the Site to recognize, serve, and hold accountable the user or users behind the Agent, and causes the Site to face the costs when something goes wrong. This post argues that in order for Sites to maximize the access they provide to Agents, the ecosystem must develop new mechanisms to preserve the relationship between Sites and Users. Traditionally, in Security and Fraud Prevention, that requires three things: Identity, Reputation, and Accountability, allowing Sites to answer: Is the person acting being truthful about who they are? Is that person trustworthy? And who answers for the action? “Personal AI Agents” (“Agents” for short) are automations that take instructions from a human (“User”) and pursue a goal by controlling a cloud computer or browser. They are usually hosted and maintained by an “Operator” as part of a managed service or consumer offering. Examples include Muse from Meta and dots from OpenAI, and more are launching all the time. Agents can potentially take any action online that their User could, without the limits that hold humans back. They don't tire, they run around the clock, they act in parallel, and they put up with friction no person would. Much of the web, from how Sites plan capacity to how they make money, assumes those limits. Fundamentally, remotely hosted Agents are intermediaries . An intermediary is anything that sits between a User and a Site, so the Site sees it instead of the User. Agents are the newest kind of intermediary, but intermediaries have existed for a long time. Cloud browsers (hosted browsers that software controls on a User's behalf) and Proxies (services that relay a User's traffic, including VPNs) are intermediaries too. What has changed is the trajectory. Agentic traffic is growing rapidly and may eclipse traditional human browsing on the Internet in the near future. This forces a reckoning for anyone operating a Site today. Historically, a Site could simply block intermediary traffic and require Users to disable the intermediary service. That stops working when the majority of traffic is agentic. Once blocking is no longer viable, Site Operators are left with the problem that intermediaries have always created. The Site loses direct information about the User and must decide whether to trust the intermediary without it. This post covers Agents hosted somewhere other than the User's device. Local agents (e.g. OpenClaw) or Agents running in the User's own browser, on their own device, are out of scope of the primary topic addressed by this post (see below, "On open source and local Agents"). This post rests on one principle: The Intermediation Principle : The business relationship between Users and Sites, and each participant’s security responsibilities, must be upheld regardless of intermediation. A Site needs new tools to recognize, serve, and hold accountable a User acting through an Agent just as it could if that User had visited directly. The Agent, and the Operator behind it, must be recognizable and accountable too, because an Agent can do what no User could. Agents are able to scale human access almost without limit, so they create new risks, even for behavior that was previously benign. The intermediary problem Meet Ezra. Ezra works as a personal assistant for people in her city. Her best client is Amy, a local CEO, but she also works for Bob, Charlie, and Debra. She runs their errands: groceries, appointments, paperwork, and flights. Ezra blends into the crowd. The corner grocer used to know Amy. He knew what she bought and set aside what he thought she'd like. Now only Ezra comes in, carrying orders for four people, and the grocer can't tell whose preferences are whose. He doesn't want…

articles.title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
articles.content: Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs. Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities. Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem. Create Editable 3D Assets With Houdini and AI Agents Creating animated 3D content requires connecting modeling, simulation, materials and rendering. Nick Scarcella, a senior technical artist on NVIDIA’s BondLab team, directed AI agents — primarily using Claude — to work with CUDA libraries and Isaac Sim to create animations. The BondLab team uses SideFX Houdini and the NVIDIA ovrtx library to develop materials, lighting and the final rendered appearance. In one experiment, Scarcella guided Astra to recreate an OP-1 portable synthesizer using product images, manuals and technical direction. He exported the model into the OpenUSD framework, tested it in Houdini and Blender, then used Astra and Opus to refine details before adjusting materials and textures for ovrtx rendering. Scarcella also used a publicly shared robot-hand checkpoint in Isaac Sim, directing the motion and developing materials and lighting in Houdini with Claude’s assistance. Working with team member Steven Dvornik, the team created an “Echos” visualization: translucent versions of the hand overlap and merge into a single hand animation, offering a visual interpretation of robot training. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Robot_Hand_Video_Omniverse.mp4 Figure: An artistic visualization of simulated robot-hand motion, developed with AI assistance and Houdini’s materials and lighting tools. These workflows bring agent-assisted creation into existing artist tools, giving teams editable content they can inspect, refine and render across applications. Explore Scarcella’s Houdini MCP tools and agent skill . Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/relay-video-v14-1080p.mp4 Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation. David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes. Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection. Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries. Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Turbine-Lab-RTX-and-What-If-under-10MB-1.mp4 Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator. The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power,…

articles.title: AI failures threaten incident management: Here are 4 ways to avoid them.
articles.content: AI is becoming woven into the fabric of digital operations and incident management. On the one hand, AI can detect, triage, and remediate incidents faster, improve coordination between teams, prevent repeat incidents, and drive process redesign. In some organizations, AI is already moving beyond assisting teams to acting on their behalf, as agents pave the way for autonomous digital operations. On the other hand, greater autonomy also introduces greater risk. Unlike traditional software systems, AI-powered incident management tools and agents fail in ways that traditional ITOps and DevOps teams aren’t used to – less predictable and harder to detect. AI has specific failure modes, including hallucinations, groundedness issues, model drift, guardrail violations, or poor tool selection. When these incidents happen, there is often no big-bang failure to set alarm bells ringing. Instead, errors cascade across services into major issues, especially in multi-agent systems. “When these incidents happen, there is often no big-bang failure to set alarm bells ringing. Instead, errors cascade across services into major issues.” The good news is that organizations can mitigate these risks by focusing on four key areas. 1. Deploy guardrails No two organizations are at the same level of maturity when it comes to AI integration. Some are in the adoption and experimentation phase, while others are building ultra-complex workflows with whole networks of specialized agents . The more autonomy an agent has, the further a single bad decision can travel before anyone notices. As organizations’ AI use matures, they need guardrails in place to enforce policy and limit risk. That includes implementing controls to ensure agents stop, self-report, or hand off to a human when they start to drift from their intended behavior. ITOps and engineering teams can then intervene before small problems become significant ones. These controls must contain risk without creating unnecessary friction for engineering teams. 2. Use AI agents to monitor and respond As organizations deploy larger numbers of agents, monitoring their behavior becomes too complex for humans alone. That creates a need for a new layer of oversight in the form of agents designed to monitor other AI systems. By assessing the signals AI systems generate, monitoring agents can identify abnormal behavior and determine when an issue needs to be escalated to a responder. In agentic systems, this responder may not be a human operator, but another AI agent designed for incident mitigation. Almost 70% of incidents stem from changes, so when AI is making changes at machine speed, organizations need to respond at the same pace. “Almost 70% of incidents stem from changes, so when AI is making changes at machine speed, organizations need to respond at the same pace.” Consider a Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) agent designed to investigate as soon as it detects a system anomaly. By the time an on-call engineer is notified, the SRE agent could be investigating, triaging, and diagnosing. Connecting the agent to code, telemetry, infrastructure, and collaboration tools makes those investigations more accurate. Where an incident is a repeat, the agent could also trigger pre-approved mitigation workflows. That provides a pathway to AI-assisted incident management and, eventually, self-healing agentic systems. 3. Identify metrics To know whether agents are behaving as intended, engineering teams need meaningful ways to measure performance. The relevance of each metric will depend on the AI agent and its associated work. However, in general, important metrics include task success (did the agent accomplish what it was supposed to?), groundedness (whether an agent’s responses are supported by the information given to it, or whether it is hallucinating), latency, tool selection, timeout rates, error rates, retry rates, step efficiency, cost, safety and ethical…

articles.title: 7 ways the midterms may affect the AI boom
articles.content: Welcome to AI Decoded , Fast Company ‘s weekly newsletter that breaks down the most important news in the world of AI. I’m Mark Sullivan, a senior writer at Fast Company , covering emerging tech, AI, and tech policy. Sign up to receive this newsletter every week via email here . And if you have comments on this issue and/or ideas for future ones, drop me a line at sullivan@fastcompany.com , and follow me on X @thesullivan . There were 41 ballot initiatives limiting data centers; all but one are on track to pass Voters in 10 states weighed in Tuesday on 41 local ballot measures related to data centers , Forbes reported. Ohio led with 21 measures, followed by Illinois with seven, Maine with four, and Kansas with three. Six other states—California, Florida, Nevada, New Jersey, North Dakota, and Wisconsin—had one each. Of the measures with reported results, all but one went against data center development, reflecting widespread opposition to the facilities. In Ohio, voters overwhelmingly backed restrictions on data centers, including outright bans in several municipalities. More than 80% of voters in Ashville rejected an agreement involving two proposed data centers, though the vote does not itself halt construction. In Kansas, Emporia approved a ban on high-impact data centers, while Ottawa voted to prohibit facilities consuming more than 25 megawatts of power. Boulder City, Nevada, rejected a proposal to permit data centers in the Eldorado Valley Transfer Area. One notable exception came in Harwood, North Dakota, where voters rejected a measure that would have required additional review of certain industrial developments, including data centers. Democrats say AI hearings and legislation are coming “Two things will change next term,” Representative Ted Lieu of California, vice chair of the House Democratic Caucus, said at a press conference Wednesday. “We will hold public hearings on AI. We will pass legislation, reasonable guardrails, on AI.” Lieu criticized Republicans for failing to regulate the industry while they controlled Congress and said Democrats would also consider restrictions on new data center construction. The odds of strong AI legislation “just shot up,” Shakeel Hashim wrote in Transformer . He argues that Democrats’ commanding congressional majorities would reduce the need for compromise. If the party wins 56 Senate seats—it currently has 54, with two races uncalled—it would need just four Republicans to overcome a filibuster. Hashim believes that support could be easier to secure as Republicans begin distancing themselves from Trump . Hashim predicts that Congress could within months pass legislation tougher than the bipartisan FRONTIER Act (cosponsored by Jay Obernolte, Republican of California, and Lori Trahan, Democrat of Massachusetts), including mandatory testing and approval of the most powerful artificial intelligence models and tighter limits on federal preemption of state laws. Stocks rallied on the blue wave Trump was supposed to be the president Wall Street and the AI industry wanted. Yet markets rallied on news that he had lost control of Congress. Global stocks initially fell as Tuesday’s midterm results trickled in, then rebounded as the scale of the Democratic sweep became clear, The New York Times reports . The S&P 500 closed 1.6% higher on Wednesday. Asian stocks initially tumbled amid fears that Democratic control of Congress would slow the AI buildout. Taiwan Semiconductor fell 1.5%, while SoftBank dropped 3.2%. But those concerns quickly faded. South Korea’s KOSPI reversed course to close up 0.6%, while European and U.S. stocks rallied. As the Times notes, investors have historically welcomed divided government, and the resolution of election uncertainty can matter more to markets than the outcome itself. articles.title: OpenAI releases GPT-6 Cyber, and promises this one stays within 'rules of engagement'
articles.content: OpenAI, on Thursday, released its latest cybersecurity-tuned model, GPT-6 Cyber, which the House of Altman says combines "stronger cybersecurity capabilities with better adherence to researchers’ rules of engagement." The new model, we’re told, is much better at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities, compared to GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 Astra. OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra in early September, and less than a month later, killed off the planned release of GPT-6.1 Astra after the model got better at pursuing tasks but worse at staying within the boundaries of what it had actually been authorized to do. The model maker said the latest cyber model was "trained to stay within authorized scope, respect restrictions and report results accurately." In OpenAI's ExploitGym training evaluation, GPT-6 Cyber scored 48.5 percent. For comparison, GPT-5.6 Cyber scored 32.1 percent on these same benchmark tests. "In a separate evaluation of whether the model respects the boundaries of an assigned task, it avoided exploiting out-of-scope services over 99 percent of the time," Open AI said. Only 0.07 percent of cases went beyond the intended scope of the training exercise. OpenAI declined to provide additional details about what happened in that 0.07 percent of cases and whether they involved any real-life safety or security incidents - like hacking companies or carrying out supply chain attacks as its earlier models have done during training. We do know, however, that OpenAI recently began denying internet access to the frontier models it is training to help prevent its models from doing bad things. The latest cyber model is also really good at finding and exploiting serious security vulnerabilities, OpenAI claimed. Its researchers used GPT-6 Cyber to find 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox, which Mozilla has started fixing . The model also helped researchers develop working exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities , including 588 previously unknown bugs. The Linux findings are being reported with potential patches for maintainer review. OpenAI classified GPT-6 Cyber as “Critical” under its Preparedness Framework . This is its highest-risk tier for cyber capabilities, and means a model can both identify and develop functional zero-day exploits in real-world critical systems, and execute end-to-end cyberattacks. As such, it’s initially only available through the API and Codex to a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers - these are customers who are authorized to use OpenAI’s models for offensive security actions such as proof-of-concept exploit development, exploit-chain validation, penetration testing, and red teaming. Over the coming weeks, OpenAI will expand access to all Daybreak Red customers, and is also making GPT-5.6 Cyber available to this group, as well. The model release comes as OpenAI makes a concerted push to improve the security of its products. Earlier this week, OpenAI raised its bug bounty reward payments , and added new bonuses for independent researchers. This includes quadrupling reward-range midpoints, on average, for medium, high and critical findings, so a critical vulnerability in a core product such as ChatGPT, Codex, or the API Platform will now earn up to $30,000 - or up to or $51,577 after bonuses - compared to the previous $6,500 payout. Exceptional critical findings on those targets remain eligible for up to $100,000, and now up to $172,000 with bonuses.®
articles.author: Jessica Lyons

articles.titleFa: انتشار مدل جدید GPT-6 Cyber از سوی OpenAI با قابلیت‌های امنیتی بهبود یافته
articles.summaryFa: OpenAI روز پنجشنبه از مدل جدید خود، GPT-6 Cyber، رونمایی کرد که به گفته خانه آلتمن، ترکیبی از قابلیت‌های قوی‌تر امنیت سایبری و رعایت بهتر قوانین تعامل پژوهشگران است. این مدل نسبت به نسخه‌های قبلی خود، یعنی GPT-5.6 و GPT-6 Astra، در شناسایی و بهره‌برداری از آسیب‌پذیری‌ها بسیار بهتر عمل می‌کند.
articles.summaryEn: OpenAI has released its latest cybersecurity-focused model, GPT-6 Cyber, which combines enhanced cybersecurity capabilities with improved adherence to researchers' rules of engagement. The new model shows significantly better performance in finding and exploiting vulnerabilities compared to its predecessors, GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 Astra.
insightsFa: GPT-6 Cyber به بهبود امنیت سایبری پرداخته و قوانین تعامل را بهتر رعایت می‌کند.
این مدل با شناسایی 81 آسیب‌پذیری جدید در Firefox و 948 آسیب‌پذیری در هسته لینوکس، قابلیت‌های خود را اثبات کرده است.
OpenAI برای جلوگیری از سوء استفاده‌ها، دسترسی به مدل‌های مرزی خود را محدود کرده است.
میزان رعایت مرزهای وظایف در این مدل بیش از 99 درصد بوده است.
عملکرد بهتر GPT-6 Cyber نسبت به مدل‌های قبلی در تست‌های ارزیابی امنیتی مشاهده شده است.
articles.whyItMattersFa: این خبر از آن جهت مهم است که نشان‌دهنده توجه OpenAI به بهبود امنیت سایبری و رعایت اخلاق در توسعه مدل‌های هوش مصنوعی است که می‌تواند تأثیرات قابل توجهی بر امنیت فناوری‌های دیجیتال داشته باشد.
